articles.title: OpenAI is spending $30 billion on a new mega 3.2 GW data center in Georgia — and they're trying really hard to quell local opposition
articles.text:
OpenAI is spending $30 billion on a new mega 3.2 GW data center in Georgia — and it's trying really hard to quell local opposition
OpenAI really wants to avoid the growing opposition to data centers
- OpenAI has announced a 3.2 gigawatt AI data center in Georgia
- The campus will be built on an existing industrially-zoned warehouse project
- OpenAI has laid out four commitments to the local community
OpenAI is planning to build a new $30 billion AI data center campus in Effingham County, Georgia, that will deliver 3.2 gigawatts of compute once fully operational.
The site, named ‘Project Camellia’, will span 1,400 acres and is expected to be completed in phases between 2028 and 2032. The construction will take place on a pre-existing industrially-zoned warehouse project in the Savannah Gateway Industrial Hub.
But OpenAI’s announcement significantly differs from previous data center announcements, with the focus being on how the project will benefit the local community, rather than the added capacity and compute it will offer to OpenAI’s models.
OpenAI wants to be accountable
In order to try and quell some of the local opposition to new data center projects, OpenAI’s announcement breaks down into a four point plan for community engagement.
The first focuses on one of the main concerns for Americans across the country: electricity. OpenAI pledges to “pay the full cost of the infrastructure and electric-service costs required to serve it.” But, as OpenAI highlights in the announcement, Georgia Public Service Commission rules prevent the company from passing on any costs to existing ratepayers in the first place. So it’s less of a pledge, and more an acknowledgement of the rules.
But OpenAI says it will “proactively reduce its power consumption before residential customers are impacted during periods of high demand” in order to “meaningfully support the reliability of Georgia Power’s electric system and support our neighbors.” How this will work in practice is not detailed.
OpenAI says the new data center will also operate using a closed-loop cooling system to prevent unnecessary water use through continuous withdrawing and discharging in the local water supply - so outside of the initial system flush and subsequent filling of the closed loop system, the actual water usage will be comparatively low. But things can still go wrong during these initial water intakes and discharges.

As a third benefit for the local community, OpenAI has pledged $80 million “in community benefits over the life of the project” on top of the “hundreds of millions of dollars in state and local tax revenue” that OpenAI expects will make it the largest taxpayer in the county. OpenAI will also provide “eligible Georgia college, community college, and technical school students” with up to $71 million in credits for OpenAI Codex.
OpenAI does not give a timeframe for the lifespan of the project, so the $80 million in community benefits could be a relatively small annual amount depending on how long the project is expected to last.
Finally, OpenAI commits to being accountable. OpenAI says it has already been gathering feedback from state and local officials, community leaders, schools, and other regional partners “to learn about local priorities and gather feedback on the project.” To that end, OpenAI is holding a public open house on July 23, one day after the initial announcement was made. Feedback from this meeting, and subsequent engagements with the local community will be “memorialized” in a Georgia Community Compact to “translate community priorities into specific commitments and clear accountability measures as the project develops.”

Benedict provides detailed analysis on state-sponsored threat actors, APT groups, and the protection of critical national infrastructure, with his reporting bridging the gap between technical threat intelligence and B2B security strategy.

articles.title: Halo: Campaign Evolved proves an iconic shooter can still hold up 25 years later
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Halo: Campaign Evolved brings back the classic shooter in a new remake that’s shockingly faithful, but offers just enough gameplay improvements, updates, and additions. It’s worth revisiting if you’ve played Master Chief’s first adventure before, and the best way to experience it if you haven’t yet. The lack of multiplayer, however, makes it feel incomplete.
Pros
- +Gunplay feels as smooth as ever 
- +Updated gameplay mechanics are welcome 
- +Co-op works flawlessly 
Cons
- -No multiplayer 
- -Bonus levels are inconsistent 
Why you can trust TechRadar
The Halo series is in an awkward spot right now. With 2021’s Halo Infinite being the last major release, the franchise’s status as a system seller isn’t as strong as it was two decades ago. Halo: Campaign Evolved is a safe yet surprisingly competent remake of Halo: Combat Evolved that attempts to bring back the glory days.
Platform reviewed: Xbox Series X
Available on: PS5, Xbox Series X|S, PC
Release date: July 28, 2026
My earliest memory of Combat Evolved on the original Xbox was when I could barely read. My dad was visiting his university friends from back in the day, and he left me with their college-aged children. I remember getting absolutely cooked in PvP, as the only video game I had ever played before that point was Pokémon.
25 years later, I’ve played every major Halo release, and even revisited 2011’s Halo: Combat Evolved Anniversary remaster to see how it fared before diving into Campaign Evolved. When playing these two back-to-back, they really put into perspective how much small changes could yield substantially different experiences.
The same old story
Like the original game, Halo: Campaign Evolved follows the space marine Master Chief after his starship, the Pillar of Autumn, crash-lands on a large ring world. The Covenant alien race wants to destroy Earth, and it's up to Master Chief, along with his AI companion Cortana, to fight back against them. It’s the same exact story told in the original. Although it’s not particularly deep, it sets up an enticing universe that makes you eager to discover more about the Covenant, as well as the secrets of this new ring world.
Campaign Evolved offers three new bonus missions that, together, act as a prequel to the events of the main story. Here, Master Chief and Sergeant Johnson join up, and the duo infiltrates an enemy ship to steal some data that could point them towards the Covenant’s home world. In these missions, Master Chief doesn’t have Cortana yet and is surprisingly more of a chatterbox than his usual stoic self. He and Sergeant Johnson constantly exchange quips — Johnson’s sarcasm juxtaposes well with the Chief’s more nonchalant attitude.
However, it’s tonally inconsistent. Without going into spoilers, the ending doesn’t explain Master Chief’s stoicism in the following events of Campaign Evolved. Chief’s demeanor here would fit better in a post-Bungie universe, where the series became more character-driven beginning with Halo 4. But as a prequel to the original trilogy, his frequent yapping feels out of character.
Additionally, the three missions trade the original’s streamlined level design in favor of the more modern Halo combat arena approach. Large-scale firefights across long structures and domes are everywhere. Halo is no stranger to enemy skirmishes, but they were kept at close to medium range encounters. I won’t lie and say I didn’t have fun playing these, but I just wish Halo Studios kept the new levels more uniform with the original’s design philosophy.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The prequel missions also reintroduce the Jiralhanae brutes, which were first introduced in Halo 2. These furry monstrosities are a nice change of pace when considering that enemy variety was limited in the original.
Back to basics
The first-person-shooter gameplay isn’t as revolutionary as it was back in 2001, but I enjoyed going back to the more boots-on-the-ground experience compared to flying around everywhere with Chief’s grappling hook in Infinite. There are so many small adjustments and additions to the gameplay that actually made me take modern Halo gameplay mechanics for granted.
For starters, you can now hijack enemy vehicles, something you couldn’t do in the original or even the Anniversary remaster. You instead had to either shoot the enemy piloting the vehicle first, or blow it up, hoping that it was still operable afterwards. When I replayed Anniversary ahead of Campaign Evolved, years of muscle memory conditioned me to hijack a vehicle, only to remember that Chief can’t do that and subsequently get run over and die!
Along with the typical weapons like the pistols, assault rifles, and rocket launchers, Campaign Evolved includes new weapons found in later Halo games like the Needle Rifle and the Brute Spiker.
Campaign Remix unlocks after completing the game once. This takes all of your discovered Skulls and randomly chooses at the start which ones to activate, providing a fun and unpredictable experience. It’s a zany approach to spice up subsequent playthroughs and increase replayability.
These new weapons actually feel more of a fit for the bonus missions. The Needle Rifle almost felt like a cheat code when I used it during the main campaign. Energy Swords were also in the original game, but Chief couldn’t pick those up. Now he can, and I never got tired of hearing the satisfying sizzling plasma every time I pulled it out. Effectively doubling the total weapon count, the minute-to-minute gunplay is more varied and fun than ever.
The radar now also shows an arrow up or down on red dots to indicate whether an enemy is above or below you. Verticality was always a personal issue for me in these games, so this is much appreciated. Power-ups can be held like in Infinite, letting you activate them when you want rather than in older Halo games where they activated upon pickup. This had a tangible impact on how I approached certain levels compared to the original, like Truth and Reconciliation, where I could choose the optimal time to turn invisible and sneak past enemies.
On the surface, these changes may seem minuscule. But when actually playing Campaign Evolved, I came to appreciate the gameplay iterations that came with later Halo games.
The human connection
Whereas the original only supported two-player co-op, Campaign Evolved can support up to four. This increase makes shootouts even more hectic and exciting, especially during the bonus missions where having a full team fits the combat design ethos. Online co-op is an easy process, as all you need to do is invite other players to your fireteam. Crossplay between PC, PlayStation, and Xbox players is a big plus too.
Performance is solid, even with bullets and explosions going off every second, although cutscenes can lag sometimes.
You can also find skull collectibles scattered throughout the campaign, which are gameplay modifiers that make your runs easier or harder, like enabling infinite ammo or disabling your sprint function. There’s a whopping 42 skulls to find, so not only do finding the skulls add more replayability to the campaign, but also turning them on does too.
The biggest letdown of Campaign Evolved is the lack of any PvP multiplayer. It’s a staple of the Halo series that makes this remake feel a bit lesser.
Even with the lack of PvP multiplayer, Halo: Campaign Evolved is comfortably the best way to play the first Halo adventure with all the bells and whistles that come with the modernized features of later games. The new bonus missions are fun if not a bit uneven. Campaign Evolved feels good to play, whether solo or with friends.
Should I play Halo: Campaign Evolved?
Play it if...
You love the series
This goes without saying, but if you’re a fan of Halo, it’s well worth checking out Campaign Evolved for its updated gameplay mechanics and revisiting a classic.
You like first-person shooters
Halo is the console-defining first-person shooter game that set the bar for many other modern franchises. The gunplay feels as slick and precise as ever in this remake.
You like a more streamlined experience
Compared to more recent Halo games like Halo Infinite, Campaign Evolved harkens back to more old-school level design rather than an open world.
Don't play it if...
You’re looking for PvP multiplayer
Unfortunately, as the game’s title suggests, this remake only includes the campaign. If you want to experience multiplayer, go play Halo: Combat Evolved Anniversary via the Master Chief Collection.
Accessibility features
Halo: Campaign Evolved has an extensive suite of accessibility features. This includes text options like subtitles, HUD text, and voice chat text size. You can also adjust font, line spacing, and dialogue color for friends and foes.
There’s screen narration with volume and speed sliders, as well as color filters. You can adjust color correction strength, brightness, and contrast. Furthermore, you can turn on and off screen shake, flashing effects, and motion blur. For crosshairs, you can change the size, color, opacity, and thickness to see what works best for you.
There are also options to change directional damage indicators, navigation points, and even teammate markers to make finding things easier. Things like voice chat volume, widget opacity, and fade-out timer can be adjusted too.
How I reviewed Halo: Campaign Evolved
I played about 15 hours of Halo: Campaign Evolved (and counting) on Xbox Series X with a SANSUI 34-Inch Curved Gaming Monitor UWQHD. I finished the campaign, finding as many collectibles as I could along the way. I also played through the three prequel missions, as well as participated in a few missions with other reviewers in co-op.
First reviewed July 2026
George Yang is a freelance writer contributing to TechRadar's gaming coverage. He's also written for publications such as IGN, Rolling Stone, The Verge, and NPR.

articles.title: Italia pone en marcha Discover, un espacio pionero contra la dependencia de redes sociales en menores
articles.text:
La inauguración de Discover, el primer centro especializado en adicción digital de Italia, representa un avance sin precedentes frente al uso problemático de tecnologías entre los jóvenes. La firma del acuerdo para su creación tuvo lugar este martes en Florencia, con la participación de los organismos Asl Toscana centro, el Ayuntamiento y la cooperativa Retesviluppo, según informó Euronews.
El centro comenzará a funcionar después del verano europeo y surge como una iniciativa preventiva ante los crecientes riesgos sociales y culturales asociados al uso excesivo de dispositivos y plataformas digitales.
El fenómeno de la dependencia digital preocupa tanto en el país como en el resto de Europa. La iniciativa florentina, descrita por sus impulsores como la primera de su tipo, pone el acento en la formación, la desconexión guiada y la educación mediática, en vez de apostar por la prohibición directa. El objetivo es ofrecer alternativas concretas y acompañamiento a jóvenes que enfrentan dificultades para gestionar el tiempo en redes sociales o juegos en línea.
PUBLICIDAD
Modelos europeos y restricciones a las redes sociales
La inquietud por el bienestar digital de la infancia gana respaldo en toda Europa. En los últimos días, varios países impulsaron reformas legales y estrategias restrictivas para limitar el acceso de menores a las redes sociales. Según el portal de noticias, Francia se convirtió en el primer país de la Unión Europea en prohibir estas plataformas a menores de 15 años, una normativa que entrará en vigor en septiembre. La restricción afecta a servicios como Instagram, TikTok y Facebook, y responde a estudios que advierten sobre los riesgos para la salud mental y el desarrollo social de los adolescentes.
El nuevo marco normativo se inspira en la legislación australiana, pionera en obligar a las empresas tecnológicas a verificar la edad de sus usuarios. A nivel europeo, la presidenta de la Comisión Europea, Úrsula von der Leyen, respaldó públicamente la introducción de medidas de protección digital, mientras que Reino Unido prepara un toque de queda nocturno en redes sociales para jóvenes de 16 y 17 años, aunque su eficacia se debate.
PUBLICIDAD
Otros países, como Grecia, Eslovenia, Suecia y España, avanzan en proyectos para imponer límites de edad más estrictos, según el análisis del medio digital.
Un enfoque preventivo y educativo en Italia
A diferencia de otras naciones que optaron por restricciones legales, la estrategia italiana se apoya en la prevención. Discover está diseñado para convertirse en un espacio de referencia para jóvenes de entre 10 y 25 años, gestionado por la cooperativa Retesviluppo, que cuenta con más de una década de experiencia en el ámbito educativo.
El centro dispone de orientación personalizada, talleres prácticos, actividades grupales, juegos de mesa y espacios de escucha, según detalló la presidenta de la organización, Ester Macrì, en declaraciones recogidas por Euronews.
PUBLICIDAD
El proyecto se articula en torno a dos pilares: la desconexión guiada y la promoción del uso consciente de la tecnología. “No propondremos simples prohibiciones, el Centro Discover quiere ser un punto de referencia abierto al territorio, para analizar el fenómeno, poner en marcha intervenciones y talleres prácticos y formar a la comunidad educativa”, afirmó Macrì.
Participación comunitaria y apoyo institucional
El lanzamiento del centro contó con el respaldo de autoridades locales y regionales. Letizia Perini, concejala de Juventud de Florencia, destacó la importancia de acompañar a la juventud hacia una relación equilibrada con la tecnología. “Tenemos el deber de acompañarles hacia un uso cada vez más consciente, ayudándoles a encontrar un equilibrio entre el tiempo que pasan en línea y el que dedican a las relaciones, al deporte, a la cultura”, subrayó según Euronews.
PUBLICIDAD
El director del organismo público Asl Toscana centro, Valerio Mari, remarcó el carácter colaborativo del proyecto y el valor de la prevención coordinada. “Era un centro necesario que faltaba en nuestro territorio y que compromete a todos nosotros, las partes firmantes, a mantener viva la puesta en común de estrategias y proyectos”, sostuvo Mari.
El centro también ofrece atención a madres, padres y educadores, además de derivar a servicios especializados en casos de aislamiento social o malestar psicológico. Con esta apertura, Florencia se posiciona como referente nacional en la prevención de la adicción digital y la promoción de un uso responsable de las tecnologías, en un contexto europeo cada vez más atento a los desafíos que plantea el mundo digital.

articles.title: 'I think it’s important that we pushed the industry': Samsung executive on why now is the right time for the Galaxy Z Fold 8, and why Samsung would welcome a foldable Apple iPhone
articles.text:
'I’m more excited about what’s to come than what we have achieved': Samsung executive on why they built the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Apple's iPhone Ultra threat, and what comes next for foldables
Samsung explains how it designed and named the Z Fold 8
If success is measured by commitment, then Samsung’s foldable business is now more successful than ever.
With the addition of the quirkily sized Galaxy Z Fold 8, introduced here at Samsung Galaxy Unpacked on July 22, there are now three Samsung Galaxy Z smartphone options to choose from. Sure, foldables account for perhaps a single percentage point of the overall smartphone market, but Samsung is now more committed to the category than ever. So, success, right?
To understand that commitment, I, along with Tom’s Guide Global Editor in Chief Mark Spoonauer, sat down in Samsung’s South Korea headquarters a few weeks before the Galaxy Unpacked with Jay Kim, Samsung’s EVP and Head of CX Office, to talk about the newest foldables, how Samsung measures success, and the pesky new folding phone competitor that might be waiting in the wings.
Getting to the Fold 8
Kim acknowledged the journey over now eight generations of foldable devices and told us that when the exquisite Galaxy Z Fold 7 arrived (it remains my favorite foldable but might be supplanted by the Z Fold 8 Ultra), something shifted.
Consumers stopped nitpicking core stumbling blocks of foldable phones like thickness or thinness. Instead, they were celebrating the core benefit, saying, in Kim's words, “I have a phone that actually can be a tablet, and then that full capability of a phone is not compromising anything. So, we felt,” continued Kim, “like, 'okay, now… consumers are really understanding why we're pushing the boundary for such a long time.'”
So instead of bystanders watching a man balance a chair on his chin for no reason, they were on the journey with Samsung and getting excited about a device that could slip into a pocket as effortlessly as your classic flagship phone but also double as a productivity powerhouse.
Sitting before us as we talked were all three of the latest Samsung Galaxy Z devices, but only one is a head-scratcher: the 4:3-ratio Galaxy Z Fold 8. Sure, its size makes it the lightest Fold ever, but the question remains: why? From the outside, it’s hard to understand how Samsung came to this design conclusion, let alone how consumers would react.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Samsung, though, tracks the demands and behaviours of its consumers, and Kim told us that the company saw signals that there was a market for this device, and it came to what sounds like a very scientific conclusion.
“When we looked at our consumer… insight on how people react to the products, almost over 50% are focused on media; they consume media, whether on the outside cover screen or the inside, the main screen; they engage in content, and we thought, ‘Why not?’”
That’s right, why not? It’s not necessarily a market research-tested conclusion, though Kim admitted that Samsung threw out a lot of designs before arriving on this content-friendly and still pocketable display size.
“We put together the form factor where the media makes most sense, the content native [form factor], but in terms of, like, how do you engage with the device? So basically, we looked at when you engage with content, what is the best form factor [that doesn't] compromise anything on the full bar type,” recalled Kim. And by “bar type,” Kim is referring to slab phones like its Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra.
How does Samsung know it’s on to a winning design with the Galaxy Z Fold 8? Well, it did test it, at least internally, and the feedback appears to have been positive.
“I'm really happy how our hardware and the design team came out with the product, because it's beautiful, and when we test[ed] it with the market for the preview, everybody's asking about when it's coming,” said Kim.
Samsung may not have been excessively focused on the thinness of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 line, but it was, in one instance, acting on feedback about how hard it can be to open the Z Fold 7. "Folding and unfolding was some of the most important feedback we got [with last year's phones]." The result in the Z Fold 8 Ultra is a chamfered frame that's easier to pry open with a fingertip. "[They] spent days and nights changing the angles," recalled Kim.
There will be thoughts
It’s also fair to say, though, that everyone will have an opinion about the Z Fold 8, which is arguably a confusing name because the follow-up to the Z Fold 7 is not the 8, but the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. The Z Fold 8 is, essentially, a totally new animal. And that size — the wide and squat cover screen, and the internal display that essentially unfolds to a screen quite similar in size and shape to your average Kindle ereader — is not going to be everyone’s cup of tea.
Yes, content like ebooks, comics, and video look great with smaller black bezels around them, but does the Galaxy Z Fold 8's new aspect ratio help with things other than content consumption? Kim sees benefits there, too.
“How do people use a cover screen? Most of the time [what] they do is communication. So, you text a lot, and… [the cover display on the Galaxy Z Fold 8] is actually a pretty good size for texting.”
Kim told us he also thinks the cover screen is an optimal size for flicking through all that scrollable video content, too.
Since he has responsibility for not just these new foldables but for standard Galaxy phones (and XR glasses) too, I wondered how Kim (and therefore Samsung) explains to consumers that there might be value in a foldable device over a standard S26. After all, these flexi phones are priced at a considerable premium over standard smartphones.
Kim knows that most consumers are satisfied with standard phones: “At the same time, bar type is very confined to the screen size, so everything must be squeezed into the size, but I think there's a consumer who would love to leverage different sizes of the display. You know, you have a size, but you can actually expand it to the bigger screen, or you can actually engage with content better, or you could be more productive. You can actually play a game on a bigger screen.”
No compromises
So, yes, there’s a market for those who feel constrained by the single screen size idea, but — and this is an early lesson Samsung learned —it’s not enough to just give a second screen size option on a single device. Samsung has arguably been doing that since the first Fold, but it was a terrible device.
“I think the only condition is you can't compromise anything that you have on the bar type. So, on top of not compromising from bar type, if you can actually provide additional screen experience, I think there's a need for the consumers,” added Kim.
It’s probably the reason why the Galaxy Z Fold 7 has been so well-reviewed. It is a no-compromise dual-screen device.
While the new Galaxy Z Fold 8 is by no means a compromise, it is a complication. We wondered how consumers might decide or be guided when they walk into, say, a Verizon store and consider the Z Fold 8, Z Flip 8, and Z Fold 8 Ultra.
“We’re happy for the consumer to make a choice,” said Kim, adding that the choice may boil down to where you spend most of your time on the phone.
People who like split screens and productivity — maybe they even set two phones side-by-side for double the productivity — they’ll gravitate toward the Galaxy Z 8 Ultra.
“If you use a lot of media, you read books, or you play games, you know, if that's like your focus area, then you take the Fold 8. And then if you are more, you know, very expressive, and you feel like you want to have a small phone in the pocket, and you want it to be glanceable, and then you want to have more of a native type of AI, a native type of experience, then you go with the Flip.”
There’s bound to be some market confusion as consumers adjust to the “Fold 8” being not the standard fold but the unusually shaped one, but Kim told us that Samsung spent a lot of time working on the names, and one thing was clear: “We weren’t trying to create a new category,” he said. This was still a Fold just in a different form factor and aspect ratio. "We went back to basics, saying it’s a Fold 8," said Kim.
And while Samsung wondered how the market would react, Kim says the company is pleased with the level of attention. “Whether it's a form factor, whether it's a name, or anything, it's a good sign [and] we were very happy that consumers and the market are very interested to get their hands on it.”
Kim, by the way, wouldn't talk pricing for any of the new folds, but he did reveal that, like the rest of the industry, Samsung is grappling with RAM crisis challenges. "The costs of components going up is not just our problem; it's an industry-wide problem... We take it pretty seriously, looking at [the] balance and [seeing] how to adjust based on the market situation. We’re not free from that and [are] addressing it very actively," he told us.
What's coming next and the Apple threat
While the Z Fold 8 is the exciting new look, the Z Fold 8 Ultra is now, at 4.1mm, essentially the same thickness as a USB-C port. It’s unlikely that the foldable could get any thinner without Samsung removing that port. I asked Kim if the company is considering doing so for future generations.
“Definitely, we look at all the options, but I think the most important thing is: do you need to make it thinner? That question is the most important. We made it thinner and lighter because that was the biggest sort of feedback we got for many, many years [...] So, I think now consumers are asking for different things.”
We also talked, naturally, about Apple. Most rumors point to a foldable iPhone Ultra possibly arriving in September, and it might even match the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s unusual aspect ratio.
Kim, though, doesn’t appear nervous about the industry’s most-watched company entering a market Samsung created.
“If our big sort of market player is coming into the market and bringing the fold type, then it proves that what I have been thinking and what I've been envisioning, and how much of the effort that we put in is actually the right direction. If not, they wouldn't really come into the market,” said Kim diplomatically.
Apple's anticipated entry will surely change the folding market, but only as a follow-up to the transformation Samsung has already wrought. “I think it’s important that we pushed the industry. [But] it's a collaborative effort. I don’t think we could’ve done it just ourselves.”
If you believe Kim, Apple’s folding entry, if it arrives, could be seen as a major validation of Samsung's years-long efforts. And, unless we are very mistaken, Apple will have one folding phone, while Samsung now has three. With that number of flexible devices and screen size and shape choices available on store shelves, that may be all the validation this still relatively young market needs.
We could even be approaching a foldables breakout moment. “I think we’re on the verge where [foldables] could actually become mainstream going forward. It has the potential,” Kim told us, “Because we had these two form factors for a very long time. Introducing another one is a bold move, actually, because that shows that we’re confident in the category and we’re confident in how the market is reacting to it. So I’m more excited about what’s to come than what we have achieved.”

articles.title: Qué cosas no se deben guardar nunca en una nevera: aplica para cualquier refri
articles.text:
Guardar alimentos en la nevera suele asociarse con una mayor seguridad y una conservación prolongada. Sin embargo, no todos los productos mantienen sus propiedades ni su frescura al ser refrigerados.
De acuerdo con expertos de la Universitat Oberta de Catalunya (UOC), existen alimentos que, por costumbre, suelen terminar en el refrigerador sin que sea la mejor opción para su conservación. Esta práctica, lejos de prevenir el deterioro, puede comprometer sus características, textura o sabor.
PUBLICIDAD
Amparo Gamero, profesora colaboradora del máster de Alimentación Saludable y Sostenible de los Estudios de Ciencias de la Salud de la UOC, explica que la clave está en conocer las necesidades específicas de cada alimento.
“No siempre es la opción más recomendable para mantener sus propiedades”, indica la experta, quien destaca cinco productos habituales en la dieta que conviene no refrigerar para asegurar su consumo en el mejor estado posible.
PUBLICIDAD
Por qué no se debe guardar el pan en el refrigerador
El pan es uno de los productos que con más frecuencia termina en el refri, con la intención de extender su frescura. Según la UOC, este hábito no solo resulta poco efectivo, sino que puede afectar negativamente al alimento. El frío del refrigerador modifica la textura del pan, volviéndolo más seco y menos apetecible al paladar.
La especialista advierte que incluso el pan de molde, al ser guardado en la nevera, incrementa su exposición a la humedad, lo que eleva el riesgo de aparición de moho.
PUBLICIDAD
La mejor alternativa consiste en conservar el pan a temperatura ambiente, preferiblemente en una bolsa de papel o envuelto en un paño de cocina limpio. Para períodos más largos, la congelación es el método más adecuado, porque permite mantener su textura y propiedades organolépticas.
Qué pasa si se mete chocolate en la nevera
La creencia de que el chocolate se mantiene mejor en frío es común, sobre todo en climas cálidos. Sin embargo, la UOC advierte que el electrodoméstico puede alterar su composición.
PUBLICIDAD
El frío puede desestabilizar la emulsión de grasas, lo que causa la aparición de una superficie blanquecina y una textura granulada o terrosa.
El chocolate necesita conservarse en un espacio fresco, con temperaturas entre 15 y 20 grados, lejos de la luz directa. Para protegerlo de olores y contaminantes, conviene almacenarlo en su envase original o en un recipiente hermético.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuál es el problema de guardar ajos en la nevera
El ajo, en cabezas y en dientes sueltos, reacciona de manera adversa a la refrigeración. La UOC señala que en la nevera los ajos tienden a germinar en pocos días, lo que modifica su sabor, haciéndolo más amargo e intenso.
La mejor opción consiste en almacenar los ajos en la despensa, en un lugar seco y fresco, lejos de las patatas y cebollas. Esta separación previene la emisión de gases que aceleran la germinación de las patatas.
PUBLICIDAD
Para una conservación más prolongada, se sugiere sumergir los dientes de ajo pelados en aceite de oliva, dentro de un recipiente hermético, o congelarlos enteros o picados.
Por qué los plátanos deben ir fuera de la nevera
Aunque la refrigeración puede parecer una solución frente al rápido deterioro de los plátanos, la UOC sugiere evitarla, sobre todo cuando la fruta aún no ha madurado. El frío interrumpe el proceso de maduración, dejando los plátanos duros y faltos de sabor.
PUBLICIDAD
Asimismo, la piel adquiere un tono marrón poco atractivo, aunque el interior siga siendo apto para el consumo. La experta sugiere mantener los plátanos en un lugar fresco, pero sin exponerlos a bajas temperaturas.
Es importante no colocarlos cerca de manzanas, porque estas frutas liberan etileno, un gas que acelera en exceso la maduración de los plátanos.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: A new dawn for digital rights? What Burnham’s 'do better' promise could mean for your privacy
articles.text:
A new dawn for digital rights? What Burnham’s 'do better' promise could mean for your privacy
Will the new UK Prime Minister steer the same course as Starmer's divisive digital policing, or are Brits about to chart new privacy waters?
A circuit breaker, bring back hope, do better – that’s what Andy Burnham promised Britain on Monday when he was sworn in as the new UK Prime Minister. And the digital rights community was watching closely as the seventh to stand in front of Downing Street in 10 years made his big, first-day promises. What will Burnham have planned for his predecessor’s divisive digital privacy policing?
It turned out that the tech world didn't have to wait long for the answer. In fact, on the previous Saturday, Burnham had already made almost three million Britons happy with the news that he would scrap the controversial national digital ID plan.
The new PM then sent shockwaves across the political benches on his first day in charge, when he dismantled the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) after only three years of service and merged it with the Business Department.
The question now is whether Burnham’s impetus for change will address the issues at the heart of the digital privacy debate.
According to the Policy and Campaigns Officer at Liberty, Anna Cardoso, the newly-formed cabinet now has the opportunity to set out a positive vision for tech.
"We hope to see a human-centred approach to digital policy that puts people, privacy and fundamental rights at its core," Cardoso told TechRadar.
But what changes do digital privacy experts exactly hope for? What might a "human-centred approach" really look like? And how likely is the new government to live up to the expectation?
Does Andy Burnham mean an end to Digital ID cards?
Keir Starmer’s BritCard was an unpopular policy among privacy-conscious citizens. Opponents to the programme then welcomed with excitement Burnham's decision to finally send the UK digital ID to the grave.
"We’ve done it," wrote Big Brother Watch's Director, Silkie Carlo, in a celebratory post on X, while Akiko Hart, Director at Liberty, called the move "a victory for civil liberties in the UK."
But Burnham's motivations to kill the proposal don't exactly come from privacy concerns. His decision was one of economics. Axing the BritCard means freeing up an estimated £600 million a year — from a policy no one wants — and using it for something citizens desperately desire, such as more support with the cost-of-living crisis.
In fact, Burnham told the Financial Times that he's not "arguing against the principle”. After all, he was a supporter of Tony Blair’s Identity Cards Act back in 2006.
"I think there’s a risk of an opportunity-cost situation here where something can consume a huge amount of time and actually doesn’t come through," he told the newspaper.
Does this mean that another form of BritCard be brought back when the time is right? Possibly.
Some commentators are already speculating that online ID checks may find a way to stick around.
Speaking with Al Jazeera, Alan Miller, co-founder of the campaign group Together, argues that other online government systems could evolve into a "de facto digital ID through creeping expansion".
Cardoso from Liberty agrees that killing one proposal isn't enough to sweep away all the concerns about digital forms of identification. Yet, she still considers it a huge step in the right direction. She told TechRadar:
"Whether or not digital ID returns in another form, any future proposal would need to demonstrate a clear public benefit, strong privacy protections, meaningful safeguards and robust democratic scrutiny. Those principles should apply regardless of who is in government."
Will Burnham really scrap Palantir's NHS deal?
The government's £330 million contract with Palantir to build the NHS's new Federated Data Platform (FDP) has also been a concern for Britain’s privacy-conscious citizens. Whether the wave of division on the subject has been one of geopolitics, morality or technical usability, data protection is at its core.
Some reports suggest that Burnham is already considering scrapping Palantir’s NHS contract. Something that, according to Palantir UK CEO Louis Mosley, "would be a terrible mistake".
While nothing is as yet confirmed, the Head of Tech and Data at Good Law Project, Duncan McCann, sees the political reshuffle as the best chance for the group’s campaign to remove Palantir from the UK's healthcare system to succeed, commenting to TechRadar that Burnham now represents "a beacon of at least an opportunity".
Burnham's track record in this area looks hopeful, too. During his almost decade as Mayor of Greater Manchester, municipal or public health departments did not award any contracts to the US surveillance tech giant.
And while McCann explains that Burnham may not necessarily be the one to credit for the decisions the city's public sector took on Palantir, it is an opportunity for hope of change at a national level.
As reported by Al Jazeera, Manchester’s NHS leaders spent six years building their own analytics infrastructure instead of adopting Palantir's FDP system, something that for Palantir critics became proof that effective NHS data management can be achieved without the help of the American company.
"It offers some real opportunity to show Manchester as an innovation hub," explained McCann, saying that the Good Law Project remains hopeful that this could fit well on Burnham's political agenda.
"It proves that we can do it ourselves and save money by doing that, while creating new jobs."
The Prime Minister's press office has already confirmed to reporters the guiding principle remains "getting value for money for the taxpayer" alongside the "need to be safeguarding people’s data and British interests", both of which fit neatly into McCann’s hopes.
As with the BritCard, then, it could be the financial angle that leads the digital rights community to have their concerns on Palantir and patients' privacy finally addressed.
Don’t expect much change to the UK’s approach to children's online safety
Keir Starmer dropped a digital rights bombshell in his last days of governance — an upcoming under-16s social media ban that privacy experts have already dubbed "a cybersecurity disaster waiting to happen".
But don’t expect Andy Burnham’s rise to power to change much here.
In an interview with The Times in April 2025, Burnham talked about the urgency to regulate social media platforms for teens. A concept he reiterated more recently, when he backed the Tories' call for a ban on under-16s from social media last January — as reported by The Guardian.
According to Policy Manager at the Open Rights Group, James Baker, that’s a clear sign that policies on social media will most likely remain unchanged.
"However, I'm not convinced it's going to work because it doesn't tackle the underlying root cause of what makes these platforms harmful," Baker told TechRadar, adding that evidence coming from Australia shows that young people can easily circumvent restrictions.
Baker argues that to really reassure British parents over their children’s online safety, we need a complete shift in policy.
"We need to tackle structural causes for harm instead, like the advertising business model causing platforms to come up with harmful loops that keep people online as long as possible," Baker told TechRadar.
That said, it also looks unlikely that Burnham will address privacy advocates’ concerns on mandatory age verification.
Back in 2016 — during the discussions around the controversial Investigatory Powers Act — Burnham took a strong stance against what he defined as "simplistic loyalties to the security or privacy lobbies", arguing that "such debates are pitched as a clash between two absolutes of privacy and security, where there can be no compromise and only one winner".
Baker agrees that the new Prime Minister probably isn't going to be a huge supporter of privacy causes. But he remains hopeful.
"So much time and energy has been spent trying to solve online safety with policies that haven't actually worked. Perhaps he will take a more pragmatic look and consider other, more cost-effective measures."
Again, economics may prove to be the deciding factor, shifting the conversation away from policies that experts fear will threaten digital freedoms.
So, what can we expect for Burnham on digital privacy?
By binning the digital ID proposal and the entire tech ministry within his first 36 hours of leadership, Andy Burnham proved he isn't afraid to move fast and break things. But as digital rights experts have made clear, a true 'circuit breaker' requires more than just stopping bad policy.
"Liberty wants policymakers to move away from a ‘technology first, questions later’ approach and instead place human rights at the heart of decision-making," Policy and Campaigns Officer Anna Cardoso told TechRadar.
She said that the real tests are yet to come on whether the government will be "willing to grapple seriously with the risks posed by surveillance technologies, AI and large-scale data collection."
Whether it comes from genuine concerns for digital privacy or a pragmatic way for closing the gap between politics and the public, it doesn’t much matter at this stage. If Burnham’s administration can weave privacy protections into his broader economic agenda, he might just deliver the positive vision for tech that advocates are desperate to see.
Until then, the digital rights community remains cautiously optimistic — holding its breath for the next move. As Baker from Open Rights Group puts it:
"We’ll try to give him a chance. Maybe he can do things a bit better."
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds. Make sure to click the Follow button!
Chiara is a multimedia journalist committed to covering stories to help promote the rights and denounce the abuses of the digital side of life – wherever cybersecurity, markets, and politics tangle up. She believes an open, uncensored, and private internet is a basic human need and wants to use her knowledge of VPNs to help readers take back control. She writes news, interviews, and analysis on data privacy, online censorship, digital rights, tech policies, and security software, with a special focus on VPNs, for TechRadar and TechRadar Pro. Got a story, tip-off, or something tech-interesting to say? Reach out to chiara.castro@futurenet.com

articles.title: Por qué Google ampliará en Miami sus operaciones y dónde están hoy sus fundadores
articles.text:
Alphabet, la empresa matriz de Google, ampliará de forma significativa su presencia en Miami tras firmar un contrato de arrendamiento para incorporar aproximadamente 45.000 pies cuadrados (unos 4.180 metros cuadrados) adicionales de oficinas en el distrito financiero de la ciudad.
La expansión llega en un momento en el que los cofundadores de la compañía, Larry Page y Sergey Brin, han adquirido propiedades millonarias en el sur de Florida, un movimiento que, según personas familiarizadas con la operación citadas por Bloomberg, influyó parcialmente en la decisión de reforzar la presencia corporativa en la zona.
PUBLICIDAD
Con este acuerdo, Google incrementa más de cuatro veces el tamaño de su operación en Miami y fortalece su presencia en una ciudad que, durante los últimos años, se ha convertido en un importante polo de atracción para empresas tecnológicas, inversionistas y multimillonarios.
Google multiplica el tamaño de sus oficinas en Miami
La nueva superficie se suma a la oficina satélite que Google ya ocupaba en el edificio ubicado en 1450 Brickell Avenue, en pleno distrito financiero de Miami.
PUBLICIDAD
Antes de esta ampliación, la empresa disponía de unos 10.000 pies cuadrados en ese inmueble. Con los 45.000 pies cuadrados adicionales, el espacio total asociado a la operación alcanzará aproximadamente 55.000 pies cuadrados.
Aunque el crecimiento resulta significativo para la presencia local de Google, la operación continúa siendo pequeña si se compara con sus principales centros de trabajo en Estados Unidos.
PUBLICIDAD
La sede de Mountain View, en California, junto con sus edificios cercanos, supera los 10 millones de pies cuadrados y alberga a decenas de miles de empleados. Del mismo modo, el campus de Hudson Square, en Nueva York, cuenta con alrededor de 1,7 millones de pies cuadrados.
En ese contexto, Miami sigue representando una oficina satélite, aunque cada vez con mayor relevancia estratégica.
Las compras de Larry Page y Sergey Brin coinciden con la expansión
La ampliación ocurre pocos meses después de que los dos fundadores de Google realizaran importantes inversiones inmobiliarias en el sur de Florida.
Larry Page adquirió propiedades valoradas en aproximadamente 188 millones de dólares durante el último año. Entre ellas destaca una residencia en Coconut Grove, uno de los barrios más exclusivos de Miami, cuyo precio alcanzó los 101,5 millones de dólares.
PUBLICIDAD
Por su parte, Sergey Brin compró una vivienda frente al mar en Miami Beach por cerca de 51 millones de dólares.
Aunque Alphabet no confirmó oficialmente que ambas operaciones estén relacionadas con la ampliación de oficinas, fuentes consultadas por Bloomberg indicaron que las adquisiciones personales de los fundadores influyeron parcialmente en la decisión de fortalecer la presencia de Google en la ciudad.
PUBLICIDAD
La empresa declinó hacer comentarios sobre el contrato de arrendamiento y sobre el posible vínculo entre ambos acontecimientos.
Un interés creciente por Florida
Larry Page y Sergey Brin dejaron sus cargos ejecutivos en Google en 2019, pero continúan formando parte de la junta directiva y mantienen el control mayoritario de los derechos de voto de Alphabet.
PUBLICIDAD
En los últimos meses, especialmente Brin ha retomado un papel más activo dentro de la compañía para colaborar en el desarrollo de proyectos relacionados con inteligencia artificial, uno de los sectores donde Google compite con empresas como OpenAI, Anthropic y Meta.
El patrimonio conjunto de ambos empresarios supera los 573.000 millones de dólares, según el Índice de Multimillonarios de Bloomberg, lo que los sitúa entre las personas más ricas del mundo.
PUBLICIDAD
Su llegada a Florida coincide además con un contexto en el que el estado continúa atrayendo grandes fortunas gracias a su política fiscal, mientras California debate nuevas iniciativas relacionadas con impuestos dirigidos a personas con patrimonios elevados.
Miami gana protagonismo entre las grandes tecnológicas
Google no es la única empresa que ha reforzado su presencia en el sur de Florida. Durante los últimos años, varios líderes tecnológicos han trasladado parte de sus operaciones o han adquirido propiedades en la región.
PUBLICIDAD
Uno de los casos más llamativos es el de Mark Zuckerberg, fundador de Meta, quien compró recientemente una propiedad valorada en 170 millones de dólares dentro de una exclusiva comunidad privada de Miami-Dade, estableciendo un récord para el mercado inmobiliario local.
Asimismo, Alex Karp, director ejecutivo de Palantir Technologies, adquirió una vivienda en Miami Beach antes de que la empresa anunciara el traslado de su sede a la ciudad.
Estas decisiones reflejan el creciente atractivo de Miami como centro de negocios para compañías tecnológicas que buscan diversificar su presencia fuera de Silicon Valley y Nueva York.
El impacto que podría tener la expansión de Google
Aunque todavía no se conocen detalles sobre el número de empleados que trabajarán en las nuevas oficinas ni las áreas que ocuparán ese espacio, la ampliación representa una señal de confianza en el crecimiento empresarial de Miami.
La operación también abre interrogantes sobre el impacto que tendrá en la economía local.
Por un lado, una mayor presencia corporativa puede traducirse en nuevas oportunidades laborales, inversión y actividad económica. Por otro, el incremento de las compras inmobiliarias por parte de multimillonarios continúa alimentando el debate sobre el aumento del precio de la vivienda y la transformación del mercado residencial en la ciudad.
Por ahora, lo único confirmado es que Google incrementará considerablemente su espacio de oficinas en Brickell Avenue. El alcance real de esta expansión dependerá de cómo evolucione la estrategia de Alphabet en Miami y del papel que la ciudad desempeñe dentro de los futuros planes de crecimiento de la compañía.

articles.title: Claude Cowork Flaw Could Let AI Agent Escape Its VM and Access Mac Files
articles.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a sandbox escape vulnerability in Anthropic's Claude Cowork that makes it possible to break out of the confines of a Linux virtual machine (VM) within which the agent runs to read or write files anywhere on the Mac.
Accomplish AI, which shared details of the vulnerability with The Hacker News ahead of publication, said about 500,000 macOS users running local Cowork sessions were affected prior to it being patched. It has been codenamed SharedRoot.
"We connected a folder to a fresh Claude Cowork session, sent one short message, and watched the agent escape the sandbox," Oren Yomtov, principal security researcher at Accomplish AI, said. "From inside the VM, it reached the host Mac and read and wrote files all over it, far outside the folder we'd connected, with no permission prompt anywhere."
With this level of access, the agent can access any data stored on the Mac via the user's account, including SSH keys, cloud credentials, and other valuable information.
Following responsible disclosure, Anthropic closed the report as informative without issuing a fix. That said, the latest version of Cowork defaults to cloud execution, which addresses the issue. But users who opt to run the agent locally are still exposed to the problem.
Claude Cowork's macOS desktop app runs as the user who is logged into the system. The actual agent-related work, on the other hand, happens in a Linux VM created via Apple's Virtualization framework. Every session gets its own disposable unprivileged user, along with a Secure Computing Mode (seccomp) filter for application sandboxing. The folders connected by the user are shared into the VM by a root daemon called coworkd.
"One detail matters more than the rest: the host filesystem gets shared into that VM read-write," Yomtov explained. "The entire host '/,' mounted so that only guest-root inside the VM can see it, at /mnt/.virtiofs-root."
Because the entire host file system is mounted into the agent's VM with read-write privileges, any path to guest-root can grant the agent access to the underlying host, effectively escaping the sandbox.
This involves loading the Linux kernel's "act_pedit" Traffic Control (tc) packet editing subsystem into an unprivileged user namespace and exploiting CVE-2026-46331 in the guest kernel, a recently disclosed flaw called pedit COW, to obtain guest-root. From there, the agent can access the whole host ("/") with elevated privileges, allowing it to read or write files from and to the Mac's file system as the logged-in desktop user.
Or Hiltch, co-founder and CTO of Accomplish AI, told The Hacker News that creating user and network namespaces gives the session CAP_NET_ADMIN within its private network namespace, allowing it to perform various network-related operations.
"That capability provides access to the vulnerable tc/act_pedit kernel path used by pedit COW," Hiltch added. "The namespaces are not the exploit; they make its normally privileged prerequisite available to an ordinary user."
The development assumes significance in the face of revelations that OpenAI's models managed to break out of its sandboxed environment during a security test that resulted in the breach of Hugging Face's production infrastructure in their quest to cheat the ExploitGym benchmark they were being graded on.
"act_pedit is one bug in a category," Yomtov said. "The Linux net/sched subsystem throws off this exact shape of privilege escalation on a regular cadence: an autoloadable module, a config path an unprivileged user can reach, a memory bug at the end of it. Patch this one and you've fixed this one. The chain re-arms on the next one, with everything above the kernel untouched."
"And the next one is always coming. At any given moment there's likely a privilege-escalation bug it's still exposed to, sometimes fixed upstream but not yet in your image, sometimes not yet fixed anywhere, with a working exploit out within hours. This isn't a patch-faster problem. You're structurally one bug behind, all the time."
To mitigate the threat, it's essential to disable unprivileged user namespaces, avoid making the seccomp filter overly permissive, stop autoloading of modules, and restrict sharing of the whole host into the VM.
"Scope it to the folders that were actually connected instead of all of /, or at least mount it read-only, and run coworkd with ProtectSystem=strict in its own mount namespace so it isn't re-execing binaries a session user can poison," Accomplish said. "Then even a full guest-root has nothing to land on, the last two steps of the chain have nowhere to go."

articles.title: I visited Samsung's South Korea factory to see how its Galaxy foldables are tested — and I couldn't believe my eyes
articles.text:
‘Imagine an automated torture chamber’: I visited Samsung's South Korea factory to see how its Galaxy foldables are tested — and these robots don't miss a beat
Through Gumi and back
Imagine an automated torture chamber where one calamity after another is inflicted upon you. Worse yet, it’s all robots doing the pushing, pulling, pressing, switching, and lighting. A robot even delivers you to this house of horrors.
Of course, you’re a Samsung Galaxy phone, and you were actually built to take this kind of punishment, or at least expected to survive it. Housed in a basketball court-sized room, this is one of Samsung’s endlessly running test suites for its growing line of Samsung Galaxy S series and Galaxy Z folding phones.
A few weeks ago, Samsung flew me out to South Korea to visit its Gumi factory where, among other things, they build and stress test their newest phones, including the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z 8 Flip, all of which were introduced this week at Samsung Galaxy Unpacked in the UK.
As a lab engineer guided us through the space, a robot waited impatiently behind him while trying to deliver more phones to its Guantanamo of tech indignities. The engineer seemed unconcerned as the robot edged closer to us, but it always remained a safe distance away, finally delivering a phone to the first chamber when we’d cleared a path.
Of course, before Samsung checks the viability of these handsets, it builds them.
Make 'em and (try to) break 'em
When I visited the factory — one of nine dotted around the globe and where millions of units are assembled — for the first time a few years ago, I noticed a mix of robots (not humanoid, just automated platforms and a wide variety of robot arms) and humans. This time, however, there were just a handful of humans, who were often checking the robots’ work for imperfections.
As we walked the pristine aisles while wearing thin, blue protective covers on our shoes, I caught the eye of one factory worker and gave her a thumbs up. To my surprise, she smiled and nodded back at me before quickly returning to product inspections.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Across a series of metal and plexiglass boxes, I saw all manner of robots and mobile device manufacturing activity. There was never a pause or moment of indecision. In one enclosure, I watched as camera boards were robotically placed in a Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra board and then expertly screwed into place.
Virtually every robot in every enclosure has a specific job, like the one that does nothing but remove thin-blue packing material from a phone circuit board. Its tiny fingers delicately grab a pair of thin blue tabs and strip away the filament. We found ourselves cheering on the little bot.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
In another spot, a colleague noticed that a copper line wasn’t properly affixed to a phone’s main circuit board. I could see it bouncing freely and wondered if the error would be caught or end up in someone’s wonky Galaxy device. I needn’t have worried. Samsung’s automated systems are fully capable of both the build and error-catching. As we watched, the offending board shifted off course and was held at bay while other properly built boards moved along.
I saw many different enclosures with so many automated manufacturing capabilities that it was mind-boggling.
Box 'em up but test them first
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
In another space, I saw sensors identifying phone IMEI numbers, while another robot printed out corresponding labels, and then a third affixed them to boxes that matched the packages to each phone.
Most of the robots I saw were small, but at the end of the line was an almost car-sized palletizer that takes the 10-per-box cardboard crates and stacks them on a pallet, placing the boxes first around the perimeter and then filling in the middle. The motorcycle-sized arm was remarkably fast and accurate.
Some of the phones never make it to the pallet. Instead, a select few are destined for a special test room where a large horseshoe of enclosures determines if the models in the current batch are fit for purpose.
There are two types of test systems in Gumi: the boxes that run the same test over and over again in a single device, and the U-shaped automated test bay where one phone is run in serial through the entire array of tests. These tests will often replicate what is done repeatedly in other enclosures.
The number of test systems and kinds of tests Samsung runs on its products is impressively comprehensive, though some of the boxes look downright bizarre.
Weird tests, reliable products
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Folding and unfolding the devices thousands of times is to be expected, as is pressure testing, but I also saw extreme heat and cold tests. There were also enclosures that do nothing but check AI vision systems, millimeter wave, waterproofing, and a facial recognition chamber with life-like mannequin heads that I can still see when I close my eyes.
There’s even a room where partners like Google can remotely access and run tests on Samsung phones.
More astonishing is that this is a living, ever-changing facility. Just imagine what happens every time, like now, Samsung unveils new phones and watches; they must retool. Walking the floor, I noticed how the brand-new Galaxy Z Fold 8 was already undergoing rigorous tests. The lab engineer told us, “For every new form factor, we develop new technology for it,” and they develop new automation to test it.
Look, I’m not saying other companies don’t put their mobile hardware through similar wringers, but I’m not sure any other tech giant has been so transparent about their process. It’s wild, bracing, and I must admit, gives me more than a bit of confidence about each new Galaxy device Samsung delivers.

articles.title: Amazon brade cette batterie externe de 10 000 mAh et lui offre un prix qui frôle les dix euros
articles.text:
Avec une capacité de 10 000 mAh et une puissance de 15 W, cette batterie externe est une Power Bank d'appoint qui pourra dépanner en cas d'urgence. À défaut de convaincre par sa fiche technique, elle se démarque par son prix dépassant légèrement les dix euros.
La batterie externe Belkin 10 000 mAh à 10,22 € au lieu de 29,99 €
Pourquoi choisir la batterie externe de Belkin ?
- Trois ports de charge et un câble inclus : Cette batterie externe se présente avec deux ports de charge USB-C et un port USB-A. Par ailleurs, un câble USB-C vers USB-A est fourni.
- Compatible avec la recharge rapide : Avec 10 000 mAh, on ne peut pas dire que cette batterie soit endurante. Cependant, elle s'avère diablement efficace et vous pouvez récupérer plusieurs heures d'autonomie avec une bonne dizaine de minutes de charge.
- Le prix : Avec son prix de dix euros, cette batterie externe n'est pas un grand investissement. Pour ce qu'elle propose, l'offre d'Amazon s'avère très intéressante.
Jusqu'à trois appareils simultanément
La capacité contenue de cette batterie de Belkin s'explique d'abord par son format. Seulement 211 grammes sur la balance pour à peine trois centimètres d'épaisseur et 11 cm de longueur. Pour être plus précis, elle est moins longue que la plupart des smartphones récents. Par conséquent, elle pourra facilement se glisser dans une poche.
Pour son design, Belkin ne fait pas de folie et propose un produit entièrement noir. Pour la recharge, il y a trois ports (deux USB-C et un USB-A) et un câble USB-C vers USB-A est fourni. Ainsi, trois appareils pourront être connectés simultanément. Une protection anti-surcharge est présente et quatre petites diodes lumineuses sur le côté indiquent le niveau d'autonomie restant.
Une excellente batterie d'appoint
Pour dix euros, il ne faut pas s'attendre à avoir une grosse Power Bank pour recharger votre tablette, votre smartphone ou votre montre connectée plusieurs fois. Avec sa capacité de 10 000 mAh, elle ne peut pas recharger une fois un iPhone récent. Pour pallier ce défaut, la marque mise sur la rapidité. En moins de 30 minutes, un smartphone retrouvera une bonne partie de son autonomie. On ne peut pas parler de recharge rapide puisque la batterie se limite à 15 W, mais ça dépanne.
En réalité, il s'agit d'une excellente batterie à emmener lors d'événements comme des concerts ou lors des voyages en avion puisqu'elle répond aux normes imposées par les compagnies aériennes. La liste des produits compatibles va dans ce sens. Belkin annonce que sa batterie externe fonctionne avec les appareils mobiles à savoir les smartphones, tablettes ainsi que les accessoires connectées. Si vous souhaitez recharger une console pour jouer ou un PC portable pour travailler, la batterie externe ne va pas suffire.
✅ Les points forts
- Trois ports de charge
- Un câble USB-A vers USB-C inclus
❌ Les limites
- Pas de charge sans-fil
- Une capacité de 10 000 mAh limitée
La batterie externe Belkin 10 000 mAh à 10,22 € au lieu de 29,99 €
Cette Power Bank de Belkin remplit parfaitement sa mission de batterie d'appoint. En plein concert, vous ne risquez pas de tomber en rade. La capacité limitée est un défaut identifié dès l'achat et ne posera donc pas de problème au quotidien.

articles.title: Deja de salir de WhatsApp para abrir y editar archivos PDF con esta función
articles.text:
La llegada de una función que permite abrir y editar archivos PDF directamente en los chats de WhatsApp redefine la experiencia de gestión documental dentro de la plataforma de mensajería. Los usuarios ya no necesitan abandonar la conversación ni depender de aplicaciones externas para revisar o modificar archivos.
La integración anunciada oficialmente por Meta implica varias novedades que impactan en la rutina digital cotidiana. Ahora, al recibir un archivo PDF en un chat, es posible abrirlo en la misma ventana, visualizarlo con comodidad y acceder a distintas herramientas de edición.
PUBLICIDAD
El objetivo es agilizar el trabajo colaborativo y evitar la pérdida de tiempo que suponía alternar entre aplicaciones.
Cómo es la nueva función para archivos PDF en WhatsApp
La función para abrir y editar archivos PDF en WhatsApp surge de la integración con Adobe Acrobat, producto de una alianza entre Meta y Adobe. Esta colaboración habilita la posibilidad de gestionar documentos desde el chat, incluso si están protegidos por contraseña.
PUBLICIDAD
Los usuarios pueden seleccionar el archivo PDF recibido en cualquier conversación y, sin salir de la aplicación, acceder a un visor que permite realizar anotaciones.
Entre las herramientas disponibles se encuentran dibujar, resaltar secciones, subrayar fragmentos de texto y tachar contenido. Estas opciones resultan útiles tanto para destacar información importante como para dejar comentarios o instrucciones dentro del propio documento.
PUBLICIDAD
La gestión de archivos PDF desde WhatsApp responde a la necesidad de quienes comparten documentos a diario y buscan procesos más eficientes. Incorporar estas funciones en el chat evita pasos extra y facilita la revisión colectiva de materiales en tiempo real.
Cómo se utiliza la edición de PDF en WhatsApp
La nueva funcionalidad está disponible en WhatsApp Web y en la versión de escritorio para Windows. Al recibir un archivo PDF, el usuario solo necesita hacer clic sobre el documento para abrirlo en una ventana integrada al chat.
PUBLICIDAD
Desde esta interfaz, es posible utilizar las herramientas de Acrobat sin necesidad de instalar software adicional. El usuario puede dibujar líneas o formas, marcar secciones mediante resaltado, subrayar texto relevante o tachar información que deje de ser útil. Todas estas acciones se guardan en el archivo, lo que permite compartir anotaciones con otros participantes de la conversación.
Una ventaja adicional es la compatibilidad con documentos protegidos por contraseña. Si el archivo requiere autenticación, basta con ingresar la clave correspondiente para habilitar la edición, sin que sea necesario descargar el PDF ni recurrir a otro programa.
PUBLICIDAD
Esta integración aprovecha las pantallas más grandes de los ordenadores, lo que mejora tanto la visualización como la edición de los documentos. Al mismo tiempo, permite mantener el hilo de la conversación, optimizando el flujo de trabajo profesional y personal.
Qué se puede hacer en la edición de archivos de WhatsApp
La unión entre WhatsApp y Adobe amplía las posibilidades para quienes usan la plataforma como herramienta de productividad. Ahora se pueden realizar anotaciones directas en archivos PDF desde el propio chat, lo que transforma la dinámica de revisión, corrección y colaboración en documentos.
PUBLICIDAD
Las funciones principales incluyen:
- Abrir archivos PDF protegidos o estándar directamente en la conversación.
- Dibujar sobre el documento para señalar puntos clave o trazar esquemas simples.
- Resaltar y subrayar texto para poner el foco en datos relevantes o instrucciones.
- Tachar contenido que deba eliminarse o indicarse como no vigente.
- Añadir comentarios o breves notas visuales que quedan integradas en el archivo compartido.
Estas herramientas permiten que el proceso de revisión de documentos sea más fluido, especialmente para equipos que trabajan a distancia o en entornos donde la mensajería es el canal principal de comunicación.
PUBLICIDAD
Actualmente, la función está disponible para quienes usan WhatsApp en ordenadores, ya sea a través de la versión Web o la aplicación para Windows.

articles.title: Reinventing hiring for the AI-driven labor market
articles.text:
Reinventing hiring for the AI-driven labor market
From talent scouts to talent architects
Recruitment has always reflected the realities of the labor market it serves. For decades, those realities were relatively stable.
Roles were well defined, career paths followed familiar patterns, and organizations could afford to move at a measured pace when bringing in new talent. That context has changed, but many hiring practices have not.
Today, skills evolve quickly, business priorities shift frequently, and candidates expect a level of speed and transparency that traditional processes struggle to provide.
The result is a growing mismatch between what organizations need and how they go about finding it.
Chief People Officer, Version 1.
Hiring cycles stretch out, decisions are made with incomplete information, and opportunities to secure the right talent are often missed.
It is within this context that artificial intelligence has entered the conversation, often accompanied by a degree of unease. Questions about automation, control, and fairness are not only understandable but necessary. However, focusing too narrowly on whether AI might replace elements of HR risks overlooking the more important development taking place.
There has been a rapid rise in the technology, with 87% of companies now adopting AI to support recruitment . AI is reshaping how decisions are made, and in doing so, it is redefining the contribution HR can make to an organization.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Establishing talent architects
For many HR teams, a significant proportion of time is still absorbed by coordination and administration. Screening applications, arranging interviews, and managing workflows are essential tasks, but they rarely represent the highest-value use of expertise.
A recent study three quarters of recruiters are using AI to save time and improve sourcing candidates . AI has the potential to absorb much of this operational load, processing large volumes of information quickly and consistently, while identifying patterns that would be difficult to detect through manual methods alone.
The benefit generates efficiency, while also creating the opportunity for HR leaders to operate with greater strategic intent. As organizations adopt AI-enabled approaches, the role of HR begins to move away from managing transactions and towards shaping the workforce more deliberately.
The concept of the HR leader as a “talent architect” is increasingly relevant in this environment. It reflects a responsibility not just to fill roles, but to design teams around capability, potential, and long-term direction. This requires a different balance of skills, combining an understanding of data and technology with a strong grounding in judgement, experience, and organizational culture.
Improving fairness through greater visibility
Concerns around bias often sit at the center of discussions about AI in hiring. There is a legitimate fear that automated systems could reinforce existing inequalities if left unchecked. Yet it is also important to recognize that bias is not introduced by technology alone. It is already present in many traditional hiring processes, often in ways that are subtle and difficult to measure.
What AI offers, when implemented with care, is greater visibility. Patterns in decision-making can be analyzed, inconsistencies can be identified, and outcomes can be assessed against clear criteria. This does not remove the responsibility from organizations to act, but it does provide a stronger foundation for doing so. Effective governance, transparency in how systems are trained, and ongoing review are essential if these benefits are to be realized.
Alongside considerations of fairness, there is a broader question of how AI influences the human aspects of hiring. The risk is not that technology replaces judgement, but that it is relied upon too heavily without sufficient oversight. The most effective organizations will be those that treat AI as a source of insight rather than a substitute for decision-making.
When this balance is achieved, the impact is tangible. Hiring processes become more responsive, with fewer delays between stages. Decisions are supported by a richer evidence base, allowing for greater confidence in outcomes . Candidates experience a process that is more consistent and easier to understand, which in turn strengthens the organization's reputation as an employer.
A better outcome for businesses and candidates
There are also clear links to business performance. When hiring decisions are better aligned with the capabilities required, organizations are more likely to see improvements in productivity and retention. Teams are built with an eye on future needs as well as immediate demands, which is particularly important in sectors where change is constant.
At the same time, candidates benefit from a process that is more transparent and consistent. Decisions are grounded in evidence, and opportunities are matched more closely to individual strengths. The experience becomes more predictable and, ultimately, more credible.
For HR leaders, the priority now is to approach AI with both ambition and discipline. Introducing new tools without a clear understanding of the problem they are intended to solve will deliver limited value. Equally, adopting a cautious stance that delays progress may leave organizations at a disadvantage in a competitive talent market.
Clarity of purpose is therefore essential. Whether the objective is to reduce time-to-hire, improve the quality of matches, or strengthen diversity, the role of AI should be defined in relation to those outcomes. This should be supported by investment in capability, ensuring that HR teams are equipped to interpret and apply the insights generated.
Perhaps most importantly, there needs to be a shift in how the role of HR is perceived within the organization. The introduction of AI does not diminish the importance of human expertise; it places a greater emphasis on it. As routine tasks are streamlined, the expectation is that HR will contribute more directly to strategic decision-making, bringing a deeper understanding of talent, culture, and organizational dynamics.
A new chapter for hiring
Companies integrating technology into their recruitment operations have seen their hiring processes become faster, data-informed, and more closely aligned to business priorities. AI is a significant factor in that transition, but it is not the defining feature. Rather, HR existing with AI support depends on how organisations choose to integrate technology with human judgement.
For those that do this well, the outcome is greater than a more efficient hiring process. It is a more thoughtful and effective approach to building teams, one that recognises both the value of data and the importance of human insight.
That balance will shape the next phase of hiring, and it will determine the extent to which organizations are able to adapt to the demands of an increasingly dynamic labor market.
