articles.title: Multi-Agent AI for Production Security Operations: An A2A and MCP Architecture in a 5G Core
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Build the reviewer agent first, with codified safety constraints (policy as code, rather than LLM prompts) and a clear escalation path to a human, built into the protocol itself
- Coordinate through an Agent-to-Agent (A2A) open protocol and integrate the environment through Model Context Protocol (MCP). Open coordination and context protocols outlive frameworks; agents written eighteen months apart will still talk if they share A2A, and each new tool exposed via MCP is immediately available to every agent at near-zero marginal integration cost.
- Gate LLM inference with classical anomaly detection. A lightweight Isolation Forest pre-filter on raw telemetry routes the LLM-driven agents only to genuinely novel samples. This approach makes the architecture reactive, where inference cost stays bounded, latency stays predictable, and the LLM does the work only humans were doing before.
- Reject both the monolithic-LLM and the GenAI-on-SIEM patterns for high-stakes security operations centers. The former is non-deterministic in ways production cannot tolerate; the latter is a productivity tool, not an architectural advance. A multi-agent layer with anomaly-gated inference, policy-gated autonomy, and a real human-in-the-loop is the durable alternative.
- Measure the right latency. The metric that matters in a production Security Operations Center (SOC) is the time between a new threat class appearing in the wild and your SOC having a deployed detection for it. Optimize the architecture for that latency.
The problem you are about to face
A 5G core in production generates more security telemetry per hour than most enterprise SOC see in a week. The bottleneck in a mature SOC is rarely analyst triage; rather, it is the detection-engineering team's ability to keep the rule base aligned with a threat landscape that evolves faster than rules can be written.
The architecture pattern described below builds on production security operations within a Tier-1 telco’s 5G core and has been continuously refined and improved over the past year through iterative operational feedback and internal deployments. It uses a multi-agent layer, coordinated through the A2A protocol and integrated with its environment through the MCP, with a privileged reviewer agent enforcing safety as code.
Measured against a baselined set of incident classes, it has reduced mean times to detect and to respond by approximately forty percent each, has autonomously generated more than eighty detection rules that would not previously have been written, and has compressed the human work required to produce a new rule from roughly three hours to fifteen minutes. The platform monitors ten to twenty 5G network functions concurrently.
Two Patterns That Don’t Work and Why
There are two dominant patterns in current industry literature on AI for security operations, and both, in my judgement, are dead ends at telco-core scale.
The Monolithic LLM
Pipe security telemetry, asset context, and operator queries into one large model and ask it to emit detections and responses. It fails in production for three compounding reasons.
First, the context window is too small for the breadth of telemetry a real SOC handles. In addition, the model is non-deterministic in ways unacceptable for outputs that trigger automated isolation on production infrastructure. Finally, a single prompt edit changes the behavior of the entire SOC, which makes change management almost impossible.
GenAI Bolted Onto a Conventional SIEM/SOAR
Most vendors are shipping an LLM assistant that summarizes alerts and drafts playbooks on top of an existing stack. It delivers analyst productivity gains. It does not change the structural shape of the SOC. Rules are still hand-written and time-to-coverage on a new threat class is still bound by your detection-engineering team's writing speed. If you are running a high-stakes SOC and you have evaluated either of these patterns and felt that something was off, this article is the alternative.
The Architectural Bet
Treat the SOC as a multi-agent system in which narrow, specialized agents collaborate through an open coordination protocol, integrate with their environment through an open context protocol, gate expensive LLM inference behind classical anomaly detection, and keep a human in the loop by design rather than by accident. The properties below are the ones we treat as non-negotiable.
Property 1: Narrow Agents with Single-Page Contracts
Each agent has several responsibilities: detection-rule synthesis, alert triage, response action proposal, environment context retrieval, and cross-agent review. Each agent’s system prompt, tool list, output schema, and escalation contract fit on a single page. If you cannot read an agent contract on one page, decompose the agent.
The temptation with large language models is to give agents rich personalities and elaborate prompts. Resist this temptation. The best-performing agents in our evaluations have terse, job-description-like system prompts; cleverness in prompts is technical debt.
Property 2: Coordination Over an Open Protocol (A2A)
Inter-agent traffic uses Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol exchanges. A2A was open-sourced by Google in April 2025 and transferred to the Linux Foundation in June 2025. In practice, the alternatives are framework-specific buses. Choosing an openly governed protocol matters because the useful life of a production multi-agent system is measured in years; the coordination layer's durability dominates any specific framework's convenience. We pair A2A with MCP (also donated by Anthropic to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025) and a CNCF substrate (e.g., Cilium, cert-manager, OPA, Kyverno, Argo CD, and Prometheus). The whole stack then sits under a single open governance umbrella, which is itself a procurement and compliance argument in regulated industries.
Property 3: Environment integration over MCP
Every interaction an agent has with the underlying environment goes through Model Context Protocol servers. This interaction includes asset inventory lookups, current network topology, recent incident history, and configuration state. MCP gives the agents a stable, schema-validated interface to a 5G environment whose internal tools evolve on their own cadence. When a new asset class is added or an inventory system is replaced, the change is absorbed by an MCP server's adapter; no agent prompt is rewritten.
Property 4: A Privileged Reviewer Agent
No agent may initiate an externally visible action without explicit approval from a reviewer agent whose safety constraints are codified, version-controlled, and independently testable. Externally visible actions here mean deploying a detection rule, executing a containment, or modifying a firewall policy. The reviewer is the safety floor of the system. In a critical-infrastructure deployment, autonomous action is acceptable only because the reviewer makes it so.
Because it is where most early multi-agent deployments fail, the instinct is to encode the reviewer's safety rules into a prompt and have the LLM reason about safety on the fly. This is a bad idea. The reviewer agent calls out to a separate policy layer (in our case, OPA) and acts on a deterministic verdict; the reviewer's own prompt is short, the policy itself is version-controlled code.
Property 5: Human-in-the-Loop Is a First-Class Output
Every consequential decision has three terminal states: auto-execute, auto-reject, and escalate to a SOC analyst with the full reasoning chain attached. The third state is reached whenever reviewer confidence falls under threshold, the asset class is on the always-escalate list, or the proposed action would exceed a configured blast radius.
The discipline this approach enforces is unfashionable but essential: Some decisions should never be automated. The protocol envelope routes those decisions to a human queue with all agent reasoning attached and before any action is taken.
What the Reviewer’s Policy Actually Looks Like
Property 4 describes the reviewer as a policy layer, not a prompt. In practice, that layer is really two layers working together, OPA and Kyverno; they do not do the same job.
The reviewer agent, backed by OPA, decides whether an action is allowed from an operational risk perspective: blast radius, confidence, reversibility, and human escalation. Kyverno independently validates how that action is expressed on the Kubernetes substrate once it reaches the cluster: trusted image sources, workload identity, resource constraints, and admission control. OPA enforces business safety invariants. Kyverno enforces platform security invariants. Together they give the system defence in depth between agent reasoning and production execution.
A quick note on the fields the OPA policy below relies on. The proposing agent estimates the blast radius and confidence at proposal time. The blast radius is the share of customer traffic a proposed action could affect if it goes wrong, while confidence is how sure the proposing agent is that its own proposal is correct. Reversible depends on the action type itself, blocking a route has a defined rollback and deleting or reconfiguring something core often does not. Config_validated is different from the other three, it is set by the reviewer, never by the proposing agent, since an agent should not be able to mark its own configuration change as safe.
The input below is not what the proposing agent sends verbatim. The reviewer agent builds it from the proposal, adding fields like config_validated that only the reviewer is trusted to set.
package reviewer.policy
# Input shape, illustrative only. Built by the reviewer agent from the proposing agent's output, not sent as-is by that agent.
# {
#   "action": {
#     "type": "deploy_rule",           # deploy_rule, execute_containment, or modify_config
#     "blast_radius_pct": 0.8,         # estimated by the proposing agent at proposal time
#     "confidence": 0.94,              # the proposing agent's own estimate that its proposal is correct
#     "reversible": true,              # set from the action type, not estimated
#     "config_validated": true         # set by the reviewer, never by the proposing agent
#   },
#   "asset": {
#     "NF_role": "upf",
#     "element_id": "upf-fr-paris-04"
#   }
# }
#
# Thresholds referenced below, data.limits, come from a separate data document, not from this file.
default decision := {"result": "escalate", "reason": "no matching rule"}
decision := {"result": "auto_reject", "reason": "configuration change is not clearly validated"} if {
	input.action.type == "modify_config"
	input.action.config_validated == false
} else := {"result": "escalate", "reason": msg} if {
	sensitive_elements[input.asset.element_id]
	msg := sprintf("%s is a sensitive network element and always escalates", [input.asset.element_id])
} else := {"result": "auto_reject", "reason": msg} if {
	input.action.blast_radius_pct > data.limits[input.action.type].max_blast_radius_pct
	msg := sprintf("blast radius %.2f exceeds limit for %s", [input.action.blast_radius_pct, input.action.type])
} else := {"result": "auto_execute"} if {
	config_ok
	not sensitive_elements[input.asset.element_id]
	input.action.blast_radius_pct <= data.limits[input.action.type].max_blast_radius_pct
	input.action.confidence >= data.limits[input.action.type].min_confidence
	input.action.reversible == true
}
config_ok if {
	input.action.type != "modify_config"
}
config_ok if {
	input.action.type == "modify_config"
	input.action.config_validated == true
}
sensitive_elements := {"upf-fr-paris-04", "sepp-fr-edge-01"}
The thresholds themselves live in a separate data document, rather than hard-coded in the policy. This approach keeps the decision logic and the actual risk tolerance independently versioned. The SOC team can tighten a threshold without touching the rule structure itself.
{
  "limits": {
    "deploy_rule": {
      "max_blast_radius_pct": 0.5,
      "min_confidence": 0.7
    },
    "execute_containment": {
      "max_blast_radius_pct": 0.2,
      "min_confidence": 0.9
    },
    "modify_config": {
      "max_blast_radius_pct": 0.3,
      "min_confidence": 0.8
    }
  }
}
Suppose the detection engineering agent generates a Kubernetes deployment for a new detection sensor, which the reviewer approves based on blast radius and confidence. That approval is not the end of the story. Before the object reaches the Kubernetes API server, Kyverno checks it independently, and it can still reject the deployment even after the reviewer said yes.
The following code snippet is a rule that rejects any deployment pulling an image from outside the approved internal registry, which matters because an agent generating a manifest could reference the wrong image source by mistake, and because a compromised dependency points somewhere it should not.
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: trusted-registry
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: verify-registry
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Deployment"]
      validate:
        message: "Images must come from the internal trusted registry"
        pattern:
          spec:
            template:
              spec:
                containers:
                  - image: "registry.internal/*"
The second code snippet is a rule that catches a different kind of mistake, an agent proposing a fix that works, but opens far more sources than intended. 
A common failure mode when an agent is asked to resolve a connectivity or access issue is to widen a NetworkPolicy or a ConfigMap until the symptom disappears, without noticing that the fix now allows traffic or access it should never have granted.
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-permissive-network-policy
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
    - name: reject-allow-all-ingress
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["NetworkPolicy"]
              namespaces: ["soc-agents"]
      validate:
        message: "NetworkPolicy must not allow ingress from all sources"
        deny:
          conditions:
            any:
              - key: "{{ request.object.spec.ingress[].from[] | length(@) }}"
                operator: Equals
                value: 0
An empty from field on an ingress rule defines "allow everything", which is exactly the kind of change that solves an immediate problem while quietly removing the network boundary on which the architecture depends. Kyverno rejects the request before it reaches the cluster, regardless of how reasonable the change looked to the agent that proposed it, or how urgent the prompting incident is.
This is not a replacement for the reviewer's judgment. OPA decides whether an action makes sense from a risk standpoint. Kyverno makes sure that whatever gets expressed as a Kubernetes object meets the cluster's own baseline, independently of how well or badly the agent that generated it reasoned about risk. Neither layer is sufficient on its own, and treating either as the final word would be a mistake.
Component Decomposition
| Agent | Responsibility | Output | Tools used | 
| Triage | Classify incoming security events; identify novelty | Event classification + novelty flag (Isolation-Forest-gated, LLM invoked only on samples above the anomaly threshold) | Asset inventory, historical detection index | 
| Detection engineering | Synthesize detection rules for newly observed patterns | Candidate rule + test fixtures | Detection index and telemetry samples, retrieved through the Context agent | 
| Response | Propose containment / mitigation actions for confirmed threats | Candidate response action + blast-radius estimate | Asset inventory and topology via Context; response actuators, read only at proposal time; retrieval of similar past remediation outcomes | 
| Context | Retrieve and structure environment data for other agents | Structured context payload | All inventory + topology MCP tools | 
| Reviewer | Validate proposals against safety constraints | Approval / rejection / escalation | Safety policy index (OPA); record of past reviewer decisions used to audit consistency over time | 
I will point out that Kyverno is not listed as a tool used by any single agent above. It sits after the reviewer, at Kubernetes admission time, and applies independently of what any agent decided.
The reviewer's safety constraints span four categories. Blast radius limits prevent proposed responses from affecting more than a configured percentage of customer traffic. Reversibility requirements require that every proposed response has a defined rollback. Confidence thresholds prevent execution of proposals below a calibrated confidence from escalating rather than auto executing all requests Finally, human-in-the-loop triggers always escalate specific asset classes. A fifth, narrower rule sits alongside these: Any configuration change the reviewer cannot validate as unambiguous is rejected outright, regardless of how the other four categories score. These constraints live outside any LLM prompt, in a policy layer the reviewer calls directly at evaluation time.
Why the System Stays Responsive
A fair objection to multi-agent LLM systems in production is latency. If every security event triggered the full fan-out, triage from context to detection-engineering, response, and reviewer, each invoking an LLM, the per-event cost in time and tokens would be untenable at telco core volumes.
The architecture solves this problem with anomaly-gated inference. Before the triage agent invokes any LLM, the raw telemetry feature vector is scored by an Isolation Forest model, which is an unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm, trained on rolling historical traffic. Isolation Forest was chosen deliberately: It is fast at inference, requires no labelling, handles high-dimensional inputs well, and degrades gracefully under distribution drift. Only samples whose anomaly score crosses a calibrated threshold are forwarded to the LLM-driven agents. Everything else is summarized at the metric level and dropped.
The practical effect is that the LLM-driven pipeline does the work that human detection engineers were previously doing (i.e., investigating novel patterns) and is not asked to look at routine traffic. Per-event latency on the LLM path is bounded by the slowest agent in the fan-out (in our deployment this boundary was low single-digit seconds end-to-end including reviewer policy evaluation), and the LLM path itself is exercised on a small fraction of events.
Two design notes are worth flagging. The Isolation Forest is retrained weekly and feature drift between retrainings is tracked as a first-class metric; a stale anomaly model would silently widen the LLM's workload. The threshold is itself a policy parameter consulted by the reviewer, so under operational stress it can be tightened to reduce LLM load without redeploying any agent.
What the Coordination Layer Looks Like
To make the pattern concrete, the following code snippet demonstrates the shape of an A2A task message between the triage agent and the detection-engineering agent. The specific schema is implementation-internal, but the envelope is representative of the structure A2A imposes:
{
  "task_id": "tsk_2026-03-24_8c1b9f",
  "from_agent": "triage.v3",
  "to_agent": "detection_engineering.v2",
  "intent": "synthesize_detection",
  "trace_id": "01HSMJ8...",
  "context_refs": [
    "mcp://asset-inventory/upf/upf-fr-paris-04",
    "mcp://detection-index/recent?window=14d"
  ],
  "payload": {
    "observation": { "...telemetry fingerprint..." },
    "novelty_score": 0.92,
    "deadline_ms": 90000
  },
  "constraints": {
    "rule_language": "sigma",
    "must_include_test_corpus": true,
    "max_false_positive_rate": 0.005
  }
}
Two things stand out. First, the agent-to-agent envelope carries a trace_id that propagates with the task. Every downstream span lives under the same distributed trace: the detection-engineering agent's call into MCP, the reviewer agent's policy evaluation, and the eventual deployment. That is what makes the system debuggable.
Second, the context_refs field carries MCP URIs rather than embedded context. The detection-engineering agent will dereference the URIs via MCP at evaluation time. This dereferencing keeps payloads small, lets the context agent enforce access control at the MCP boundary, and causes a single asset-inventory change to be immediately visible to every agent.
The shape of an MCP call into the asset inventory looks like this example:
GET mcp://asset-inventory/upf/upf-fr-paris-04
  Headers: { agent-identity: spiffe://company.com/sa/detection_engineering }
  Returns: { hostname, customer_segments, NF_role, last_seen, ...}
The agent’s identity is a workload identity attached at the mesh layer; the MCP server enforces authorization on the inventory based on that identity. Identity-as-traffic-policy is the right place for it.
A Representative Request Flow
Suppose the triage agent receives a previously unseen control-plane signalling anomaly on a User Plane Function (UPF) in the 5G core:
- Triage classifies the anomaly, queries the context agent via MCP for the UPF’s metadata, customer impact, and recent history, and determines that the pattern is novel.
- Triage dispatches an A2A task to the detection-engineering agent, such as "Synthesize a detection rule that would have caught this pattern earlier, with a small test corpus".
- In parallel, triage dispatches an A2A task to the response agent, such as "Propose a containment action assuming this signaling pattern is malicious".
- Both proposals are submitted to the reviewer agent via A2A.
- The reviewer evaluates each proposal against the policy bundle (OPA-style rules). If both pass, the rule is deployed and the response action is executed. If either fails, the case escalates to a human SOC analyst with the agents’ full reasoning chain attached.
Across hundreds of such flows per day, this approach produces the rule-creation compression and the autonomous coverage growth we measure at the operator level.
Measured Outcomes
Against the baseline architecture, using the same incident classes during internal evaluation, we measured:
- An approximate forty percent reduction in MTTD and an approximate forty percent reduction in MTTR.
- More than eighty detection rules generated autonomously on the 5G core, validated through the reviewer agent and human-spot-audited.
- Approximately twelve times the compression of human time to produce a new detection rule (three hours being reduced to roughly fifteen minutes).
- Concurrent monitoring of fifteen to twenty 5G network functions.
The figures above need two pieces of context, drawn from the platform's internal benchmark and the operator's incident-response metrics, rather than from a third-party study. They are baselined against the previous architecture at the same operator; your baseline will look different.
Trade-Offs and Limits of Applicability
The pattern fits well when your SOC is event-rich and the rule base is large enough that maintenance is a structural bottleneck, when the cost of a missed detection is high (e.g., critical infrastructure, financial services, and telco core) and when you have the engineering maturity to treat the reviewer's safety policy as a first-class artifact.
It is the wrong pattern if rule volumes are small enough that human detection engineering is not your bottleneck, if regulation mandates fully deterministic, statically-auditable detection logic, or if the operator lacks the engineering function to own the reviewer's safety policy. That last case matters most: Without that ownership, the platform is unsafe regardless of how well the rest is designed.
A few caveats are worth stating plainly. The architecture shifts detection engineers' work from rule authorship to reviewer-policy curation and agent-output audit, but it does not eliminate that work. A2A and MCP are still evolving, so any reviewer safety constraint that has not been red-teamed should be assumed insufficient.
What I Would Do Differently
With hindsight, two things would have gone differently. I underestimated the work involved in writing useful OPA policies; the code is small, but designing the right invariants, especially the right blast-radius constraints, required several iterations with the SOC team for which I had not budgeted. I also built the reviewer as a single agent. Having learned from the experience, I would now split the reviewer into a pre-execution reviewer (i.e., does this action satisfy policy?) and a post-execution auditor (i.e., did this action have the expected effect?), with the auditor's findings feeding back into reviewer policy tuning.
A few lessons emerged during the implementation and evaluation of this architecture.
Build the Reviewer First
The safety floor is set by the reviewer. Investing in its constraints before scaling the rest of the agent layer would have saved retroactive constraint patches.
Add the Anomaly as a Pre-Filter From Day One
We initially fanned events out to the LLM-driven agents too early and discovered the cost and latency problem only under production load. Placing an Isolation Forest in front of the LLM tier from the start would have saved a quarter of operational firefighting; the same is true of treating the anomaly threshold as a reviewer-consulted policy parameter rather than a configuration constant.
Resist Clever Prompts
Terse, single-page system prompts beat elaborate personalities every time in production. Cleverness compounds as technical debt and obscures the change-management story.
Publish the Schemas Earlier
A2A and MCP are open, but the SOC-domain agent schemas built on top of them have stayed internal. There is industry value in publishing reference schemas for SOC-domain agents and in opening up the policy language used by the reviewer. The field will converge on shared schemas in 2026-2027; getting there sooner is better.
Closing
Multi-agent AI for security operations, coordinated through A2A and integrated through MCP, is no longer a future choice for us; it is a current production pattern with measured outcomes. That pattern does not make it a universal answer; the trade-offs are real. But for cloud-native SOCs at the scale where rule maintenance is the structural bottleneck, it is, in my experience, the most durable architectural bet available today.
Two questions I keep hearing since presenting this architecture at KubeCon are how do you keep it reactive and where does the human sit. These questions have the same underlying answer: Be disciplined about where you put the LLM, putting cheaper more predictable mechanisms in front of expensive ones. Open protocols rather than bespoke buses, prioritizing safety in policy-as-code, rather than in the system prompt. Maintain a human-in-the-loop path that is a normal output of the system, rather than an exception bolted on the side.
The interesting work for the next eighteen months will not be in scaling models. It will be in hardening reviewer agents, standardizing SOC-domain agent schemas, and writing the safety policies that turn a clever architecture into one that is operationally trustworthy.

articles.title: Iran claims it destroyed Amazon's main data hub in Bahrain. Nobody has confirmed it
articles.text:
What just happened? Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard says it launched several cruise missiles at Amazon's data infrastructure in Bahrain, claiming the attack destroyed the facility. The alleged strike marks the latest escalation in the renewed conflict between Tehran and Washington, though neither Amazon nor US or Bahraini officials has confirmed that it actually happened.
The IRGC's Aerospace Force said it targeted what it described as Amazon's central data infrastructure in Bahrain. Iranian state-linked media made the announcement on Tuesday, adding that US air defense systems and radar installations in the Bahraini areas of Muharraq and Riffa were also attacked.
Iran said the operation was retaliation for a US strike on the Darkhovin nuclear power plant, which is still under construction in southwestern Iran. The United States has been carrying out nightly attacks across Iran since hostilities resumed earlier this month, while Tehran has targeted American military facilities and other US-linked sites throughout the Gulf.
There is currently no independent evidence confirming the IRGC's claim. Amazon did not comment when contacted by reporters, while officials in Bahrain and the US have remained silent.
– RedWave Press (@RedWavePress) March 31, 2026
AWS's public health dashboard states that its Middle East Bahrain region, known as me-south-1, is currently unavailable. However, this doesn't necessarily prove that Tuesday's attack took place. The region has been offline for months following earlier strikes connected to the conflict, and AWS's last public update on the situation was posted on April 30.
Iran has previously made clear that American technology companies are considered potential targets in this conflict. In April, the IRGC threatened Nvidia, Microsoft, Intel, Apple, Google, Meta, Oracle, and several other US firms, accusing them of supporting military operations against Iran. Employees were warned to evacuate their workplaces.
Days later, Iran threatened to annihilate the $30 billion Stargate UAE AI data center in Abu Dhabi. The planned 1GW facility is backed by OpenAI, Oracle, Nvidia, Cisco, G42, and SoftBank.
With the Bahrain AWS region already unavailable, the effect of any new damage may be limited, but Iran's latest claim is a reminder of the risks facing American-owned digital infrastructure across the Middle East.

articles.title: Caída de Instagram en España: reportaron problemas para iniciar sesión y enviar mensajes
articles.text:
Durante la tarde del miércoles 22 de julio de 2026, miles de usuarios en España experimentaron problemas al intentar acceder a Instagram. La incidencia comenzó alrededor de las 16:00 (hora peninsular), con reportes masivos de fallos tanto en la versión móvil como en la web.
El servicio presentó errores para iniciar sesión, visualizar publicaciones, enviar mensajes y, en algunos casos, los usuarios se encontraron con desconexiones continuas. Por el momento, la compañía no ha ofrecido detalles sobre el origen de la interrupción.
PUBLICIDAD
Este tipo de incidentes vuelve a poner sobre la mesa la dependencia diaria de las plataformas sociales y cómo una caída temporal puede afectar tanto la comunicación personal como la actividad profesional de miles de personas.
Así fue la caída: qué problemas reportaron los usuarios
La plataforma Downdetector, que recopila reportes de usuarios sobre fallos en servicios digitales, registró un pico significativo de incidencias a partir de las 16:00. El mayor número de quejas se centró en la imposibilidad de iniciar sesión y el mal funcionamiento de la versión móvil, aunque también hubo problemas en la versión web.
PUBLICIDAD
Entre los fallos más comunes se encontraron:
- Imposibilidad de acceder a la cuenta o iniciar sesión.
- Publicaciones que no cargaban o no se actualizaban.
- Mensajes directos que no se enviaban ni se recibían.
- Desconexiones frecuentes sin motivo aparente.
A pesar de la magnitud del problema, la caída no fue global, ya que afectó principalmente a usuarios en España, con reportes dispersos en otras regiones.
PUBLICIDAD
La respuesta oficial: silencio y rápida normalización
Hasta el momento, Meta, la empresa matriz de Instagram, no ha emitido ningún comunicado oficial explicando las causas del fallo. Sin embargo, la actualización del servicio fue relativamente rápida: hacia las 17:45, Downdetector reflejaba una reducción notable de los reportes, y la mayoría de los usuarios confirmaban que la plataforma volvía a funcionar con normalidad.
Este tipo de caídas, aunque temporales, generan inquietud entre los usuarios, especialmente cuando no hay información oficial sobre lo sucedido. La falta de comunicación inmediata suele dejar espacio para rumores y especulaciones, aunque en esta ocasión la recuperación del servicio fue casi tan rápida como la propagación del problema.
PUBLICIDAD
¿Qué hacer si Instagram no funciona?
Ante una caída de este tipo, conviene seguir algunos pasos para descartar que se trate de un problema individual:
1. Comprobar la conexión a Internet
Asegúrate de que tu conexión WiFi o datos móviles funciona correctamente. Un fallo local puede confundirse fácilmente con una caída global de la app.
2. Consultar plataformas de monitoreo
Accede a portales como Downdetector y busca “Instagram” para verificar si hay reportes masivos de fallos en tu zona o país. El sitio muestra gráficas de incidencias y mapas que permiten identificar las áreas afectadas.
PUBLICIDAD
3. Probar en diferentes dispositivos
Intenta acceder a Instagram desde otro dispositivo o usando la versión web. Si el fallo persiste en ambas, es probable que el problema sea generalizado.
PUBLICIDAD
4. Esperar la recuperación del servicio
En la mayoría de los casos, estos errores se solucionan en cuestión de minutos u horas. Mantén la aplicación actualizada y evita hacer cambios en la configuración hasta que el servicio se restablezca.
PUBLICIDAD
La caída de Instagram en España refleja cómo las plataformas sociales se han convertido en infraestructura clave para la comunicación cotidiana. Mensajes, noticias, promociones y hasta negocios dependen de su disponibilidad. Un fallo temporal pone de manifiesto la vulnerabilidad de estos ecosistemas y la importancia de contar con canales alternativos para mantener la comunicación y la actividad.
Aunque hoy la incidencia se resolvió rápidamente, la recomendación para los usuarios sigue siendo la misma: informarse a través de fuentes confiables y estar atentos a los canales oficiales de la plataforma ante cualquier interrupción relevante.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Kevin Feige revela el ambicioso plan tras 'Avengers: Doomsday' y 'Secret Wars': ¿Hasta cuándo habrá UCM?
articles.text:
El debut del tráiler de Avengers: Doomsday revitalizó el interés por el próximo gran evento del Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel, que marcará el regreso de figuras como Robert Downey Jr y Chris Evans. El filme de los hermanos Russo busca levantar a una saga en caída tras Avengers: Endgame (2019), con una historia que concluirá el próximo año en Avengers: Secret Wars. Sin embargo, Marvel Studios tiene planes bastante ambiciosos para el futuro, como ha confirmado el propio Kevin Feige.
El líder del estudio le concedió una entrevista a un portal chino (vía GamesRadar), donde dio a conocer algunos detalles interesantes sobre el futuro del UCM después de Avengers: Doomsday y Secret Wars. Según Feige, Marvel Studios ya ha planificado los próximos 16 años de la franquicia.
De acuerdo con el citado medio, la compañía pretende lanzar nuevas producciones al menos hasta 2042. Ojo, que eso no necesariamente implica que ese año se vaya a terminar el Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel. Aunque el propio Kevin Feige ha dicho que tampoco saben si realmente van a llegar hasta esa fecha.
"Acabamos de estar en una sala de reuniones de Marvel Studios, planeando películas hasta el año 2042. ¿Llegaremos a 2042? ¿Quién sabe? ¿Serán esas [mismas] películas? ¿Quién sabe?", explicó el líder del estudio.
Tras Avengers: Doomsday y Secret Wars, Marvel planifica el UCM al menos hasta 2042
Por sorprendente que parezca, planificar el UCM hasta 2042, con 16 años de antelación, no es descabellado. Tengamos en cuenta que la franquicia de Marvel Studios lleva ni más ni menos que 18 años de vigencia, tomando Iron Man (2008) como punto de partida.
Con Avengers: Doomsday y Secret Wars, la compañía parece estar gastándose los últimos cartuchos para ganarse el beneplácito de los fanáticos. El nivel de la franquicia cayó considerablemente tras Endgame, especialmente por la superpoblación de proyectos destinados a Disney+. Marvel Studios ha gozado de algún que otro éxito esporádico, pero en líneas generales las sensaciones del público y la prensa especializada han quedado lejos de la etapa más gloriosa. A esto hay que sumarle el cambio de rumbo obligado por el despido de Jonathan Majors como Kang, el Conquistador.
El regreso de Robert Downey Jr, Chris Evans y los hermanos Russo busca recuperar la fase más exitosa del UCM. De allí a que Avengers: Doomsday y Secret Wars lo logren, es una discusión diferente. Pero planificar con anticipación el resto de la saga seguramente busque recuperar el componente más épico. Por ejemplo, la gestación gradual de un conflicto a lo largo de varios títulos, como sucedió con Thanos y las gemas del Infinito.
Por lo pronto, Kevin Feige ha revelado que la intención a futuro es trabajar en un único universo que ponga a los X-Men en un espacio predominante. "Se creará un universo único, simplificado y coherente que podremos seguir. Algunas cosas nos resultarán familiares, pero muchas serán completamente nuevas. Volviendo a lo que mencionamos antes sobre atraer a los jóvenes y conectar con una nueva generación de público, de eso tratará precisamente el próximo universo. Y, fundamentalmente, los X-Men serán su eje central", remarcó.
Sea como sea, el Universo Cinematográfico de Marvel tiene dos títulos de peso programados para los próximos meses. Primero llegará Spider-Man: Brand New Day, cuyo estreno se dará el próximo 31 de julio. En tanto que el 18 de diciembre llegará a la cartelera la esperada Avengers: Doomsday.

articles.title: What Apple’s OpenAI lawsuit is really about
articles.text:
Today on Decoder, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the major trade secrets lawsuit between Apple and OpenAI and what this tells us about OpenAI’s future.
Apple’s OpenAI lawsuit is about who gets to define the post-smartphone era
OpenAI can’t afford another lawsuit, especially not with a company like Apple.
By now I’m sure most Decoder listeners are familiar with Apple’s allegations in this case. The company says a number of ex-Apple employees at OpenAI targeted Apple’s trade secrets in job interviews and even downloaded files from Apple’s servers related to hardware manufacturing. The claims are shocking, although OpenAI denies them, and we have yet to see the company’s legal response.
Hayden has been covering OpenAI for years now, and she also just talked to a bunch of lawyers who specialize in intellectual property and trade secret law to get a sense of how serious this case is. The answer is not entirely positive for OpenAI, which spent $6.5 billion to acquire legendary Apple designer Jony Ive’s AI hardware startup, io Products, back in 2025.
As you’ll hear Hayden explain, Apple is a notoriously tenacious litigant, and we have lots of tech industry history to back up that reputation. But those cases were against companies at the scale of Microsoft and Samsung, giant corporations that could afford the cost and distraction of this kind of litigation.
OpenAI isn’t yet that kind of company. It’s still burning cash and a little strategically adrift as it tries to compete in both enterprise and consumer markets, and it’s turning over executives on a regular basis. So Hayden and I spent a lot of time talking about what this case might mean for a company that defined the early part of the AI boom, but which lately always seems to be in a crisis of one sort or another.
Okay: Verge senior AI reporter Hayden Field on the Apple-OpenAI lawsuit, and how the AI industry might change because of it. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Hayden Field, you’re the senior AI reporter for The Verge. Welcome back to Decoder.
Thanks. Great to be here.
Once again, we’re going to talk about OpenAI, Hayden.
Once again, it never stops.
We’re going to talk about whether OpenAI can maintain focus at a time of great distraction, which seems to be a theme with that company. Although this time, it’s not their own distraction. It’s a distraction from out in the world, maybe caused by some of their own behavior.
Of course, we’re talking about the Apple trade secret lawsuit. It feels like a big deal. Apple is accusing OpenAI of stealing all kinds of information from that company, even in job interviews — asking people in job interviews to tell them what they know about Apple products. Tell us briefly about this lawsuit and what’s going on here.
Definitely. So, it is crazy. I wrote a piece last week titled “Sam Altman didn’t need another lawsuit,” and that’s really the situation here. It seems pretty egregious from some of the claims that Apple is making. A former Apple employee was allegedly soliciting trade secrets over interviews, asking people to maybe bring pieces of hardware outside the Apple office to OpenAI to do a “show and tell” in interviews, things like that.
There’s a lot of allegations being made that are pretty crazy. But then when I actually interviewed a bunch of experts last week, they said they’ve seen all of this before, a lot. It’s just they haven’t seen all of it in one case with two key players.
Some of this stuff is pretty egregious, if it turns out to be true. But also, to the experts in the space, they’re saying, “Oh, we see this all the time with trade secrets cases. It’s not crazy. What’s really crazy is that it’s all in one case and that it’s two really large companies.”
It’s really interesting. It’s just a pattern, maybe not worth diving into at great length, but in the ‘90s, Apple pushed copyright law to the limit. They sued Microsoft for allegedly infringing on how the Mac looked and felt with Windows. I will point out that Windows still exists, Microsoft is fine.
And then in the 2000s and early 2010s, Apple pushed patent law to the limit, suing Samsung for allegedly violating a bunch of patents with Android and Galaxy phones because Apple felt that they had protected the iPhone. Samsung eventually paid about $1 billion in damages and those cases just went around in circles forever.
But I’ll point out that Android still exists, Samsung is doing just fine. Apple may have redefined patent law around 3G and 4G licensing, but fundamentally, it did not actually succeed in stopping its competitors with intellectual property lawsuits.
So, you go from copyright to patent and now trade secrets, which is the third big intellectual property, and Apple’s doing it again with OpenAI. My big question is whether OpenAI can just pay the money the way that Microsoft and Samsung were able to just pay the money. If you look at Samsung, spending $1 billion in penalty fees to get Galaxy phones off the ground and be a major competitor in mobile is maybe the easiest and best investment that company ever made.
But I don’t know if OpenAI is the same company at the same moment. It certainly seems like all of the Apple employees that went over to OpenAI maybe pushed the limit too much, at least from the story that Apple’s telling us right now.
It’s pretty crazy reading the wildest claims from the lawsuit and also the messages that were being exchanged. One of them allegedly accessed Apple confidential information on a device and then said, “LOL! So funny that I can access this.” There’s a lot there.
I’ve been wondering the same thing. It really depends on Apple’s willingness to be petty or be super logical here. When I interviewed a bunch of lawyers about this, they said Apple is a notoriously tenacious litigant, as we’ve seen in those past cases. But also, they really will take things far. They have a lot of money and they’re willing to use it. It really just depends on how mad they are.
I think that they would potentially settle if OpenAI paid them enough, but will OpenAI be able to do that? They’re already having a really tough year. They’re about to IPO, all the investors are looking at their bottom line, wondering when they’re going to turn a profit. It’s a tough time to be shelling out a ton of money to Apple. We’ll have to see what they do.
I think it’s going to go to trial and be a very drawn-out years-long thing. That’s what a lot of the lawyers I interviewed said as well. But I could see a world in which they just figure out a way to get all this money together and pay and maybe Apple accepts it.
In the Samsung patent cases, they lasted forever. In the middle of it, Tim Cook was at a Code Conference and I asked him, “What are you doing? Is this accomplishing anything?” And he looked at me very seriously and he said, “Well, we think the fees for licensing standard essential patents are out of whack.” And I was like, “That is not the reason you’re doing any of this. That’s not the point, the point is that you were mad and you wanted to run this lawsuit to ground and you’re going to run this lawsuit to ground no matter what the nominal reason is.”
That feels like a big piece of the puzzle here. OpenAI has taken a bunch of Apple employees. Famously Jony Ive, Apple’s most famous designer, is working with OpenAI on hardware devices. Tang Tan, who is OpenAI’s chief hardware officer. He had a reputation at Apple for “playing fast and loose,” that’s from Mark Gurman at Bloomberg.
He seems like the central character in the story, not so much Jony Ive, but Tang Tan. And that piece where it’s a bunch of ex-Apple people maybe playing too fast and loose almost feels like it’s personal, almost feels like there’s a lot of emotions involved. Talk about Tang Tan and talk about what all these folks are alleged to have done that feels like it’s a little more personal than your standard big corporate dispute.
On what you said about talking to Tim Cook, I truly believe people underestimate companies’ pettiness. We’ve seen it in recent years, like with the OpenAI-Elon Musk lawsuit. There are so many things that could have been avoided if companies weren’t trying to just be petty, which is fine. They can do that, they have enough money to do that. But people underestimate how much that plays a part sometimes in these things.
As for Tang Tan, yeah, he worked at Apple for 24 years. He was the VP of the Apple Watch. He left in 2024 to work on Jony Ive’s hardware company, io Products, which obviously OpenAI ended up purchasing.
OpenAI then appointed him as chief hardware officer. So he had a C-suite role at OpenAI, but this is after 24 years at Apple. According to Apple’s lawsuit claims, he was the mastermind of a lot of this trade secrets gathering, regarding interviews that he would conduct and ask about secret code-named projects. And then the person being interviewed would feel like maybe they were able to tell him stuff because, oh, well, why would he know the name of this project or these details about it if he wasn’t involved also? So, they felt they could speak more freely, allegedly.
There were other times that he asked, “Hey, why don’t you bring some batteries or other pieces of hardware outside the Apple office that you’ve worked on in the past so that we can do a show and tell?” It’s very interesting to go through these claims. It just seemed like he really was not worried about what was going to come of this, if these claims are true.
The other major character here is Jony Ive, Apple’s very famous ex-designer who worked with Steve Jobs and all of those famous projects. I would say Ive reportedly has a very testy relationship with Apple.
Now that he’s left, he’s certainly made that clear in various interviews and statements. And he’s working with Sam Altman on new devices. He made a video with Sam Altman, which I can only describe as a romantic coffee date.
Absolutely.
In which they described the phone and the laptop as legacy devices.
It was instantly memed. I have to say the memes were amazing.
It’s very good. And they shut down half of San Francisco to make it. I thought Ive calling the phone and the laptop legacy devices in that video was just a straight shot at Apple. These are the things that he made, that he revolutionized in many, many ways. And he’s like, “These are over now.”
You can say a lot about whether that’s true, whether that can come true, and I want to talk about that in a little bit. But it’s notable to me that Jony Ive is not mentioned in this lawsuit. There’s a line Apple wouldn’t cross, and it’s mentioning the fact that it’s Jony Ive who went to OpenAI and started hiring all of his old designers, who sold a big portion of his company to OpenAI. And now, they’re trying to make hardware and allegedly stealing trade secrets. But Jony Ive, he’s not part of it. We’re just going to leave his name out of it.
Is that because he’s too famous? Is that because it’s too nuclear? Is it because he’s still friends with Laurene Powell Jobs? What do you make of that?
I think it may be more that he knew how to cover his tracks. It could be that he’s too powerful or any of the things you said, but I really feel like it’s just that he has other people doing his dirty work for him. The other stuff in this lawsuit is pretty egregious, and they’ve found it all. So if they found some really intense stuff on Jony Ive, would they really not put it in the lawsuit? There’s some bad blood between them. I just feel like they would put it in there.
This is just speculation, but when you’re in a powerful enough role, you don’t have to do all this stuff yourself. You have other people doing it for you and you also know how to cover your tracks. So, to me, maybe they just didn’t have anything on him.
Yeah, or he’s distracted designing Ferraris no one likes or whatever it is he’s doing, but he’s not in this. I do think that’s notable because the reason Sam Altman would hire Jony Ive is to make a credible claim to the next device. Whatever that category of AI-powered device is going to be, you hire the most famous designer to say, “I made the iPhone and I’m going to make this thing.”
And then it seems like OpenAI also wanted a bunch of Apple’s know-how in order to make that thing. What do you make of that, that OpenAI needed hardware know-how from Apple? Or at least Apple alleges that OpenAI needed hardware know-how from Apple to make whatever the next thing is?
To some extent, whether you’re talking about trade secrets or just regular legal aboveboard know-how from hiring their employees, of course they needed it. They’ve seen a ton of hardware in AI crash and burn and they’re trying to not become the next Humane AI Pin. It can be incredibly embarrassing to make an AI hardware device in this day and age. Chances are you’re probably going to fail miserably and become a laughingstock. And so, if you want to avoid that, of course you need to get the best people on your side.
Hardware is hard, as everyone says, so of course they want to get experts in there that have experience actually being incredibly successful at hardware. That’s not surprising to me and I think it’s a smart decision. OpenAI has demonstrated in the past — and this is typical of every tech company, it’s not just OpenAI— that sometimes they’re a little bit disconnected from what the consumer actually wants.
You roll something out, no one really wants it. Okay. With software that’s a little easier to pivot from, as we’ve seen from OpenAI deleting its side quests and stuff. They’re like, “Oh, we’re not doing this anymore. We’re not doing this anymore. We’re rolling this into that.” With hardware, you can’t do that. You’d better have it right from the get-go.
I’m glad you said consumer, because that brings me to what I think is the heart of the matter for OpenAI, which is that it was going to be the consumer AI company, Anthropic famously focuses on enterprise and it’s been lucrative for them; maybe that’s where all of the money is. But OpenAI was going to take down Google, maybe through Bing, maybe through its own app. It was going to be a consumer company.
The only reason you would make hardware is to go attack the consumer, to go attack the iPhone. So, OpenAI’s ambitions, at least as I could see them, were first to take market share from Google, which is one of the most lucrative businesses in the history of the world, and then to go attack the iPhone, which is the most famous and culturally dominant tech product that has ever existed.
I don’t know how it can do either of those things. It doesn’t seem like consumers even want these products or want AI at this scale. I don’t know where that revenue comes from in consumer, and the college students are all booing AI at graduation. Does OpenAI just need to pivot to enterprise? Does it need to spend its time spinning its wheels at consumer hardware devices before it figures out its business?
OpenAI has pivoted so many times internally. Its most recent pivot was that it was going to focus on its key revenue drivers, which are enterprise and coding. They’ve said that a million times. OpenAI folded Sora, Atlas, the sexting feature. It feels like years ago, but it’s crazy that that was in the past year.
They’ve done a lot of this, and so, everyone thought, “Okay, they’re going for it, they’re doing enterprise,” because that’s the tried-and-true money maker here, especially in a year that they’re going to IPO. To be fair, yes, they had already planned to do the hardware device before this whole pivot and cutting out the side quests. I guess they can’t afford to cut out this potential side quest because they’ve already spent a lot on it, it’s happening no matter what. So now they’re just trying to make it as successful as it can.
I’ve only been on the AI beat for six years. That is a long time in AI, and maybe I’m missing something, but I just do not see a market when everyone is buying an OpenAI hardware device. If I’m wrong, we can come back on here and laugh at my clip from July 2026. A smart speaker, okay, maybe people buy it just to be a smart speaker like Google Home, that’s what I use mine for.
I think it’s going to be one of those things that a few people really, really, really love and that the general public probably does not adopt because it’s difficult to get them to adopt anything unless all their friends have it. There’s a social aspect. You’re going to be a laughingstock with green text if you don’t have an iPhone. No hate to Android people, I’m just saying sometimes you don’t get added to the group text or something. It’s sad and it’s not right, but there’s got to be some public buy-in if you’re going to be adopting a new piece of hardware a lot of the time.
We founded The Verge at the start of the smartphone boom. Just thinking back on it, it was never a question of whether people would adopt smartphones. That was obvious. It was obvious to us, maybe it wasn’t obvious to everyone, but we were in it and the only thing that wasn’t obvious was who would win.
After a while it became obvious that Apple would win. How many iPhone killers did we cover 15 years ago? And they all came and went, and they looked like new operating systems. Windows Phone existed. The Palm Pre ran an operating system called webOS. Android was ascendant. Nokia tried to do its own thing and then they pivoted to Windows Phone.
At the end of the day, we ended up with iOS and Android and everything else fell into line. Maybe the whole tech industry hates this and they hate paying the App Store fees, but this feels like that same kind of moment where OpenAI is going to put out a hardware device, it’s going to run its own operating system. Elon Musk is fulminating about Starlink and xAI putting out their own phone, maybe running their own operating system, apparently the run-up to IPO, they were showing it to people.
I just have really dumb questions that, to me, mirror the same questions we asked about new smartphone operating systems 15 years ago. Are you going to make a Gmail client? Is it going to have Instagram? Because if you don’t have those things, you don’t actually get to replace the phone. And if you don’t replace the phone, well, I’ve got the beta of iOS 27 on my iPhone right here and Siri AI is definitely good enough to just get through the day.
That’s what really gets me here, because the smartphone replaced the dumb phone. So okay, you’ve got to have something way better than the smartphone. Are you going to? Doubtful, but we’ll see.
But the other thing that gets me here is how many devices OpenAI is reportedly working on. Reportedly it’s five hardware devices, and the screenless smart speaker is the first one. How can they come up with five? That’s what I want to know. What are the five? And shouldn’t you be putting all your resources toward one? It’s already hard to make one. I’m a little dubious of five successful AI hardware devices. Even one is a long shot, but five is a little bit crazy.
I’m sure there’s a lot and some will come and go. The thing that I think about, particularly when it comes to Jony Ive and his approach to hardware — which is familiar at this point, we’ve watched him launch a lot of hardware at Apple — is Ive tends to focus on new input methods for new devices.
The iPod had the click wheel and that really defined the form and function of the iPod. The iPhone has a multitouch screen that really defined the form and function of the iPhone and then the iPad. If you’ll remember the Apple Watch, they launched it with great fanfare about the scroll wheel on the side. I don’t know if that came to pass, but they really thought that was a big deal when they launched the Apple Watch.
This is Ive’s go-to path: “We find a new input mechanism, we’re going to define the product around it.” I know exactly what that should be for AI — it’s a natural language input. You can just tell the computer whatever you want and it’ll figure it out and it’ll go off and do it for you.
But we’re however many years into the AI revolution?Three or four years into this version of it? And it doesn’t quite work yet. I think this is why the AI devices keep failing, as you keep mentioning. Because you can talk to a Humane Pin all day and all night and it will pretend to understand you and then not actually be able to do the things on the other side of it.
That feels like the problem in AI right now. There’s these flashes of brilliance and then there’s these limits of capability. Where do you think we are in that process of figuring out exactly what it can and can’t do? And how do you think that limits a hardware device?
We’re still in the midst of it. I personally use AI all the time, obviously in my personal life to test things out, see what it can do. Month to month, I see how it’s improved, at least from my own personal experience, which is all anecdotal.
But just the other day I was trying to look up a lot of addresses of companies because I wanted to map something out. I would say maybe 60 percent of the ones I looked up were completely wrong, just wrong. It made me a whole table. And it was like, “Yeah, don’t worry, all these are definitely correct.” And then 60 percent wrong. I’m like, “A lot of these are wrong.” They’re like, “Oh, sorry, my mistake.”
Yeah, my favorite.
It’s like, “Oh yeah, you’re right. You caught me.”
It’s right about a lot of stuff a lot of the time. But as we all know from when we were an intern back in the day, or if we’ve ever had an intern, there are certain things that are just easier to do yourself if you’re not 100 percent sure the person is going to get it right.
So what I wonder is, for a hardware device like this, there are a lot of low-stakes questions you can ask it and it’ll be fine. But for higher-stakes things, it’s simpler to just look it up yourself or do it yourself even than put it out there when it’s going to be a potentially wrong answer.
Is this going to end up like a Google Home situation, where you’re just using it as a speaker and you’re asking it what the weather is because it doesn’t really matter that much if it’s wrong? But as we know, it can only really be super useful if you can trust it with those higher-stakes types of questions. And so, saying, “Hey, what time does Emily’s flight get in tonight because she’s staying with me? What flight is she on?” Or, “Is it delayed?” If it gets that wrong, okay, I’m not going to be ready for her to come in from the airport.
This does seem like the core problem. Will there be enough progress? Certainly the industry will claim that it’s made great progress on hallucinations. Whether that’s the lived experience of people who use these products, I think that’s up for debate. But the industry claims they’ve made great progress here.
The other piece is, will OpenAI have access to all of your data and personal context to make this useful in an environment with a smart speaker, where you can just say whatever you want to it? That, again, brings you back to whether it’s going to have a Gmail client. Where’s the Gmail client going to run? Are you going to let OpenAI log into your Gmail, so when you ask for flight information, it can go look at it? Or are you just going to default to opening Gmail on your phone and asking it because Google already has it? This seems like a version of competition that really depends on how comfortable you are handing over all of your data to various AI providers. And I’m just not sure OpenAI is that one.
The other part of this is that — and obviously this is a vocal minority here, it’s not like the majority of OpenAI users — a lot of people are extremely worried about ads. Anthropic capitalized on that with its Super Bowl ads that were anti-AI ads. OpenAI has been dealing with that fallout and just trying to say, “Hey, don’t worry, we’re not going to influence answers, we’re just going to raise a similar ad underneath the answer.”
But it can be unnerving, whenever I use ChatGPT and an ad surfaces. It just makes me feel like it’s less private. It’s just a little bit strange and I feel like everyone gets that unnerved feeling. Even if it’s not affecting the actual answer, it’s still reminding you that it’s not a space where they’re not trying to sell you something. Someone is always trying to sell you something.
There’s already a lot of loss of trust right now in AI labs, if anyone trusted them to begin with. Right now, it’s at an all-time low. We’re seeing the rise of AI populism. We’re seeing lots of death threats against AI CEOs, as The Wall Street Journal covered the other day. There’s a lot of backlash, like you were saying about college kids booing AI at graduations. We’re seeing a huge backlash right now, and I just think it’s a strange time to be releasing a public-facing, “every consumer should buy this” AI hardware device.
That connects to a bigger issue for OpenAI in this Apple lawsuit, which is that the AI industry right now is basically built on unauthorized taking. I’m saying that instead of theft because there are a lot of lawsuits. I know our audience wants me to just call it theft and maybe it is just theft. And maybe we can just say that when we get to the end of the road of 10,000 different lawsuits. But that part of the AI industry feels like we have to studiously ignore it.
There’s a trillion-dollar question over whether training data is fair use that is as of yet unresolved. We can just go down the list of lawsuits where all of these companies have to defend themselves about training data. And if they lose any one of them, maybe this whole industry cost structure falls apart.
The inputs to AI right now are free. They just took the internet and they took all the books. We just saw, as a result of a hack, that Suno had to basically admit that it had scraped all of the music off of YouTube illegally. It just didn’t have permission, and I think YouTube feels a certain way about that and certainly the artists on YouTube feel a certain way about that.
Here’s Apple saying OpenAI also took its hardware designs and its manufacturing know-how. It didn’t have permission for that either, those are Apple’s secrets. OpenAI hired people and they concocted this scheme to take all of that stuff without permission.
Again, culturally, this just feels like part of the AI industry to me, that they think they can just take everything to build super intelligence as fast as they can. And once they get there, all will be forgiven. But the public doesn’t seem to like it. Certainly, artists and writers and musicians don’t seem to like it, and now Apple doesn’t like it.
It feels like this lawsuit is going to be a proxy for that as much as anything else. Can you take all this stuff without permission? I’m not sure OpenAI has the cultural capital to fight back. What are they going to say?
It’s really ironic that this whole industry is only possible because of the amount of data it’s consumed, whether aboveboard or not. And AI labs, as well as just tech companies in general, get so litigious when others take that information elsewhere. So this whole thing is pretty ironic.
The AI industry is really famously cliquish. It’s almost incestuous, it’s like you work with the same people here, then you depart and go elsewhere. Then that same company buys your start-up that you created and then you leave that start-up to go somewhere else and you get acqui-hired by your old friend that worked at this other place. A lot of industries are like that, but this industry specifically is so much like that. And so yeah, I think it’s a bit ironic on both counts.
People are going to leave Apple, and okay, they’re going to take some trade secrets. Was this incredibly egregious? Yes, some of these claims are crazy. But also, like you were mentioning, a lot of the reason that any of these companies are even successful in the first place is because of all the unauthorized taking they’ve done. It’s an interesting time to be watching all this play out.
All the AI companies get really mad when, I don’t know, Chinese AI companies distill their models. I’m just thinking about a jury and how Apple will play this case to a jury and be like, “You stole all the music, didn’t you? And then you also stole our manufacturing designs. And don’t you get mad when the Chinese companies distill ChatGPT?” 
In the course of your reporting, does it ever occur to the people in the AI industry that being mad about distillation is the exact same feeling that artists and musicians have about all of their work being put into the model in the first place?
I haven’t seen any of them even acknowledge that or at least even hint toward it one time, which is crazy. It just feels like there’s a disconnect there. They get so, so angry about distillation, they’re saying, “It’s against our terms of service!” They can’t even say it’s illegal, just against the terms of service. They write open letters to the government. They even come together with their mortal enemies and other AI labs to unite against distillation. So, it’s just interesting to me thatI’ve never seen that occur to them.
I know a lot of people are probably listening to this and that they’re mad at me, and mad at us, for not making the claim that Apple is just filing this lawsuit because it was behind in AI. It missed with Apple Intelligence, it took a long time to catch back up, it’s only shipping it now. It had to go to Google and distill Google’s Gemini models and put them in its new Private Cloud Compute system, and all the stuff that it needed to do. But that is shipping now.
Do you feel like the broader AI industry is just looking at Apple lashing out at being late? Because I have heard a lot of glimmers of that, that this is just Apple trying to slow down the biggest threat in consumer as it launches Apple Intelligence and tries to catch back up.
That could be definitely part of it. Everyone knows Apple has been famously incredibly behind in AI and it’s been a big topic of conversation and an embarrassment for the company for years. So, that could definitely be part of it.
But this lawsuit is not about someone “stealing trade secrets” for Siri. It’s about hardware, specifically “show and tell” of hardware, things like that. Hardware is something that Apple does amazingly and they are pretty much by all accounts the best at.
So, I think some people are thinking that. It’s a benefit for Apple if they’re able to kneecap a competitor from pulling ahead in any way. But the fact that this is a trade secrets lawsuit about hardware specifically I think has rolled back a few of those claims; it’s not like they’re trying to claim that OpenAI is stealing Siri AI’s secrets that it may not have many of.
[Laughs] They’re like, “Please take everything we know about Siri AI. That will truly kneecap you.” Apple can afford the distraction, you’ve mentioned this already in this conversation. Apple can just hire a bunch of lawyers and set them off to be as tenacious as they want. Maybe the rest of Apple won’t even notice that that’s happening, because they’re busy making the next iPhone.
Apple spent however many years and like $10 billion trying to make a car and it just didn’t work. It didn’t even occur to the rest of Apple that was happening. They just kept shipping phones and laptops and everything was just fine.
OpenAI is not that company. OpenAI might not even have enough executives to absorb the cost of another distraction. They keep leaving. Greg Brockman, who’s the president of OpenAI, seems to be running the entire company himself.
As you’ve been reporting on the story, has it occurred to OpenAI that they’re going to need more people to do more things? Because I look at that company and they just keep shedding all of their talent and pivoting, as you said, from one thing to the other and they’ve landed on “we need to compete with Anthropic.” But it doesn’t seem like they can afford distraction at this scale in any way, shape, or form.
They can’t. This is like the final battle. Actually, there are going to be a lot more battles, but this is a key battle in the longstanding AI arms race. This is the IPO year. Things are coming to a head. Investors are looking very closely at these companies in a way they haven’t before. They’re looking for them to turn a profit, or at least have a way to turn a profit in a way that they have not really paid too much attention to before, and it’s all coming down to the line. They cannot afford a distraction right now.
They are reshuffling, restructuring, changing executives around. When I’ve asked them about this, they will say, “Well, it’s all been one large plan that we’ve just been doing in little pieces. It’s not like we’ve pivoted a million times, we’ve always been going towards one thing and these are just different steps along that journey.” But it doesn’t always read that way to the general public.
In some ways, yes, Greg Brockman is taking control of product. That’s because Fidji Simo, the AGI chief, took leave because of her health and then she left permanently because of her health. So, it’s not all things that the company could control, but I do think there have been a lot of defections even from the rank-and-file staff. They’ve got to get more people. They’ve got to hire more, which will require even more money, and it’s not the time to get distracted by anything.
It’s worth noting that there’s some reporting saying OpenAI will delay its IPO. And as you and I are sitting here speaking, SpaceX’s stock price has dipped below its IPO number. These mega IPOs, they’re in some kind of danger. It might not be a good idea to do this, especially if you don’t have the revenue or, more importantly, the profits to back it up. Do you think there’s some risk that this lawsuit is the straw that pushes OpenAI to delay its IPO?
Absolutely. Reporting showed that Sam Altman was originally worried about filing its Form S-1 before Anthropic. Then it didn’t do that. Anthropic did it first and then — and this is me just speculating — it seems like after Anthropic won that part of the race, OpenAI backed off and said, “Okay, well, should we actually do this right now? We were trying really hard to win, but let’s look at the facts here.” That’s why it said, “Okay, it might be early next year, it might not be this year.”
That was before Apple’s lawsuit dropped. So now of course I’m sure OpenAI is thinking, “Okay, should we delay it even more? Especially because there’s no way we’re going to beat Anthropic to an IPO.” It seems like that might be a smart idea.
If you can put out a great hardware device and make some big splashy profitable entry into the consumer market, that’s a good story to tell in an IPO. But if you can’t do that because everything you do is going to end up in litigation or in messy discovery on the way to litigation, maybe that all just has to be set to the side.
That’s pretty much my last question here. I feel like my thesis on this show and on The Verge generally has been, “Okay, I understand how this is going to work for software development and I understand how this is going to work in enterprise, although even that’s pretty shaky still. But consumers don’t love this stuff.” That there are 900 million free ChatGPT users is not a reflection of anything other than, well, Google Search got really bad and this thing will tell you it loves you.
But it hasn’t turned into, “We should build more data centers.” It hasn’t turned into, “We culturally love the products of AI.” It’s turned into, “Get this slop out of my face and we’re going to boo you at graduation and we’re going to come to the town board meetings and say we don’t want data centers.”
There’s some huge gap there. Do you think OpenAI can close that gap? Because it has always been the company chasing the big consumer product vision, the big consumer market. If it can’t close the gap, it should just shut it down and compete with Anthropic for enterprise uses. I don’t know which one it’s going to be. Do you have a sense through all this reporting if OpenAI has realized how existential the consumer side of the debate is?
I think they know to some extent, but not the full extent. tThey will get at it in speeches, in research papers, in tweets. They have some PR lines where they will acknowledge that this is a thing, but I just don’t think they realize how deeply this crevice goes. The gap is so wide. I don’t see them being the only company to close it — if it’s ever going to be closed. People are extremely worried about so many things when it comes to AI and they’re very emotional about it.
It’s not just logic. I think if it was just a logical gap — some people logically think it’s not good, some people logically think it is good — I think they could probably close that. But when emotions come into play, no, I don’t think that they will be able to fully bridge that gap.
For me, when I became an AI reporter six years ago, none of my friends really knew or cared what I wrote about. That was fine. It was really niche, whatever. Starting four years ago, it would come up at the bar, at the club. I’ll be walking down the street, someone’s asking me about it, and they don’t know I’m an AI reporter. So, when they learn I’m an AI reporter, it happens even more. But just randomly, this is coming up for people and making them extremely emotional. So yeah, I just don’t think OpenAI is going to be the company to bridge that gap.
We’ll see what happens with the hardware of it all. A lot of people I’ve been seeing — TikTok creators, creators on other platforms — are trying to change the narrative here, saying, “Hey, don’t get left behind. Learn how to use this stuff.” And it’s something that can be valid, but the way that they’re framing it a lot of the time is more, “Oh, it’s such a high learning curve. You must learn how to use it before it leaves you behind.”
It’s not that high of a learning curve, it depends on how you’re using it, but you know what I mean. Sometimes it is, yeah, if you’re using Codex and doing all sorts of intense vibe coding, yes, of course it is. But if you’re just chatting with a chatbot, it’s really not a high learning curve.
I personally believe all that algorithmic social video content is an astroturfing campaign. That’s just me. That’s a conspiracy theory, we’re going to leave that aside. I do want to pitch you a video series called “Hayden in the Club,” where you just go to the club and talk to people about AI.
[Laughs] I would love to do that officially instead of just having it happen to me unofficially all the time.
It’s been a long time since I was in the club. That was not what the club was like when I was younger. Things have changed.
Hayden, this has been great. I have a strong suspicion you’re going to be back on this show talking about this lawsuit and OpenAI for the rest of this year. We’re going to have to have you back very soon.
Can’t wait. Thanks.
Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
Decoder with Nilay Patel
A podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems.

articles.title: Les meilleurs jeux narratifs de SF de la décennie arrivent sur PS5 en précommande
articles.text:
Citizen Sleeper 1 et 2 sont à la science-fiction ce que Disco Elysium est au communisme. Ça ne veut rien dire et pourtant, vous voyez parfaitement ce que ça veut dire. Les deux jeux narratifs, sortis respectivement en 2022 et 2025, sont développés par le petit studio Jump Over The Age, composé principalement de Gareth Damian Martin, et se sont vite imposés parmi les meilleurs jeux du genre sortis ces dernières années. La version physique réunissant les deux jeux débarque sur PS5 en précommande.
Précommandez Citizen Sleeper 1+2 Helion Collection au meilleur prix
Citizen Sleeper 1+2 Helion Collection est un bundle réunissant les deux jeux Citizen Sleeper dans une version physique sur PS5 avec les textes en français. La date de sortie est le 6 novembre 2026, et le jeu est déjà disponible en précommande.
Notez également que la version Switch 2 de Citizen Sleeper 2: Starward Vector est aussi en précommande en version physique, au prix de 49,99 €, et sortira à la même date du 6 novembre 2026.
C’est quoi, Citizen Sleeper ?
Citizen Sleeper et Citizen Sleeper 2: Starward Vector sont deux RPG narratifs de science-fiction qui vous plongent dans un univers futuriste où chaque décision compte. Dans le premier, vous incarnez un Sleeper, un être artificiel ayant échappé à son propriétaire et cherchant à survivre sur une station spatiale en ruines. Dans le second, vous prenez le contrôle d’un androïde amnésique traqué par une mystérieuse organisation, et devez accepter des contrats pour survivre avec votre équipage. Les deux jeux possèdent des histoires indépendantes l’une de l’autre.
Visuellement, Citizen Sleeper et sa suite se démarquent par une direction artistique particulièrement soignée, portée par les illustrations de Guillaume Singelin, l’artiste français, connu notamment pour ses travaux dans la bande dessinée (PTSD, Frontier et Shin Zéro). L’univers de science-fiction possède un style coloré, expressif et immédiatement reconnaissable. Les personnages comme les environnements bénéficient d’un véritable travail d’illustration, qui donne aux deux jeux une identité visuelle forte, accompagnée d’une musique évocatrice et magnifique.
L’autre force de Citizen Sleeper, c’est son ambiance mélancolique et immersive, à base d’amitié et de solidarité dans un futur où les humains et les machines tentent de trouver leur place. L’écriture, les personnages et les choix proposés donnent envie de rester sur la station ou de poursuivre son voyage, simplement pour découvrir ce qui arrivera ensuite. Deux expériences narratives singulières qui misent sur l’atmosphère.
