articles.title: AMD Ryzen 7 7700X3D Review
articles.text:
AMD is not finished with Zen 4 just yet. The Ryzen 7 7700X3D is the company's latest 3D V-Cache-enabled processor, arriving four years after the first Zen 4 desktop CPUs and three years after the launch of the now-legendary 7800X3D.
The 7700X3D is essentially a slightly downclocked version of that processor. It launched at $329, representing a healthy 27% discount compared with the 7800X3D's original MSRP. However, with the 7800X3D commonly available for less than $400, the value proposition was not immediately clear. Then, just days after release, Newegg discounted the 7700X3D to $279, making this new model considerably more interesting.
You might think it is odd that AMD is releasing a "new" Zen 4-based processor in 2026, but by now, you should be used to this. We fully expect the company will still be releasing "new" binned variants in 2030, and we are not convinced we won't see another new AM4 processor later this year.
As for the specifications, the base clock has dropped from 4.2 GHz on the 7800X3D to 4.0 GHz, a 5% reduction, while the boost clock has fallen from 5.0 GHz to 4.5 GHz, a larger 10% reduction. Everything else remains the same: 96 MB of L3 cache, a 120W TDP rating, eight cores, and 16 threads.
| Ryzen 7 7700X3D | Ryzen 7 7800X3D | Ryzen 7 9800X3D | Ryzen 7 9850X3D | |
| Price MSRP (USD) | $330 | $450 | $480 | $500 | 
| Release Date | Jul 16, 2026 | Apr 6, 2023 | Nov 7, 2024 | Jan 29, 2025 | 
| Cores / Threads | 8c / 16t | |||
| Base Clock | 4.0 GHz | 4.2 GHz | 4.7 GHz | |
| Boost Clock | 4.5 GHz | 5.0 GHz | 5.2 GHz | 5.6 GHz | 
| L3 Cache (Total) | 96 MB | |||
| Box Cooler | N/A | |||
| Chiplets | 1 × CCD, 1 × I/O Die | |||
| Core Configuration | 1 × 8 | |||
| TDP | 120 W | |||
The key question, then, is how much performance has been sacrificed and whether the 7700X3D makes sense at its $329 MSRP or its discounted $279 price. Let's get into the benchmark data.
Test System Specs
| CPU / Platform | AMD Ryzen 9000 / Ryzen 7000 MSI MAG X870E Tomahawk Max (BIOS 7E59v5A32) G.Skill Trident Z5 RGB 32GB DDR5-6000 CL30-38-38-96 AMD Ryzen 5000 MSI MPG X570S Carbon MAX WiFi (BIOS 7D52v1D1) G.Skill Trident Z Neo RGB 32GB DDR4-3600 CL14-15-15-35 Intel Core Ultra Asus ROG Maximus Z890 Hero (BIOS 2201) G.Skill Trident Z5 CK 32GB DDR5-8200 CL40-52-52-131 CUDIMM | 
| Graphics Card | Asus ROG Astral RTX 5090 OC Edition | 
| Power Supply | Kolink Regulator Gold ATX 3.0 1200W | 
| Storage | TeamGroup T-Force Cardea A440 M.2 PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSD 4TB | 
| Operating System | Windows 11 25H2 | 
| Display Driver | Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver 610.74 WHQL | 
Operating Behavior
Before we get into the blue bar graphs, here is a quick side-by-side comparison with the 7800X3D while running an all-core workload in Cinebench 2026. Under full load, the 7800X3D clocked at 4.85 GHz, while the 7700X3D reached 4.55 GHz, making the 7800X3D 7% faster in this test.
Looking at the maximum recorded frequency during the single-core test, the 7800X3D clocked at 5.05 GHz, whereas the 7700X3D reached 4.55 GHz, making the original model 11% faster.
The 7% increase in clock speed during the all-core workload raised power consumption by 7%, from 85W to 91W. This also increased the peak core operating temperature from 75°C to 80°C. Everything is therefore behaving as advertised: the 7700X3D is simply a downclocked 7800X3D.
Gaming Benchmarks
Rainbow Six Siege X
Starting with Rainbow Six Siege X using the Medium quality settings, we see that the 7700X3D is 8% slower than the 7800X3D. This also made it slower than the 7600X3D, delivering performance comparable to the 7500X3D. Compared with the 270K Plus, it was 6% faster, while it outperformed the 250K Plus by 21%.
Using the Ultra+ preset increased the GPU bottleneck, allowing the 7700X3D to roughly match the 7600X3D. It was just 3% slower than the 7800X3D, though it trailed the 9800X3D by 10% for those wondering. At these higher visual settings, it remained 6% faster than the 270K Plus and 24% faster than the 250K Plus, while also delivering a 27% improvement over the older 5800X3D.
Marvel Rivals
Next, we have Marvel Rivals, tested using the built-in benchmark. At 1080p with the Medium preset, the 7700X3D averaged 216 fps, with 1% lows of 165 fps. This placed it among Intel's latest processors, sitting just ahead of the Core Ultra 5 250K Plus and narrowly behind the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus.
Although it was roughly 10% slower than the 7800X3D on average, it maintained a comfortable lead over the six-core 7600X3D and outperformed the older 5800X3D by more than 20%.
Increasing the visual settings to 1080p Ultra+ narrowed the margins considerably as the GPU took on more of the workload. The 7700X3D averaged 149 fps, with a stable 1% low of 116 fps, making it just 4% slower than the 7800X3D.
Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered
Next is Horizon Zero Dawn Remastered, again tested using the built-in benchmark. At 1080p Medium, the Ryzen 7 7700X3D delivered a strong result, averaging 232 fps with 1% lows of 150 fps. This placed it comfortably ahead of the six-core 7600X3D and Intel's 270K Plus.
It trailed the 7800X3D by just 4%, while maintaining an impressive 19% lead over the older 5800X3D.
Increasing the visual settings with the Very High preset created a larger GPU bottleneck, narrowing the performance gap. Here, the 7700X3D averaged 198 fps, with a stable 1% low of 121 fps. That placed it within reach of the 7800X3D's 210 fps result while extending its lead over the mid-range alternatives.
Baldur's Gate 3
In the heavily CPU-bound city districts of Baldur's Gate 3, the 7700X3D thrives, much like the other 3D V-Cache-enabled processors. At 1080p Medium, it averaged 197 fps, allowing it to dominate Intel's offerings and beat the 270K Plus by an impressive 35%.
Moving to the Ultra preset, the 7700X3D maintained an exceptionally smooth 163 fps average. This was essentially identical to the 7600X3D, while placing it comfortably ahead of the 5800X3D and once again well ahead of the Arrow Lake processors.
Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty
Next is Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty, tested in-game rather than with the built-in benchmark. Using the Medium preset, the 7700X3D delivered a very strong result, averaging 203 fps with 1% lows of 148 fps.
This placed it comfortably ahead of the six-core 7600X3D and roughly 7% behind the 7800X3D. It also outperformed the Intel competition, establishing a noticeable lead over both the 270K Plus and 250K Plus while beating the older 5800X3D by 13%.
Switching to the Ray Tracing: Ultra preset dramatically increased the GPU load, compressing the results across the entire field. Under these heavily GPU-limited conditions, the 7700X3D matched the real-world gaming performance of the flagship 9800X3D. Keep in mind that we are using an RTX 5090 at 1080p, so for those chasing maximum visual quality, the CPU becomes considerably less important.
Battlefield 6
Moving on to Battlefield 6, we will again start with the Medium preset data. Here, the 270K Plus put up a strong fight, splitting the difference between the 7800X3D and 7700X3D. The 7700X3D averaged 181 fps, placing it effectively on par with the 7600X3D.
With the Overkill preset enabled, we found similar results, though the slightly more GPU-limited test conditions allowed the 7700X3D to close the gap to the 7800X3D. It averaged 191 fps, making it just 4% slower than the 7800X3D.
Space Marine 2
In Space Marine 2, the demanding swarm simulation tests both core count and cache efficiency. Using the Medium preset, the 7700X3D hit a solid sweet spot, averaging 121 fps with 1% lows of 103 fps. This allowed it to comfortably outperform the 270K Plus while maintaining a steady lead over the six-core 7600X3D. The 7800X3D pulled ahead by around 10%, demonstrating the benefit of its higher clock speeds in CPU-limited scenarios.
Shifting to the Ultra quality preset compressed the results as the GPU became the primary performance-limiting component. Even so, the 7700X3D performed well, averaging 116 fps and reducing its deficit against the 7800X3D to a negligible margin.
The Last of Us Part II
Next, we have The Last of Us Part II Remastered. Using the Medium preset, the 7700X3D delivered a highly playable 180 fps average. Interestingly, Intel's Arrow Lake processors performed particularly well in this title, with the 250K Plus beating most of the X3D lineup. The 7700X3D performed virtually identically to the 7800X3D and 7600X3D, suggesting that cache scaling reaches its limit fairly early here.
Stepping up to the Very High preset reinforced this behavior. The 7700X3D averaged 173 fps, perfectly matching the 7600X3D and trailing the 7800X3D by just a single frame.
Spider-Man 2
Next is Spider-Man 2. Testing with the Medium preset allowed the 7700X3D to stretch its legs, averaging 217 fps. This placed it just behind the 7600X3D and slightly ahead of the 270K Plus.
The Ultimate Ray Tracing data produced an interesting result, with Intel's processors handling the engine's high-overhead settings particularly well. This pushed the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus to the top of the chart with 109 fps. Meanwhile, the 7700X3D averaged 89 fps, placing it roughly in the middle of the X3D lineup.
Mafia: The Old Country
Moving on to Mafia: The Old Country, the 7700X3D averaged 130 fps using the Medium preset. Intel's Arrow Lake architecture held a slight advantage in this title, with the 250K Plus and 270K Plus establishing a minor lead over the 7700X3D. The new Ryzen processor performed almost identically to the 7600X3D, though it still maintained a substantial 20% advantage over the 5800X3D.
Jumping to the Epic preset introduced a significant GPU bottleneck, causing virtually all of the modern processors to deliver similar results. The 7700X3D averaged 101 fps, matching the 270K Plus and finishing just one frame behind the 7800X3D.
Assetto Corsa Competizione
Switching gears to the racing simulator Assetto Corsa Competizione, the large pool of 3D V-Cache once again provided a substantial performance advantage. Using the Medium preset, the 7700X3D averaged 264 fps, outperforming Intel's 270K Plus by an impressive 25% while trailing the 7800X3D by less than 10%.
With the Epic preset enabled, the story remained much the same. The 7700X3D delivered an excellent 216 fps average, keeping it tightly grouped with the other Zen 4 X3D processors while leaving Intel's lineup well behind.
Borderlands 4
Borderlands 4 serves as a textbook example of a heavily GPU-limited game. Even at 1080p using an RTX 5090 and the Medium preset, the chart is remarkably flat. The 7700X3D averaged 158 fps, matching the 7600X3D and finishing just 2 fps behind the 7800X3D.
This behavior became even more pronounced with the Badass preset, producing almost entirely GPU-bound results. The 7700X3D averaged 102 fps, matching the 9800X3D, 7800X3D, and 7600X3D frame for frame.
Arc Raiders
Finally, we have Arc Raiders. Using the Medium preset, the 7700X3D averaged 234 fps, giving it a slight advantage over the 270K Plus, while the 7800X3D maintained a healthy 10% lead.
Increasing the visual settings with the Epic preset naturally tightened the margins, but the 7700X3D remained very strong, averaging 220 fps. This again made it 10% slower than the 7800X3D, though it remained faster than the 270K Plus.
13 Game Average
Across the 13 games tested, the 7700X3D was 7% slower than the 7800X3D on average and 15% slower than the 9800X3D. In turn, it was just 3% faster than the 7600X3D and 6% faster than the 270K Plus.
Those margins narrowed under the more GPU-limited maximum-quality test conditions, where the 7700X3D trailed the 7800X3D by just 4% and outperformed the 270K Plus by a mere 3%.
Cost per Frame
Using the average results from the Medium quality testing, here is a look at cost per frame based solely on the current retail price of each processor.
There are a few interesting takeaways. First, if you could simply buy the CPU and start gaming, the Core Ultra 5 250K Plus would be the best-value option. It costs almost 30% less per frame than the 7700X3D while also offering considerably stronger productivity performance.
Platform Cost: Motherboard and Memory
Now here's how each CPU compares in terms of value when the cost of a full platform upgrade is included. For the AM5 and Arrow Lake processors, we have factored in a $170 X870 or Z890 motherboard and 16GB of DDR5 memory, bringing the combined motherboard and memory cost to $230. The 5800X3D can be paired with a $100 B550 motherboard and 16GB of DDR4 memory for a combined cost of $130.
Adding everything together, the 7700X3D costs 8% more per frame than the 250K Plus while offering similar value to the 7500X3D and 270K Plus. When factoring in the cost of a decent motherboard and 16GB of DDR5 memory, the 7700X3D is a strong-value gaming CPU at $330, though that depends on how cheaply you can find the 7800X3D.
We also see that the 5800X3D makes more sense once the lower cost of an AM4 platform is taken into account. A decent B550 motherboard can still be purchased for $100, while 16GB of DDR4 brings the combined motherboard and memory cost to $130. This takes the total package price to $580, making the 5800X3D an even better value per frame than the 250K Plus.
That said, if we were investing in a platform with no meaningful upgrade path, we would choose the 250K Plus package over the 5800X3D. It not only delivers better gaming performance but also offers considerably stronger productivity performance.
A Good CPU at $329, a Great One at $279
The "new" Ryzen 7 7700X3D is between 4% and 7% slower than the 7800X3D, depending on the game and test conditions. Given that it clocks up to 10% lower in core-heavy workloads, a performance reduction of around 7% in CPU-limited gaming scenarios is a reasonable expectation.
The lower clock speeds also reduced power consumption slightly, and because AMD has used the same thermal interface, we recorded a 5°C reduction in peak operating temperature.
Based on those results, the 7700X3D is worth considering whenever it costs at least 10% less than the 7800X3D. At its $329 MSRP, the value proposition depends heavily on the price of the older model. With the 7800X3D currently selling for around $389, the 7700X3D is about 15% cheaper, which is enough to make it a reasonable alternative, though hardly an exciting one.
However, just a few days after launch, Newegg discounted the 7700X3D to $279 via a promo code. At that price, the verdict changes considerably. It is around 28% cheaper than the 7800X3D while delivering gaming performance that is typically only 4% to 7% lower. That makes the 7700X3D an excellent-value gaming processor and a much easier recommendation.
Of course, it has been less than a week since launch, so we cannot know whether this discount is a sign of things to come or simply a limited-time promotion from a single retailer. AMD has, on occasion, reduced pricing fairly quickly. For example, the Radeon 9070 GRE has already been spotted for $500, a $50 discount just one month after release.
Our CPU cost-per-frame charts were calculated using the $329 MSRP, but at $279, the 7700X3D would perform substantially better in those comparisons.
The broader problem remains DDR5 pricing. With memory costs still painfully high, it is difficult to get excited about building a new platform around a CPU based on a three-year-old product. Still, for anyone already planning an AM5 gaming build, the 7700X3D makes sense at $329 and becomes a standout option at $279.
So that is the Ryzen 7 7700X3D. Let us know what you think about this latest release from AMD, and we will be sure to read your comments.

articles.title: From Star Wars to King Arthur: 10 European startups with names drawn from fiction, folklore and religion | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Choosing a startup name is difficult. It needs to be memorable, available as a domain and sufficiently distinctive to survive an investor’s overflowing inbox – so its no surprise to see references to famous fiction such as Dune, Start Wars and even The Matrix.
The obvious and most famous example is Palantir, named after the all-seeing stones in J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings – an interesting choice for a company built around making sense of vast amounts of data.
We at EU-Startups, have seen an increasing startup landscape populated by gods, guardians, legendary weapons, digital worlds, and at least one desert planet crawling with enormous sandworms.
Here are 10 European startups whose names have escaped from fiction, folklore and mythology – in alphabetical order.
Ariadne Maps (Garching, Germany) – Greek Mythology
Founded in 2019 by Georgios Pipelidis and Nikos Tsiamitros, Ariadne Maps develops location analytics technology for indoor and outdoor spaces.
Based in Garching, near Munich, the startup helps retailers, transport operators and venue managers understand how visitors move through physical environments without requiring dedicated apps or tracking hardware to be installed on users’ phones.
Its name is directly inspired by Ariadne from Greek mythology. After Theseus entered the labyrinth to kill the Minotaur, Ariadne gave him a thread that allowed him to retrace his route and escape rather than wandering indefinitely through the maze. The company has described its own location intelligence as a comparable guiding thread through complex physical spaces.
It may be one of the neatest examples in this list: a mapping company named after the woman who solved antiquity’s most notorious navigation problem.
Arondite (London, UK) – King Arthur
Founded in 2023, Arondite is building software and AI systems for defence and national security organisations. The London-based startup raised more than €10.5 million in Seed funding in May 2025, following an earlier €1.9 million pre-Seed investment involving Concept Ventures and Creator Fund.
Its co-founder and CEO, Will Blyth, previously served in the British Army and worked at Palantir and Helsing, while co-founder and CTO Rob Underhill brought experience from BAE Systems and cybersecurity company Garrison.
Arondite has not publicly confirmed a medieval naming story, but its spelling is extremely close to Arondight, the sword traditionally associated with Sir Lancelot. The weapon is better known from later Arthurian tradition and modern popular culture.
A legendary sword belonging to one of the Knights of the Round Table is an almost suspiciously appropriate reference for a DefenceTech startup.
Arrakis (London, UK) – Dune
Arrakis is emerging from stealth after raising €33 million in just over three months. The company was founded by former Accel investor Rafael Quintanilla alongside a team with experience at Palantir, Revolut, Delivery Hero, Datadog and ASML.
Arrakis develops AI agents for mission-critical industrial operations, targeting sectors including energy, aerospace, logistics and manufacturing.
The name is an unmistakable nod to Arrakis, the desert planet at the heart of Frank Herbert’s Dune. Also known as Dune, the planet is the only natural source of spice, the substance upon which the fictional universe’s economy, politics and interstellar travel depend.
For a company entering the high-stakes world of industrial infrastructure, it is a suitably dramatic choice.
The spice must flow, and apparently so must the enterprise workflow.
Babbel (Berlin, Germany) – The Bible
Founded in Berlin in 2007 by Thomas Holl, Markus Witte, Lorenz Heine and Toine Diepstraten, Babbel is one of Europe’s best-known language-learning companies.
Babbel offers a subscription-based platform offering structured lessons, podcasts, vocabulary practice and interactive speaking exercises. The company says it has sold more than 25 million subscriptions and now provides around 60,000 lessons across 14 languages.
EU-Startups included Babbel in its June 2020 overview of European language-learning apps. Its name, however, reaches considerably further back than the app economy.
Babbel takes its name from the Tower of Babel, adding an extra “b” to create its distinctive spelling. In the Book of Genesis, God gives the tower’s builders different languages, leaving them unable to understand one another and causing them to abandon the project and scatter.
The added letter also evokes “babble”, neatly combining mythology, conversation and the awkward early stages of learning a language.
Bending Spoons (Milan, Italy) – The Matrix
Founded in 2013 by Luca Ferrari, Francesco Patarnello, Matteo Danieli, Luca Querella and Tomasz Greber, Bending Spoons is a Milan-based technology company that develops and acquires digital products. Its portfolio has included well-known platforms such as Evernote, Meetup, Remini, WeTransfer and Vimeo.
EU-Startups has followed the company’s rapid expansion, including its raise of more than €500 million in 2025 and its subsequent filing for a Nasdaq IPO in June 2026.
The company has confirmed that its unusual name comes from The Matrix, specifically the scene in which a child appears to bend a spoon using only his mind. The moment leads to the film’s memorable lesson that the spoon itself is not really bending; Neo must instead recognise that the rules governing his surroundings are not as fixed as they appear.
It is a suitably mind-bending reference for a company known for reshaping established digital products. The only disappointment is that its growing portfolio is managed through software and corporate strategy rather than telekinesis.
Daedalus (Karlsruhe, Germany) – Greek Mythology
Karlsruhe-based Daedalus is applying AI, robotics and software to precision manufacturing. Founded in 2019 by Jonas Schneider, a former OpenAI technical lead, the startup operates automated factories capable of producing complex components for industrial customers.
Daedalus is one of Greek mythology’s great engineers. In Greek legend, he was an exceptionally skilled inventor, architect and craftsman, best known for designing the labyrinth that imprisoned the Minotaur. He also built the wings used by himself and his son Icarus in their attempted escape from Crete.
For a startup building advanced manufacturing systems, Daedalus is close to perfect. The only slightly awkward detail is that his most famous aviation project had a famously poor safety record. Perhaps the company should keep its robots away from the sun.
Heimdall Power (Oslo, Norway) – Norse Mythology
Founded in 2016, Heimdall Power develops technology that helps electricity-grid operators monitor power lines and make better use of existing infrastructure. Its hardware sensors, nicknamed Neurons or “Magic Balls”, gather real-time information about factors such as line temperature, weather conditions and available transmission capacity.
The Oslo-based company raised €22.9 million in Series B funding in July 2024. The round was co-led by ORLEN, NRP Zero and the Steinsvik Family Office, with participation from existing investors including Investinor, Eviny, Hafslund, Lyse and Sarsia.
Heimdall is the watchman of the gods in Norse mythology, stationed at the entrance to Asgard and gifted with extraordinary sight and hearing. The company has explicitly drawn a comparison between the mythological guardian and Heimdall Power’s role in watching over electricity infrastructure.
The original Heimdall guarded the rainbow bridge Bifröst. His technological namesake watches high-voltage power lines. The scenery may be less colourful, but the monitoring brief remains broadly similar.
Mimir (Oslo, Norway) – Norse Mythology
Mimir uses AI to automate customer support and operational tasks for e-commerce companies. Founded in 2024 by Jørgen Vartdal Halse, Jens Kristoffersen and Øyvind Monsen, the startup raised €518.3k in pre-Seed funding in June 2026.
The round was led by Sondo, with participation from angel investors connected to companies including VILLOID, Kry, Enode and Whitson. Mimir’s platform is intended to help online retailers handle repetitive enquiries and workflows while drawing on information scattered across their existing systems.
While the company has not officially made the connection, Mímir is an unmistakable figure from Norse mythology. Renowned for his wisdom, memory and counsel, he guarded a well whose waters offered knowledge. Odin famously sacrificed an eye for the opportunity to drink from it.
An all-knowing adviser is a natural mascot for an AI platform expected to answer questions quickly and accurately. Thankfully, modern e-commerce teams can access Mimir’s knowledge without surrendering an eye every time a customer asks where their parcel is.
Naboo (Paris, France) – Star Wars
Founded in 2022 by Maxime Eduardo, Antoine Servant, Lucien Bredin and Jean-Louis Villeminot, Naboo provides a platform through which companies can search for, book and manage corporate events.
The Paris-based startup has raised €86.2 million across rounds of €7.5 million, €20 million and €58.7 million, with investors including Lightspeed Venture Partners, Notion Capital, ISAI, Ternel and Kima Ventures.
Its name comes from the planet Naboo in Star Wars, the picturesque homeworld associated with Queen Amidala, grand palaces, rolling green countryside and the occasional trade blockade.
The company has connected that natural setting with its emphasis on organising more local events and reducing unnecessary international travel. It is a surprisingly thoughtful explanation for a name that might otherwise sound like someone booked the company retreat while binge-watching the prequel trilogy.
No word yet on whether lightsaber workshops are available as a team-building activity.
Valarian (London, UK) – Game of Thrones
Valarian develops AI infrastructure designed to help organisations deploy and manage AI. The company was co-founded by Max Buchan and Josh McLaughlin, who previously spent more than a decade at Palantir – another technology company with a famously fantasy-inspired name.
Valarian has not publicly confirmed the origin of its name, but the apparent reference is difficult to miss. Its spelling closely resembles Valyrian, the language, civilisation and legendary steel associated with Valyria in George R. R. Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire and its television adaptation, Game of Thrones.
The theory is strengthened by McLaughlin’s Palantir background, making another fantasy-adjacent company name feel potentially deliberate.
Either way, a name evoking an advanced but mysterious lost civilisation is suitably dramatic for an AI company – although Valarian will presumably be hoping to avoid Valyria’s rather explosive ending.
From myth to reality
From Naboo’s green plains to the deserts of Arrakis, these names do more than make companies easier to remember. They provide a miniature origin story, signalling what a startup wants to represent before anyone has read its pitch deck.
Ariadne offers guidance, Heimdall keeps watch, Mimir supplies knowledge and Daedalus builds.
Some connections are confirmed, others remain educated guesses, but all demonstrate the same useful lesson: when the available domain names are disappearing, several thousand years of stories can be a very productive place to look.

articles.title: Upbound Group Says Data Breach Led to $13 Million in Fraudulent Contract Losses
articles.text:
Texas-based consumer finance company Upbound Group, Inc. says recent cybersecurity incidents led to a data breach that resulted in millions of dollars in fraudulent contract losses.
Upbound offers lease-to-own and flexible payment solutions through brands like Rent-A-Center, Acima, and Brigit.
In a filing with the SEC, the company said non-sensitive customer information and other documents were recently obtained by hackers.
Upbound believes “the information was subsequently used to facilitate fraudulent lease-to-own agreements, contributing to elevated fraudulent contract losses of approximately $13 million in the Company’s Acima segment during the second quarter of 2026.”
The company has notified law enforcement and hired external cybersecurity experts to help boost the security of its systems.
Upbound’s investigation is ongoing, but at the time of the SEC disclosure it believes the incidents are not material.
It’s unclear who is behind the attacks on Upbound. No known cybercrime group appears to have listed the company on its leak website.
A longtime cybersecurity executive recently launched The Hacker in a Hoodie (HIH) Index, a tracker for material breaches that can be useful to cybersecurity professionals, journalists, policymakers, and others.

articles.title: MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view
articles.text:
MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view
New breakthrough could help create smaller and more durable sensors for vehicles, drones, and industrial sites.
- Date:
- July 22, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- MIT engineers have found a way to give chip-based lidar a wider, clearer view without relying on moving parts. Their design uses differently shaped antennas that can sit close together without scrambling one another’s signals. In tests, the system sharply reduced interference while steering a single precise beam across a broad field of view.
- Share:
Lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment. This allows autonomous vehicles to detect objects in their path and respond quickly. However, conventional lidar sensors are often large and costly, and many rely on moving components that can wear out over time. These limitations make the systems difficult to use in a wider range of settings.
MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts. Their advance centers on a new silicon-photonics chip, a type of semiconductor device that controls light instead of electrical signals.
Existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view. As a result, they struggle to scan areas located toward the edges of a scene. Previous attempts to expand this viewing range have often introduced extra noise and reduced measurement accuracy.
The MIT team addressed those problems by creating an array of integrated antennas that greatly limits unwanted crosstalk, which occurs when neighboring antennas interfere with one another. The design allows the chip to scan across a broader field of view while producing less noise than other silicon-photonics-based methods.
A Smaller Lidar System With a Wider View
The advance could support the development of more capable lidar sensors for challenging uses, including autonomous vehicle navigation, aerial mapping, and the monitoring of construction sites.
"The functionality we demonstrated in this work solves a fundamental problem for integrated optical-phased-array technology, enabling future lidar sensors that can achieve significantly higher performance than we could demonstrate previously," says Jelena Notaros, the Robert J. Shillman Career Development Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) at MIT, a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and senior author of a paper on this innovation.
The study also includes lead author and EECS graduate student Henry Crawford-Eng, along with EECS graduate students Andres Garcia Coleto, Benjamin M. Mazur, Daniel M. DeSantis, and Tal Sneh. The findings were published recently in Nature Communications.
How Lidar Maps Its Surroundings
Many traditional lidar systems use a large rotating unit to direct light pulses across a scene. When the light strikes nearby objects, it reflects back toward the sensor. The returning signals provide the information needed to reconstruct a detailed map of the environment.
Silicon-photonics-based lidar works differently. Rather than rotating a mechanical device, it scans a beam of light electronically in several directions with a system known as an integrated optical phased array (OPA).
At the heart of an OPA is a group of integrated antennas. Each antenna contains tiny, regularly spaced variations along its length. These features, known as corrugations, cause light from an input source to scatter upward and out of the photonic chip.
Researchers can control the direction of the outgoing beam by changing the phase of the light sent to each antenna. Adjusting these phases changes the angle at which the array releases light, making it possible to steer the beam without moving any physical components.
The Antenna Spacing Problem
Placing the antennas close together creates a serious obstacle. Neighboring antennas can couple with one another, scrambling the light they produce. Engineers have traditionally prevented this interference by increasing the distance between antennas, but wider spacing creates a different set of problems.
When antennas are too far apart, the array produces several copies of the same beam at different angles. The primary beam can only be moved a limited distance before it becomes difficult to distinguish from these additional copies.
"This limits our field of view, so the autonomous vehicle now only knows what is in front of it for a certain angular range," Garcia Coleto explains.
The unwanted beam copies, called grating lobes, can confuse the sensor and generate false detections. They also consume energy that could otherwise be directed into the main beam.
To overcome this tradeoff, the MIT researchers developed antennas with reduced crosstalk that can be positioned close together without strongly coupling.
Three Antenna Shapes Reduce Interference
In a conventional OPA, every antenna has an identical structure and uses the same pattern of corrugations. When these matching antennas are placed close together, they interact very strongly.
The MIT team instead created a repeating set of three antennas with distinct shapes. They changed the width of the antennas as well as the size and placement of the corrugations. Because the antennas have different geometries, each one also has a different propagation coefficient, which describes how light moves through the structure.
"Because the antennas have very different propagation coefficients, when we put them close together, essentially each antenna doesn't 'see' the antenna next to it. Therefore, it won't couple with its neighbor," Garcia Coleto says.
Making Different Antennas Behave the Same Way
Reducing the coupling was only part of the challenge. Although the antennas needed different propagation coefficients, they still had to release light in the same consistent manner.
The team designed the antennas around three essential requirements.
Each antenna had to emit the same amount of light. Every antenna also needed to release its beam at the same angle when receiving the same wavelength. Finally, the angle of emission had to change evenly across the entire array as the beam was steered.
"We have this challenge where we require the antennas to have different geometries to reduce the crosstalk, but we need to simultaneously design the antennas to have the same emission characteristics. While it is possible to engineer this, it is extremely difficult because, typically, when antennas are designed with different geometries, they tend to behave differently," Crawford-Eng says.
The researchers began by developing the basic electromagnetic theory describing how radiative modes couple. They then used this theoretical framework to guide the design and computer simulation of the antennas.
Based on those calculations, the team manufactured an OPA containing the reduced-crosstalk antennas. The antennas were placed much closer together than those in a conventional system, and the completed device was then tested experimentally.
Interference Falls From About 100 Percent to 1 Percent
Under the conditions of the experiment, a typical OPA would have produced coupling of approximately 100 percent. The MIT design lowered that coupling to about 1 percent while still generating one clean and precise beam.
The system accurately steered the beam across a broad field of view without producing any grating lobes. This combination of wide scanning, low interference, and strong beam quality addresses one of the central obstacles facing integrated lidar technology.
The researchers now plan to refine the method so the system can cover an even broader viewing range. They are also studying another possible approach to wide field-of-view performance that emerged while they were developing the underlying theory.
"This work addresses a longstanding challenge in integrated optical phased arrays: simultaneously achieving both a wide field of view, which requires dense antenna spacing, and high beam quality, which requires low crosstalk between neighboring antennas. The authors solve this problem with an elegant antenna design. Their innovation is an important step forward for chip-scale, solid-state beam-steering technology," says Joyce Poon, professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Toronto and director of the Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics, who was not involved with this work.
The Semiconductor Research Corporation, the National Science Foundation, an MIT MathWorks Fellowship, the U.S. Department of War, and the MIT Rolf G. Locher Endowed Fellowship supported the research, in part.
Some of the work was carried out using MIT.nano facilities.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Adam Zewe. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Henry Crawford-Eng, Andres Garcia Coleto, Benjamin M. Mazur, Daniel M. DeSantis, Tal Sneh, Jelena Notaros. Reduced-crosstalk antennas for grating-lobe-free and wide-field-of-view integrated optical phased arrays. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-71832-y
Cite This Page:

articles.title: Lookout launches tool to expose vulnerable code hidden inside mobile apps - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Lookout launches tool to expose vulnerable code hidden inside mobile apps
Mobile security company Lookout Inc. today launched the Lookout Mobile Software Exposure Center, a tool that lets organizations continuously identify, assess and prioritize the software exposure risk buried inside the mobile apps running on their employees’ devices.
The capability is delivered as a core part of the company’s Lookout Mobile Endpoint Security platform, using the same console and agent that customers already run across their mobile fleets.
Lookout argues that most enterprise security tools were built for desktop and cloud environments and largely overlook mobile applications, which are assembled from a patchwork of open-source libraries, embedded software development kits and third-party application programming interfaces. That leaves an exposure gap that mobile device management platforms cannot inspect, the company said.
The timing is tied to the arrival of frontier artificial intelligence models such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5, which Lookout says have compressed the work of finding exploitable bugs from months of specialized research into hours. The company points to its own Threat Labs discovery in March of DarkSword, a full-chain iOS exploitation framework that targeted vulnerabilities hidden inside legitimate apps, as evidence that automated attacks on unexamined code have already arrived.
The Mobile Software Exposure Center inspects Android and iOS apps at the binary level, without ever seeing their source code. For each one it fingerprints the compiled code and builds a software bill of materials. The tool then checks every component against Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures databases and third-party threat intelligence feeds. Outdated libraries and vulnerable SDKs get flagged for the security team.
Security teams can query their fleet to find which apps contain a given component. The tool also scores applications for abandonment and patching hygiene and can push policies into existing device management and unified endpoint management workflows to restrict high-risk apps automatically.
“In a frontier AI model world, the threat landscape has changed so fundamentally that traditional malware is akin to a toy in a sandbox,” Chief Executive Jim Dolce said in the announcement. “By unpacking application binaries at machine speed, we are giving enterprises the required control points to surface hidden vulnerabilities and neutralize automated, mobile AI-driven threats before they can hit the enterprise.”
Lookout said the tool builds on more than 15 years of mobile threat work and telemetry from more than 235 million devices and 400 million applications. Existing customers get it natively, with no new agent to deploy.
The launch follows Lookout’s April release of its AI Visibility and Governance product, which focused on discovering and controlling AI use on mobile devices. Where that tool addressed outbound AI activity, the Mobile Software Exposure Center targets the inbound software supply chain running on the device.

articles.title: Xiaomi S40 vale a pena? Confira uma análise completa do robô aspirador
articles.text:
Robôs aspiradores são dispositivos quase indispensáveis atualmente, já que eles são capazes de facilitar (e muito) a faxina de casa. Modelos mais avançados vão além de uma simples aspiração, contando com mapeamento de ambiente que otimiza a limpeza e garante que todos os cantos dos cômodos sejam aspirados.
Um dispositivo de destaque no mercado atualmente é o Xiaomi S40. O Olhar Digital preparou uma análise completa do robô aspirador com mapeamento de ambiente; confira abaixo e saiba se ele é o modelo ideal para a sua casa:
Xiaomi S40: design e construção
O Xiaomi S40 tem um design que não se distancia muito de robôs aspiradores convencionais, com um corpo de plástico fosco. Na parte superior está posicionada uma pequena torre que abriga os sensores a laser, além de dois botões: um para ligar, e o outro para fazer o aparelho retornar à base.
Ele é baixo o suficiente para entrar debaixo de boa parte dos sofás e camas, mas a presença da torre do laser exige um pouco de atenção caso os móveis da sua casa sejam muito baixos. O reservatório de poeira e o de água ficam armazenados na parte interna do dispositivo e precisam ser retirados manualmente na hora de esvaziar a sujeira e adicionar mais água.
Na parte inferior do aparelho estão as rodas de borracha e as escovas. A escova principal foi projetada para evitar que fios de cabelo e pelos fiquem enrolados com facilidade, embora em alguns casos ainda seja necessário que o usuário remova fios presos manualmente.
Funções de limpeza
Assim como a maioria dos robôs aspiradores da atualidade, o Xiaomi S40 tem função tripla: ele aspira, varre e passa pano, podendo fazer tudo isso no mesmo ciclo de limpeza. Ele tem boa força de sucção para limpar desde a poeira fina até sujeiras maiores, como migalhas de pão e grãos de ração. O motor tem quatro níveis de potência, e, quanto mais forte é a aspiração, mais barulhento fica o dispositivo.
Para passar pano, ele conta com um pano de microfibra preso na base, além do reservatório de água que solta o líquido aos poucos. Por mais que seja uma funcionalidade que ajuda bastante na faxina, é importante ressaltar que ele não é capaz de esfregar o chão, só cuidar de sujeiras mais superficiais. Para manchas secas, gordura de cozinha ou qualquer coisa mais pesada, o pano de chão tradicional continua sendo a melhor opção.
Desempenho em diferentes pisos
No geral, o robô aspirador da Xiaomi se sai bem em diferentes tipos de piso, ainda que com algumas particularidades. No caso dos pisos frios, porcelanato, laminados e tacos, ele consegue puxar a sujeira que fica acumulada nas frestas do piso, e, com o pano úmido, finaliza ao tirar o pó residual. A roda emborrachada garante que ele não risque o chão durante o funcionamento.
Em tapetes finos e carpetes, ele aumenta a força de sucção automaticamente para puxar a sujeira presa nas fibras. Mas há um porém: o modelo pode se enroscar e travar as rodas em tapetes mais grossos, felpudos ou com franjas compridas, o que faz com que ele não seja exatamente adequado para lidar com a limpeza deles. Nesse caso, é bom ajustar pelo mapa no aplicativo para que o robô passe longe desses tapetes.
Mapeamento do ambiente e aplicativo para smartphones
Uma das principais características do Xiaomi S40 é o mapeamento de ambientes, que faz com que o robô entenda como é a configuração do cômodo e planeje uma rota mais eficiente para fazer a limpeza. Isso ocorre a partir do laser abrigado na torre que fica na parte superior do dispositivo.
O uso é simples: na primeira vez que você pede para ele fazer a faxina, ele já cria esse mapa (que pode ser acessado pelo aplicativo para smartphones) e passa a realizar a limpeza em linhas retas, em vez de sair batendo em objetos como se estivesse sem rumo.
Os sensores também evitam colisões fortes contra a parede e impedem que o robô caia de escadas ou degraus. Caso você more em um sobrado ou casa com mais de um andar, ele consegue armazenar mapas diferentes pelo app. A única questão é que você precisará levar o robô e a base até o outro andar manualmente para a limpeza acontecer.
O aplicativo da Xiaomi, que está disponível para Android e iOS, é por onde você controla quase tudo. Ele exibe o mapa da sua casa em tempo real, indicando por onde o robô já passou e quanto ele ainda tem de bateria. Você pode criar paredes virtuais para evitar que o robô se aproxime de lugares que podem ser arriscados para ele – dá para impedir que ele limpe perto do prato de água do seu cachorro, por exemplo.
Pelo app também é possível organizar a limpeza por cômodos: você pode programar o aparelho para aspirar a sala com mais potência, e usar menos água quando for limpar o piso de madeira no quarto. O aplicativo também avisa quando as peças — como o filtro e as escovas — estão gastas e precisam ser trocadas ou limpas.
Xiaomi S40: pontos fortes e fracos
A navegação por laser e a configuração personalizada a partir do aplicativo para smartphones fazem deste um excelente robô aspirador para quem precisa de mais do que os modelos básicos oferecem. O robô realmente consegue entender o espaço da casa e não fica perdido, e a customização pelo app é simples e eficiente. Ele vem com boa potência de sucção para a categoria e lida muito bem com a sujeira do dia a dia.
Por outro lado, ele ainda exige alguns ajustes manuais pelo usuário, já que não esvazia o reservatório de sujeira automaticamente, o que significa que você vai precisar abrir para limpar o filtro com alguma frequência, dependendo do tamanho da sua casa. Outra fraqueza é a função de passar pano, que cumpre apenas o básico e definitivamente não substitui uma limpeza mais pesada com um pano de chão. Além disso, ele pode passar sufoco em alguns tipos de tapetes.
Para quem o Xiaomi S40 é indicado
Quem quer manter a casa limpa no dia a dia sem precisar varrer ou aspirar manualmente o chão o tempo inteiro tem neste robô aspirador um grande aliado. Ele pode muito bem limpar apartamentos e casas de médio ou grande porte, e a navegação a laser permite gerenciar vários cômodos diferentes sem se perder.
Ele também é indicado para quem tem pets que soltam muito pelo na casa, já que o sistema de aspiração dá conta do recado e a escova segura bem os fios sem travar o tempo inteiro. Se o objetivo é eliminar a poeira diária e você precisa de mais do que os modelos básicos oferecem, este robô aspirador é uma excelente opção. Mas, se você precisa de algo voltado para limpeza mais pesada, não vai encontrar nele o que procura.
Aviso: este artigo contém um ou mais links gerados a partir de um programa de afiliados. O valor não muda para você e o Olhar Digital poderá receber uma comissão. Nenhuma empresa participou da escolha para os links e não existiu aprovação prévia deste conteúdo, que segue independente como sempre foi.

articles.title: Xbox por fin permite jugar tus juegos de consola en PC
articles.text:
Xbox ha anunciado una de las funciones más pedidas por los usuarios desde hace años. La compañía anunció un programa de retrocompatibilidad que permitirá jugar títulos de consola en PC. La función estará disponible tanto en ordenadores como en consolas portátiles como la ROG Ally X, siempre y cuando cumplan con los requerimientos de hardware.
De acuerdo con una publicación en su web, el programa Xbox Backward Compatibility para PC arranca con cuatro juegos originales de la consola Xbox clásica. BLiNX: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge y Fuzion Frenzy podrán comprarse en la tienda en línea para jugarse en PC. Los títulos también estarán disponibles para los suscriptores de cualquier plan de Game Pass.
Aquellos que ya cuenten con estos juegos en formato digital no tendrán que volver a pagar por ellos. Xbox confirmó que la licencia se traslada automáticamente a PC o a dispositivos portátiles, ya que los cuatro cuentan con la función Xbox Play Anywhere y partidas guardadas en la nube. Jason Ronald, jefe de próxima generación en Xbox, dijo que este lanzamiento es apenas el comienzo de un esfuerzo más grande por preservar juegos y llevarlos al PC de manera progresiva.
Vale la pena aclarar que el programa de retrocompatibilidad se trata de una preservación estrictamente digital. Si compraste estos juegos hace más de 20 años, no podrás instalarlos o ejecutarlos desde el disco en tu PC. Existen rumores de que Microsoft trabaja en un proyecto para digitalizar los juegos físicos desde la era de Xbox One, aunque gran parte de ese equipo fue víctima de los recortes de personal en los últimos años.
Los juegos de Xbox ya son compatibles en PC y no necesitas emulador
Hasta hace poco, el único modo de jugar los títulos clásicos de Xbox en PC era a través del emulador xemu. La versión más reciente es compatible con un 80% del catálogo completo, por lo que puedes convertir tus discos originales a formato XISO o bajarlos de algún rincón oscuro de la web.
Al parecer, el equipo de retrocompatibilidad de Xbox se inspiró en el trabajo de xemu y ofrece mejoras con esta iniciativa. Los cuatro juegos soportan escalado de resolución hasta 4x, soporte para VSync, modos de pantalla completa y ventana, filtrado anisotrópico y antialiasing mejorado. La compañía adelantó que seguirá sumando funciones a través de actualizaciones futuras, incluidos los logros.
Si te interesa jugarlos, lo primero que necesitas hacer es comprobar que tu ordenador cumpla con los requerimientos mínimos. El procesador más bajo que puedes usar es un Intel Core i3-8100 o un AMD Ryzen 3 1200, con al menos cuatro núcleos, además de 8 GB de RAM. En cuanto a gráficos, necesitas una NVIDIA GTX 950, AMD Radeon RX 550, Intel UHD 770 o una Intel Arc A310.
Para una mejor experiencia de juego, Xbox recomienda un procesador de seis núcleos como el Intel Core i5-10400 o el AMD Ryzen 5 3600, así como una NVIDIA GTX 1070 Ti, Radeon RX 6800, Intel Arc A770 o cualquier otra tarjeta gráfica más reciente con al menos 8 GB de VRAM y compatibilidad con DirectX 12. Eso sí, el programa de retrocompatibilidad requiere Windows 11, por lo que si todavía estás en Windows 10 tu única alternativa será emularlos con xemu.
¿Bofetón a PlayStation?
El anuncio de Xbox llega a unas semanas de que PlayStation anunciara la muerte de los juegos en disco. Aunque la compañía quiere aprovechar el momento, la realidad es que esta iniciativa llega a pocos días de un recorte masivo de empleados. Entre los despidos se encuentra Kevin LaChapelle, responsable del programa de retrocompatibilidad que llevó los juegos de Xbox y Xbox 360 a la Xbox One.
Sin alguien como LaChapelle, es difícil saber a qué ritmo se añadirán nuevos juegos al catálogo. Tampoco se sabe o si la compañía implementará alguna forma para digitalizar aquellos que compraste en formato físico con tu consola original.

articles.title: Samsung announces dive-focused Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 and Watch 9
articles.text:
Samsung has announced the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 and the Watch 9, the company’s newest pair of smartwatches. Unfortunately, if you’re a fan of the ‘Classic,’ you’re out of luck, but otherwise these flagship watches are pretty impressive.
The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is now 10ATM rated, allowing users to dive up to 100m with the watch. It also has a Diving Standard Certification, making it a perfect watch for diving, with Health Coach training helping you with your diving abilities. In the past, I’ve wanted to learn how to properly dive, as I used to be a very strong swimmer, and this would have been perfect for me.
Plus, the smartwatch has Ocean Swimming, which is great for people like me. Every year, I go to Hawaii and having to remember to take off my watch before a late-night ocean swim is a struggle. I tend to just not wear my smartwatch at night, and with the five/six hour time difference, wearing a watch is clutch.
The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 also has a MIL-STD rating, which should help with bumps and dings — something that I definitely need. Sometimes at the end of my review period of smartwatches, I’ll see scratches around the body of the device, and it’s definitely user error, but a rugged smartwatch seems made for people like me.
But the Watch Ultra 2 is more for the sporty, hikers, and some people may prefer the Watch 9 instead. This device comes in two sizes: 40mm and 44mm. While it lacks the 10ATM rating, it still has a 5ATM rating, letting you go as deep as 50m. It’s also MIL-STD graded for more protection.
The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 starts at $949.99, and the Watch 9 starts at $519.99.
