articles.title: Débutant, amateur ou expert : quel appareil photo Canon choisir selon votre niveau et votre pratique ?
articles.text:
Débutant, amateur ou expert : quel appareil photo Canon choisir selon votre niveau et votre pratique ?
Choisir un appareil photo adapté à son niveau et à ses besoins n’est pas toujours évident. Entre les nombreux modèles disponibles et les dernières innovations, il est facile de s’y perdre, surtout si vous débutez ou si votre boîtier commence à dater.
Que vous souhaitiez faire vos premiers pas en photographie, progresser techniquement, vous lancer dans la vidéo ou vous équiper pour un usage professionnel, voici un tour d’horizon des modèles Canon les plus intéressants en 2026.
Découvrir la photo et la vidéo : EOS R50
Vous voulez un premier hybride simple, performant, polyvalent et accessible côté budget ? Le Canon EOS R50 coche clairement beaucoup de cases.
Compact et léger, il se transporte partout et peut être associé à de nombreux accessoires qui renforcent encore ses capacités. Son capteur APS-C de 24,2 mégapixels est couplé à un autofocus Dual Pixel CMOS AF II, réputé pour son excellent suivi automatique. Un duo efficace qui permet d’obtenir des photos nettes et précises, même lorsqu’on débute.
Et son usage ne se limite pas aux souvenirs de vacances… il s’adresse aussi aux créateurs de contenu avec une partie vidéo très efficace.
L’appareil filme en 4K jusqu’à 30 images par seconde, avec un suréchantillonnage à partir de la 6K pour offrir un rendu plus détaillé et réaliste. Il est également possible de le connecter à un smartphone pour ajuster les réglages, cadrer ses prises de vue, déclencher la capture ou encore enregistrer à distance. Le transfert des fichiers se fait facilement via l’application Canon Camera Connect. Enfin, on peut même l’utiliser pour la diffusion en streaming ou des appels vidéo via la connexion USB.
Progresser sans exploser son budget : EOS R6 Mark II
Pour les photographes qui veulent franchir un cap sans doubler leur budget, l’EOS R6 est une pépite, la valeur sûre.
Son capteur plein format de 24,2 mégapixels et sa rafale électronique jusqu’à 40 i/s en fait un choix naturel pour les scènes rapides que ce soit pour de la photographie animalière ou sportive… rien ne lui échappe. L’autofocus utilise d’ailleurs l’IA pour verrouiller les sujets en mouvement, où qu’ils se trouvent dans le cadre.
Ajoutez à cela une stabilisation allant jusqu’à 8 stops, et vous gagnez en polyvalence pour toutes les prises de vue à main levée, notamment en basse lumière. En vidéo aussi, la stabilisation combinée (IBIS + optique + numérique) permet des séquences très fluides, sans forcément sortir un trépied.
Une polyvalence qui change tout : EOS R6 Mark III
Le R6 Mark II était déjà très complet. Le Mark III pousse encore plus loin la logique de polyvalence.
Sport, paysage, portrait… un seul appareil pour tout faire
La présence d’un capteur plein format de 32,5 mégapixels décuple ses capacités en offrant davantage de détails, une meilleure capacité de recadrage et un rendu plus précis pour l’impression grand format.
Avec une cadence pouvant atteindre 40 images par seconde en obturation électronique, l’EOS R6 Mark III conserve une philosophie orientée action. Cette réactivité est soutenue par son autofocus Dual Pixel CMOS AF II, capable d’analyser la scène en temps réel et de reconnaître les personnes, les animaux ou encore des véhicules. Qui plus est, la performance ne faiblit pas en conditions de faible luminosité. Le système de mise au point reste opérationnel jusqu’à environ –6,5 IL, un niveau qui permet de conserver un autofocus précis dans des environnements très sombres, comme des concerts ou des scènes de nuit.
Le petit plus bien pratique de cet autofocus, c’est sa gestion des visages. Il mémorise plusieurs sujets, un vrai atout pour les événements, les conférences ou toutes les situations où plusieurs personnes partagent le cadre.
Une polyvalence hors du commun pour les créateurs
Sa stabilisation mécanique sur cinq axes, associée à la stabilisation optique des objectifs compatibles, offre jusqu’à 8,5 stops de compensation. Un atout majeur pour réaliser des images nettes à main levée ou obtenir des séquences vidéo plus fluides, sans recourir systématiquement à un trépied ou à un stabilisateur.
Justement, cette polyvalence s’exprime aussi dans ses capacités vidéo. Le boîtier peut enregistrer en 7 K RAW jusqu’à 60 images par seconde en interne et propose un mode Open Gate, qui exploite toute la surface du capteur. L’utilisateur dispose ainsi d’une plus grande liberté pour recadrer leurs images ou adapter leurs contenus à différents formats en post-production, sans perte de définition.
Canon a également soigné l’ergonomie destinée aux professionnels. Les deux emplacements pour cartes mémoire (CFexpress Type B et SD UHS-II) permettent d’enregistrer simultanément les fichiers sur deux supports, de séparer les photos et les vidéos ou encore de basculer sur la seconde carte lorsque la première est pleine.
Enfin, l’EOS R6 Mark III hérite de nombreux outils issus des caméras Cinema EOS. Les fonctions zebra, false color et waveform apportent un contrôle précis de l’exposition, tandis que les profils Canon Log 2, Canon Log 3, HLG et PQ offrent une belle latitude d’étalonnage et une meilleure gestion de la plage dynamique.
La référence des professionnels : l’EOS R5
Pour les usages les plus exigeants, où la qualité d’image est une priorité absolue (photographie publicitaire, mode, studio, paysage ou impression grand format), l’EOS R5 reste la référence.
Son capteur plein format de 45 mégapixels produit des clichés d’une richesse exceptionnelle. En vidéo, il conserve également une longueur d’avance avec son enregistrement 8K RAW. À cela s’ajoutent une stabilisation mécanique du capteur pouvant atteindre 8 vitesses, le système autofocus Dual Pixel CMOS AF II assisté par l’intelligence artificielle, une construction robuste en alliage de magnésium ainsi qu’un double logement pour cartes CFexpress Type B et SD UHS-II, pensé pour répondre aux contraintes des professionnels.
Quel Canon est fait pour vous ?
Que vous découvriez la photographie avec l’EOS R50, que vous souhaitiez franchir un cap avec le R6 Mark II, profiter de la polyvalence du R6 Mark III ou investir dans la puissance du R5 pour un usage pro, Canon propose des solutions adaptées à chaque profil.

articles.title: El rechazo a la IA y el CGI se convierte en la mejor herramienta de marketing de 'La Odisea' de Nolan
articles.text:
¿Qué te ha parecido el trailer de 'Vengadores: Doomsday'? Hay algo en él que suena a "ya visto", y no es solo lo que se adivina de un argumento que parece que va a seguir punto por punto lo que ya contó 'Endgame'. También hay algo en esa estética de puro CGI, donde no hay ni un escenario, ni un efecto especial, ni siquiera un solo traje que no sea una invención digital, que no huela a pasado. Porque paradójicamente, el éxito de 'La Odisea' de Nolan ha traido consigo un estimulante digestivo para el empacho CGI: el futuro es analógico.
140 kilos de cámara. Christopher Nolan rodó 'La Odisea' con cámaras IMAX, algo que ningún largometraje no documental había hecho antes. La cámara pesa más de 140 kilos, y va encerrada en una carcasa insonorizada, porque sin ella suena, según contó el propio Matt Damon, "como una batidora pegada a la cara". Esa carcasa permitió a Nolan filmar diálogo íntimo con la máquina a pocos centímetros de los actores. El rollo revelado pesa aún más: cada copia en 70mm supera los 360 kilos y mide 2,1 millones de pies. Fabricar la cámara cuesta entre 40.000 y 50.000 dólares, y moverla requiere una carretilla elevadora.
Le gusta al hombre. El director lleva desde 2008 apostando por el formato. 'El Caballero Oscuro' fue la primera película de Hollywood en usar cámaras IMAX para escenas de acción, y 'Oppenheimer' estrenó el primer rollo IMAX de 65mm en blanco y negro. 'La Odisea' cierra el círculo al haberse rodado íntegramente con cámaras de ese tipo. Eso sí: solo 41 salas en todo el mundo pueden proyectarla en su formato IMAX 70mm de 1,43:1, lo que ha generado quejas de "elitismo" y también un evidente efecto FOMO. La exclusividad, aquí, vende tanto como la propia técnica: cuanto más difícil es ver la película como Nolan quiere que se vea (una frase que ya tiene categoría de meme), más se comenta.
El polvo que se note. La estética analógica no solo afecta al formato, al celuloide (en este caso, como se ve, carísimo de rodar), sino también al propio acabado visual de la película. Nolan quería, capas de suciedad reales en el vestuario y platós que parecieran lugares que se parecieran a los que se vivían de verdad en la época que retrata el film. Se buscó en todo momento un realismo sucio y tangible, no brillo CGI, y esa búsqueda de textura física llevó al equipo a rodar en Marruecos, Grecia, Italia, Islandia y Escocia a lo largo de 91 días, y a subir a los actores a barcos auténticos.
Del mismo modo, Nolan utilizó efectos prácticos siempre que pudo: quería que los monstruos, los dioses y las tormentas de la mitología resultaran fantasiosos pero verosímiles, y que el cansancio de la tripulación en las tormentas se notara porque era real, no que estuviera simulado delante de una pantalla verde.
El caballo de Troya. Mientras promocionaba la película, Nolan calificó la inteligencia artificial generativa de "caballo de Troya", en una entrevista. Días antes había dicho sentirse animado por la rapidez con la que el público joven rechaza la peor cara visual del fenómeno. Nolan calificó ese rechazo de "rápido y masivo" y dijo no haber visto nunca algo así ante un supuesto salto tecnológico fundamental. Como prueba cita el éxito comercial entre público joven de películas de bajo presupuesto y efectos prácticos como 'Obsession' o 'Backrooms' y de paso lo convierte en el argumento comercial de su propia película.
La estrategia. Nolan no está adoptando una postura tradicionalista o pasada de moda, más bien al contrario: sabe que una visión de 'La Odisea' rebosante de CGI y efectos que, estéticamente, quedarán anticuados dentro de unos meses, es la forma menos inteligente de adaptar un texto clásico. Lo analógico (sea en el soporte o en la estética) no solo garantiza atemporalidad sino que, en estos tiempos, equivale a cierta ambición y lujo estético: antes solo las superproducciones se podían permitir CGI. Hoy es al contrario: lo digital es el recurso económico, es la serie B la que acude a los ordenadores para solucionar cualquier problema.
Nolan ha tenido la suerte de que Disney, que ha declarado que la IA es uno de los tres pilares de su estrategia de crecimiento, haya lanzado un vídeo de 'Doomsday' que garantiza más de lo mismo con la estética de siempre. Paradójicamente, Nolan ha recurrido a los clásicos para plantear que soplan vientos de cambio... hacia lo que tan bien funcionaba hace tiempo.

articles.title: Space startup ecosystem soars to 450-plus ventures as policy reforms fuelled growth: IN-SPACe Dir
articles.text:
Space startup ecosystem soars to 450-plus ventures as policy reforms fuelled growth: IN-SPACe Dir
The number of space startups has risen from a single digit six years ago to more than 450, said PK Jain, Director, Program Management and Authorisation Directorate at INSPACe.
India's space startup ecosystem has grown from single digits to over 450 ventures in six years, with funding gathering pace as policy reforms reshape the sector, a senior official at the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) said on Wednesday.
Addressing IAFI's Space Policy Conference 2026, PK Jain, Director, Program Management and Authorisation Directorate at INSPACe, noted that the sector has witnessed a series of policy measures since the government announced space reforms, and various initiatives have brought certainty and predictability in the regulatory regime.
India's space sector reforms have helped create a thriving private ecosystem, with the number of space startups rising from a single digit six years ago to more than 450 today, Jain said.
He said the collective efforts have built the momentum and "now we are ready to take off". Highlighting the growth of the private space ecosystem, Jain said IN-SPACe has received more than 800 applications for facilitation and authorisation over the past four years.
"Collectively, more than 800 applications for facilitation and authorisation have been received in the last four years. We have issued about 113 authorisations...when it comes to technology transfer, more than 100 technologies have been transferred to the private industry," he said.
Jain said Skyroot has become India's first space startup unicorn and recently achieved a successful maiden launch of its privately developed launch vehicle, making it the first private company globally to succeed on its first launch attempt.
Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 recently became India's first privately developed rocket to successfully reach orbit, marking a historic milestone for the country's private space sector and commercial launch capabilities.
On the investment front, Jain said Indian space startups have attracted about $380-390 million in funding over the last three years. In the current year alone, they have already secured $150-160 million, aided by IN-SPACe's efforts to connect domestic startups with global investors.
He also pointed to government-backed initiatives such as the $120 million venture capital fund and the Technology Adoption Fund to support emerging companies.

articles.title: Apple colmate la faille « Masquer mon adresse e-mail » : la fonction iCloud+ exposait vos vraies adresses
articles.text:
Apple vient de colmater la faille qui exposait les vraies adresses de ses abonnés iCloud+. Treize mois après le signalement. Pendant tout ce temps, un simple message rejeté comme spam suffisait à démasquer l'utilisateur dans les logs de messagerie.
Payer 0,99 euro par mois pour masquer son adresse e-mail, c'est l'une des promesses centrales d'iCloud+. Début juillet, nous relations cette faille : la fonction « Masquer mon adresse e-mail » exposait les vraies adresses des abonnés dans les logs de messagerie, depuis le signalement initial du 13 juin 2025. Apple a déployé un correctif le 3 juillet 2026, soit treize mois plus tard, et après deux tentatives avortées en mars puis le 30 juin 2026.
Un spam suffit : comment l'alias exposait votre vraie adresse
Le mécanisme technique, gardé confidentiel depuis le signalement de juin 2025 pour éviter d'alimenter l'exploitation, a été publié une fois le correctif en place. Il est d'une simplicité déconcertante.
Quand un message est envoyé vers une adresse générée par « Masquer mon adresse e-mail », il est redirigé vers la vraie adresse de l'abonné. C'est le principe de base de la fonction. Là où ça déraille : si ce message est automatiquement rejeté comme spam par le serveur destinataire, la vraie adresse de l'abonné apparaît en clair dans les logs de messagerie générés au passage.
- Intégration profonde dans les terminaux Apple
- Simplicité d'utilisation
- Partage entre utilisateurs Apple
- Fonctionnalités limitées
- Intégration profonde dans les terminaux Apple
- Simplicité d'utilisation
- Partage entre utilisateurs Apple
- Fonctionnalités limitées
Résultat : un expéditeur qui connaissait un alias pouvait, en quelques minutes et avec peu de compétences techniques, obtenir la vraie adresse derrière cet alias. Chaque adresse devait être ciblée individuellement. Les chercheurs précisent que chez beaucoup de grands fournisseurs, le simple rejet automatique d'un e-mail légitime détecté comme spam suffisait à déclencher la fuite. L'abonné ne voyait rien dans sa boîte de réception.
Apple était informée depuis le 13 juin 2025. Deux tentatives de correctif ont échoué (mars 2026 et 30 juin 2026) avant que le 3 juillet ne marque un début de déploiement. Nuance à retenir : AppleInsider a reproduit la faille le 17 juillet sur certains serveurs de messagerie, deux semaines après le patch annoncé. Le déploiement semble avoir été progressif côté serveur. Apple n'a pas répondu aux questions sur ce point.
Une class action, une promesse payante et des alternatives
L'inaction d'Apple pendant treize mois est au cœur d'une class action déposée le 15 juillet devant le tribunal fédéral du district Nord de la Californie. Le recours collectif Alvarez v. Apple reproche à l'entreprise d'avoir commercialisé « Masquer mon adresse e-mail » comme une protection de confidentialité payante tout en sachant, depuis au moins juin 2025, qu'elle ne fonctionnait pas. La procédure vise aussi bien la version complète d'iCloud+ que les adresses relais gratuites générées via Sign in with Apple. La plainte est sèche sur ce point : à aucun moment Apple n'a désactivé la fonction, prévenu ses utilisateurs ou corrigé ses engagements publics en matière de vie privée.
La situation concerne aussi les abonnés iCloud+ en France pour une raison concrète. Les adresses créées avant le 7 juillet 2026 ont potentiellement vu leur vraie adresse fuitée dans des logs de messagerie, sans qu'il soit possible de le vérifier soi-même. La fonctionnalité reste active, le correctif est en place. Mais si votre alias a été ciblé pendant cette fenêtre, l'information a peut-être transité quelque part.
Si vous souhaitez une alternative moins dépendante des délais de patch propriétaires, des services comme SimpleLogin (intégré à Proton Mail) ou Firefox Relay proposent le même principe d'alias e-mail, en open source, avec des politiques de transparence plus explicites. La décision de changer d'outil dépend de votre niveau d'exposition et de confiance dans l'écosystème Apple.
Apple présente « Masquer mon adresse e-mail » comme un outil pour « garder votre adresse personnelle privée ». La formulation est calibrée : elle ne promet pas l'anonymat. Pour les abonnés qui ont payé en faisant confiance à l'esprit de la fonctionnalité plutôt qu'à sa lettre, la class action californienne est peut-être l'endroit où cette nuance sera testée.

articles.title: Warum dein nächstes Macbook hässlich werden könnte
articles.text:
Günstiger als der Neukauf: Warum dein nächstes Macbook hässlich werden könnte
Manchmal stimmt das Timing einfach perfekt, obwohl man es gar nicht beabsichtigt hat. Anfang Juni hatte Swappie angekündigt, fortan neben Refurbished-iPhones und -iPads auch wiederaufbereitete Macbooks zu kaufen. Nur wenige Wochen später erhöhte Apple die Preise für zahlreiche seiner Mac-Computer. Schließlich, das erklärte der noch amtierende CEO Tim Cook im Vorfeld, ist selbst eines der größten Unternehmen der Welt nicht gegen die steigenden Speicherpreise für Consumer-Geräte immun.
Das günstigste Macbook, das Macbook Neo mit iPhone-Prozessor, kostet bei Apple nun rund 800 Euro, das Macbook Air in der Grundausstattung liegt mittlerweile bei 1.399 Euro. In Zeiten, in denen ohnehin viele Produkte aufgrund globaler Krisen teurer werden, ist das sehr viel Geld. Nicht nur deswegen lohnt ein Blick auf den sogenannten Zweitmarkt, also das Geschäft mit den wiederaufbereiteten Macbook, in das Swappie gerade erst eingestiegen ist.

articles.title: Zürich-based Immitra Bio secures €2.58 million to scale its scalable in-vivo genetic medicine platform | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Immitra Bio, a Zürich-based genetic medicine platform bringing scalability and commercial viability to gene editing therapies, has announced the completion of an upsized €2.58 million (CHF 2.4 million) pre-Seed financing round.
Venture capital and private investors contributed €2.42 million (CHF 2.25 million), while an additional €161.8k (CHF 150k) was obtained through non-dilutive funding sources. The round was led by Backbone Ventures and co-led by OCCIDENT with participation from Another VC, Kickfund, Venture Kick, Zürcher Kantonalbank, FONGIT, ETH Foundation, and select private investors.
Jan Nelis, CEO and co-founder of Immitra Bio, said, “At Immitra Bio, we are advancing a fundamentally new approach to gene editing therapies and are proud to be backed by a syndicate of early-stage and life science specialist investors. This pre-seed financing enables important value inflection points for the company and lays the foundation for establishing Immitra Bio as a leader in in-vivo gene editing.
“Our goal is to make gene editing therapies scalable, commercially viable, and accessible to patients. Our platform has the potential to generate dozens of highly differentiated therapeutic assets in an accelerated fashion.”
Founded in 2024 by Nelis, Amir Taheri, and Jacob Corn, Immitra Bio is developing a platform for scalable, one-time curative in-vivo gene editing therapies based on its novel mutation-agnostic gene editing technology and digital target identification platform.
The company notes that its approach is designed to overcome key limitations of current gene editing therapies by avoiding complex ex-vivo cell manipulation, patient conditioning, stem cell transplantation and personalised therapies.
According to the company, today’s approved stem cell therapies for genetic disorders are toxic, unscalable, slow, and expensive, all rooted in ex-vivo approaches. Immitra Bio claims to be developing an in-vivo alternative, a single, off-the-shelf injection that cures patients without chemotherapy or cell transplantation.
Immitra Bio’s digital target discovery platform and novel mode of editing enables the development of off-the-shelf drug formulations designed to treat all patients within a given disease, regardless of the underlying mutation.
Paul Sunzenauer from OCCIDENT said, “Recent advances and growing market adoption of gene therapies have validated the enormous potential of curative genetic medicine. However, current approaches still face significant challenges, such as chemotherapy-related toxicities, manufacturing complexity, and limited scalability.
“Immitra Bio’s differentiated in-vivo platform is designed to address these challenges head-on. We believe that combining non-viral delivery with a mutation-independent therapeutic approach has the potential to transform the treatment of genetic diseases and make curative therapies accessible to a much larger patient population. We are impressed by the team’s bold vision and scientific excellence, and we are excited to support Immitra Bio in advancing the next generation of genetic medicines.”
This fresh capital will primarily support preclinical proof-of-concept studies for Immitra Bio’s lead candidate, IB-003, a potential one-time curative in-vivo gene editing treatment for an inherited anaemia.
In addition, the financing will support further discovery and validation work across Immitra Bio’s select pipeline, enabled by the company’s digital target discovery platform, as well as continued refinement of the platform.

articles.title: What the sudden demise of the UK’s department of science means for the future of research
articles.text:
The obituaries were being written before the body was cold. Within hours of Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirming that Whitehall’s responsibilities for science and technology would be absorbed into a new Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST), Sir Paul Nurse, president of the Royal Society, was on Radio 4 warning that “science isn’t a slave to business”. The trade association TechUK declared it “the wrong change at the wrong time”.
You might imagine that something ancient, ineffable and essential to British science had been ripped away. In fact, the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) was only born in February 2023 – a surprise late tweak to the machinery of government under Rishi Sunak’s faltering premiership.
Science has never enjoyed a settled home in Whitehall. For most of the period from 1995 to 2023, it sat precisely where Burnham has put it now: inside a business super-department. Notably, the single most important protection UK science secured in that era – a ring-fenced budget through the George Osborne austerity years – was won from inside the Business, Innovation and Science department, under then-business secretary Vince Cable.
The historian David Edgerton has long argued that Britain’s fondness for tinkering with the machinery of government is a form of displacement activity. What actually shapes the fortunes of research is money, people and demand for what they produce, not the nameplates on London’s Victoria Street.
On that test, the outlook for science is far calmer than some reactions to this latest move would suggest. Under plans published last October, the UK’s total research and development budget is locked in at £58.5 billion over the four-year spending review to 2030 – a real-terms increase.
Machinery changes move budget lines across departments; they don’t unravel them. As yet, nothing we’ve heard from the Burnham government suggests the settlement for UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) is at risk.
A US wrecking ball
If we want to be reminded what real damage to a science system looks like, we only need to glance across the Atlantic. While London rearranges the departmental furniture and dishes out new email addresses, Washington is taking a wrecking ball to the foundations of its public science system.
A 2027 budget request will halve the size of the US National Science Foundation, if passed. A draft White House rule, due to take effect in October, will hand political appointees the power to vet federal research grants against “the president’s priorities” and terminate awards mid-stream.
A predictable exodus has begun. The Nobel laureate Omar Yaghi has just left the University of California, Berkeley for Tsinghua University in China.
Set against political commissars patrolling the borders of knowledge, the UK’s science soap opera feels deeply provincial – a debate about which secretary of state sponsors oversight of a gradually swelling budget.
And the institutional layer beneath this is in better shape than doomsayers allow. UKRI’s new strategy has set a clear five-year path: priority programmes in AI, quantum and clean energy, faster funding decisions, and a welcome seriousness about experimentation with the modes and means by which we manage public investment in research.
Not everyone is happy with UKRI’s approach to prioritisation. But a funder with a published strategy, agreed budget and hard targets is a more durable asset than a three-year-old ministry. The research councils have outlasted every department that ruled over them, and UKRI will outlast this too.
Nor should the science community be spooked by closer proximity to business. When I leave my office at UCL and stroll down the Euston Road through London’s Knowledge Quarter – dubbed “the new square mile” – I pass by the Wellcome Trust, the Crick and Turing institutes, the British Library, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. Day in, day out, this dense weave of labs, firms and cultural institutions delivers what the triple helix of government, industry and academia is all about.
And we can find versions of the same story unfolding in Manchester, Sheffield, Cambridge and Glasgow. Rather than science being subordinate or “enslaved”, the UK’s world-leading universities have spent the past decade aligning themselves with agendas for regional growth and frontier technologies.
But there’s a harder truth lurking here too. Public money accounts for less than a third of UK research and development investment. The rest is financed and largely performed by the private sector.
UK science’s chronic weakness has never been the quality of publicly funded research. It is the R&D intensity of UK firms, and their ability to convert discoveries into products, services and revenue streams generated and owned in the UK.
If yoking science to industrial strategy in a single department reminds Whitehall to treat these as a single problem, some good may come of Burnham’s reorganisation.
AI policy concerns
With DSIT’s disappearance, a particular source of concern has been the future of AI policy. This at a time when the radical possibilities and risks of AI frontier models, fluctuating US export controls, and the latest “Sputnik moment” jolt from China’s Kimi K-3 demand sustained and technically fluent policy attention.
We are also seeing a sharp acceleration in the ways AI is transforming science itself – whether by cracking mathematical problems that stumped humans for the past 87 years, or collapsing decades-old models of grant writing and peer review.
Splitting AI from science just as they converge in practice would have been the least defensible element of this reorganisation. So it is reassuring that cross-government oversight of AI, including the AI Security Institute and AI public sector adoption, is moving to a new “AI taskforce” in the Cabinet Office – alongside the promotion of Kanishka Narayan to the status of AI minister attending Cabinet. Much now rests on his shoulders.
Government departments come and go. Those of us who have long advocated for research policies built on evidence rather than gut can allow ourselves a wry smile at the fuss created by this latest reorganisation – and then get back to work.
DSIT is dead, but UK science will be fine. Keep your eyes on the AI prize – and be thankful we are arguing about organograms, not survival.

articles.title: Taming existing tech: A strategic approach for insurance modernization
articles.text:
Insurance remains an incredibly data-heavy industry with deep roots. Based on product offerings and strict regulatory data retention rules, a significant number of existing systems, some decades-old, are still in operation. It's not uncommon to find COBOL-coded applications or AS/400s continuing to run mission-critical workloads.
There's a valid reason for this: the insurance sector was an early adopter of these data-heavy environments, and the technology worked well.
However, managing this data over decades created heavy technical debt. For example, liability insurance policies often require data retention periods of up to 20 or 30 years beyond a policy's lifetime. If a policyholder lives to be 100 years old, it is possible that mandates would compel operational teams to secure and correct 100 to 120-year-old data.
We once hoped cloud computing would provide a fix for this specific legacy problem, but no single technology offers a complete answer. Cloud is a significant component, but virtual machines remain a necessity as well. Because of this, IT teams must piece together environments or extract data into separate storage layers to keep operations running.
Today, insurers manage hybrid environments composed of new cloud-driven systems, old legacy applications, and a complicated middle layer where operational teams try to tie everything together. This infrastructure sprawl can make accelerating claims adjudication and other critical business functions incredibly difficult.
Risks of a “rip and replace” strategy
When confronted with this level of complication, a "rip and replace" strategy might feel like a natural response. The instinct is to build something entirely new and transition operations to the newly constructed environment. However, moving away from working infrastructure—even if it's duct-taped together—comes with substantial risk and potentially high expenses.
Massive overhaul projects can take years to complete, and IT teams often don’t have full visibility into existing systems.
- Data may have been placed into storage decades ago for compliance reasons.
- Insurance organizations often don’t have years to modernize and can incur unnecessary risk when choosing a "rip and replace" strategy.
A better strategy is an iterative approach. Developing an incremental plan to outline upgrades, modifications, or an approach to replace systems 1 by 1 creates a more controlled risk environment.
Controlling potential chaos with a unified platform
To reduce operational complexity, organizations require a robust application management platform. Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization provides a central layer to control older systems alongside new, modern applications. Traditional virtual machines and modern containerized applications can operate together in a single unified view.
With a heavy reliance on third-party data, a strategic platform that supports multiple formats, processes information faster, and accelerates routine claims adjudication is critical for future success.
Practical steps for iterative modernization
To effectively mitigate risk and resolve technical debt, insurance leaders should adopt a focused, iterative approach to modernizing their infrastructure. Consider the following:
- Commit to an open source platform: Selecting a unified application management platform built on open source principles provides the operational agility needed to navigate evolving regulatory data requirements without vendor lock-in.
- Enforce central control: Modernization often stalls when disconnected IT initiatives emerge across various business units. Success requires executives to champion and enforce a unified, central strategy across the organization.
- Target a single specific business function: Avoid the pitfalls of a massive overhaul by focusing on a single target area first. Whether it's a vertical line like personal auto insurance in specific regions or a horizontal function like claims fraud, starting with a self-contained environment enables faster validation.
By demonstrating success in 1 concentrated area, teams can build the necessary momentum and confidence to scale the migration to subsequent business functions.
Learn more to take the next steps
Modernizing insurance technology doesn't require risking the entire business on a massive, multi-year overhaul that could become obsolete before completion. By embracing a standardized, open source platform and an incremental approach to manage virtual machines and modern containers, organizations can systematically reduce technical debt and increase their competitive advantage. Start by identifying 1 distinct business function for migration to prove the value of your new architecture. Prove it out and use the lessons learned to expand.

Monique is a global insurance executive with a deep passion and fascination for how technology and data can support insurers and their customers. She has held senior positions in Europe and the USA in companies such as Zurich, Chubb, CIGNA, Mutual of Omaha, as well as Accenture and Cloudera. Ms. Hesseling has chaired the global insurance data standards body ACORD for many years, and supports starting insurtechs as a board member or advisor. Monique resides in the Philadelphia area in the USA with her husband and enjoys traveling to visit her adult children, sailing, doing long distance walks and supporting the local sport teams.

articles.title: AMD Advancing AI 2026 Keynote Live Coverage
articles.text:
Taking place in San Francisco this week is AMD’s annual enterprise and AI-focused event, Advancing AI. Once one of a few differently yearly(ish) events spread across AMD’s different product segments, the rise of AMD’s fortunes in the data center market has meant that the AI-focused event is quickly becoming AMD’s marquee event of the year due to the importance of the products that get announced here.
AMD tells us that this is their biggest event yet; and with the show filling the entirety of the Moscone Center West, AMD does not need to exaggerate there. Driving the major turnout is a few different elements, the first of which being that AMD has turned what was previously a press conference into a full blown trade show with developer sessions, product booths, and more. The event has effectively turned into AMD’s equivalent to NVIDIA’s GTC – just 60 miles down the road.
AMD Advancing AI 2026 Keynote Preview
But like GTC itself, the prime event is the keynote speech, where AMD CEO Dr. Lisa Su will be revealing a suite of data center and AI product announcements for the company. AMD, for its part, has not been shy about laying out its plans for 2026, so we have a solid idea of what to expect from the keynote.
The big news year? AMD’s first rackscale system, Helios, and all the chips that will go in it. Previously teased by AMD at last year’s event, Helios is the fusion of AMD’s MI455X GPUs, EPYC “Venice” CPUs, and Pensando DPUs, with a complete system fitting into a single rack and employing a speedy scale-up networking architecture to allow the rack to function as a single machine. The rack is AMD’s answer to NVIDIA’s NVL72 racks, and while it has technically not even been fully detailed yet, AMD has already publicly lined up customers for the system, including perennial partner Microsoft.
To that end, we are expecting much of the 2 hour keynote to focus on Helios and the components of it, with Su and her lieutenants delivering new details on the MI455X GPUs, the EPYC “Venice” CPUs, the Pensando DPUs, and the latest iteration of AMD’s ROCm software stack. Any one of those would be significant news on their own, but from AMD’s perspective they are all meant to work together and are going to be presented together as such.
Besides promoting Helios, we expect today’s keynote to also solidify when the various components of the system will go into volume production and when the first racks will ship. To date AMD has said that they will ship in the later part of 2026, but they have not said anything beyond that. Hopefully we will also get a refreshed roadmap for future AMD chips and racks beyond Helios, though AMD may opt to keep their focus on the near future here as opposed to last year’s future-centric showcase.
And, of course, we are keeping our eyes peeled for any surprise announcements from AMD.
The Advancing AI 2026 keynote kicks off at 9:30am PT/12:30pm ET/16:30 UTC. Please come join us here at ServeTheHome for our live blog coverage of the keynote.
As always, we suggest opening the keynote in its own browser, tab, or app for the best viewing experience.

articles.title: Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought
articles.text:
Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought
- Date:
- July 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Illinois Grainger College of Engineering
- Summary:
- A new study suggests the brain begins making decisions much earlier than scientists previously thought. Researchers found that even primary sensory regions are influenced by higher brain areas through rapid feedback loops, rather than simply passing information forward. This more dynamic view of brain function could help engineers design future AI systems that think more like biological brains while using far less power.
- Share:
Scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence. Their findings suggest that decision making begins much earlier in the brain than traditional theories propose, offering fresh ideas for designing future AI systems that are more capable and far more energy efficient.
Led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS). The study points to an unexpected role for early sensory brain regions in decision making, challenging the long accepted view that decisions emerge only after information moves through a strict hierarchy of brain regions.
Rethinking How the Brain Makes Decisions
The human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe. Scientists still do not fully understand how it works, which is why reverse engineering the brain was identified by the National Academy of Engineering in 2008 as one of the 14 grand challenges for engineering in the 21st century.
For decades, many artificial intelligence systems, including convolutional neural networks, have been inspired by the idea that the brain processes information in a one way sequence. According to this traditional model, sensory information travels upward through increasingly complex brain regions until it reaches the frontal cortex, where decisions are made.
Vlasov and other researchers have increasingly questioned whether that picture is complete.
Instead, they are exploring a model based on natural intelligence, which has been refined through evolution over hundreds of millions of years. In this framework, the brain does not rely only on a step by step flow of information. Decision making also depends on interconnected feedback loops that allow information to move in both directions between brain regions.
Because biological intelligence performs remarkably complex tasks while using far less energy than today's AI systems, understanding this architecture could help guide the development of future artificial intelligence.
"We want to learn from a billion years of evolution," Vlasov said. "How is that biological intelligence organized architecturally? Can we learn from the architectural side of the brain and emulate that to make AI more effective, less power hungry, and more intelligent than it currently is? In the level of decision-making, that's where current AI is lacking."
Early Brain Regions Show Decision Making Activity
To investigate how these processes work, the research team focused on the brain's earliest stages of sensing and perception.
The scientists recorded neural activity in mice as they navigated a virtual reality corridor and made perceptual decisions. They found evidence of decision related activity in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), one of the brain's earliest sensory processing areas.
Rather than simply passing information forward, S1 appeared to be influenced by higher brain regions through feedback loops. This top down regulation suggests that decision making involves continuous communication across multiple brain areas instead of a simple one direction flow of information.
"The neural code of the brain is still mostly an unknown language," Vlasov said. "But this systems-level understanding can be viewed as a potential impact on how more efficient artificial neural networks can be built -- how the next generation of AI can be thought through. Maybe with these analogies that we learn from real brains, we can improve AI further."
What the Findings Could Mean for Future AI
The researchers emphasize that the study does not provide a blueprint for building better artificial intelligence. Instead, it offers new insights into how the brain organizes decision making that could eventually inspire future AI architectures.
Next, Vlasov and his team plan to investigate the timing of these brain signals in greater detail. They also intend to develop new technologies for measuring neural activity to better understand how feedback loops emerge and coordinate different levels of brain processing.
"By looking at the fast temporal dynamics of neural activity, maybe we can understand better how these feedback loops are engaged in making decisions," Vlasov said. "Maybe that's the approach that potentially uncovers these currently unknown mechanisms -- how these feedback loops are organized dynamically and how they form and shape different levels of processing. Maybe that can be implemented in new architectures for AI."

articles.title: US Warns of Iranian Hackers Targeting Siemens, Schneider, and Rockwell ICS Devices
articles.text:
The US government has updated a recent cybersecurity advisory describing Iran-linked attacks on critical infrastructure organizations, warning that hackers have been targeting industrial control systems (ICS) made by Siemens, Schneider Electric, and Rockwell Automation.
The advisory was initially published in early April, when federal agencies said Iranian hackers had been conducting disruptive attacks targeting operational technology (OT) devices at organizations in the government services and facilities, energy, and water and wastewater sectors.
The authoring agencies said at the time that threat groups had hacked internet-exposed programmable logic controllers (PLCs), naming Allen-Bradley devices made by Rockwell Automation.
The hackers had used malicious PLC project files and manipulated the data displayed on human-machine interfaces (HMIs) and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems.
The updated advisory, published on July 22, adds Schneider Electric and Siemens to the list of vendors whose PLCs have been targeted by Iranian APT actors and notes that devices from other companies may also be targeted.
In the case of one victim in the United States, FBI investigators discovered that the attacker had used configuration software to download a malicious project file to a PLC.
“Analysis indicated the project file retained ladder logic for downstream function but added logic that overrode specific instruction sets responsible for maintaining safe operating parameters in the victim’s environment,” the updated advisory explains.
Investigators are aware of attacks against Rockwell Automation CompactLogix and Micro850, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 (BMX P34), and Siemens S7-1200 series PLCs.
The attacks targeted ports 44818, 2222, 102, 502, and 22, and the hackers connected to the vulnerable PLCs via manufacturers’ programming software and leased third-party-hosted infrastructure.
The vendor configuration software targeted by APTs includes Rockwell Automation Studio 5000 Logix Designer, Schneider Electric EcoStruxure Control Expert, and Siemens TIA Portal.
According to the updated advisory, the hackers extracted and exfiltrated PLC project files and then modified and deleted the logic in those files. The attackers included add-on instructions and manipulated data on HMI and SCADA displays.
“Additionally, the changes disabled critical shutdown and alarm logic, allowing systems to enter unsafe conditions without notifying operators of the anomalies,” the advisory notes.
The advisory now includes new guidance for detecting malicious activity, as well as updated indicators of compromise (IoCs).
Iranian hacker groups targeting ICS/OT
The Iranian government has been using hacktivist personas to carry out many of the attacks targeting ICS/OT. The group named CyberAv3ngers made many headlines in the past years for its attacks on such systems.
A group named Handala has taken the lead this year, starting with a highly disruptive attack on the US medical technology giant Stryker.
Last month, Handala claimed it could have disrupted the water supply after hacking systems owned by California Water Service (Cal Water).
The hackers’ statements suggested they had gained deep access to ICS, but the water utility said it had found no evidence of activity in its OT environment.
While cyber adversaries once focused primarily on exposed, poorly secured ICS, these latest findings demonstrate that their capabilities are steadily advancing, underscoring the need for organizations to maintain proactive, up-to-date defenses.
